description: An interactive timeline of Indian history, from the Indus Valley Civilisation to the twenty-first-century republic: drag through major events by era and open any event for details and pictures.

eras.name: Prehistory
eras.desc: Early humans spread across the subcontinent, leaving stone tools, rock art and the first farming villages

eras.name: Indus Valley Civilisation
eras.desc: Planned cities with drains, standard bricks and a still undeciphered script rise along the Indus

eras.name: Vedic Period
eras.desc: Indo-Aryan tribes settle northern India, compose the Vedas, and the varna order and Brahmanical religion take shape

eras.name: Age of the Mahajanapadas
eras.desc: Sixteen great states and new cities arise on the Ganges; the Buddha and Mahavira found new faiths as Magadha grows strong

eras.name: Maurya Empire
eras.desc: Chandragupta builds the first empire spanning most of the subcontinent, and Ashoka promotes dharma and Buddhism

eras.name: Age of the Middle Kingdoms
eras.desc: Shunga, Indo-Greek, Kushan and Satavahana kingdoms rule side by side as Silk Road trade, Mahayana Buddhism and Gandhara art flourish

eras.name: Gupta Empire
eras.desc: Northern India is reunited and Sanskrit literature, mathematics and astronomy reach a peak often called India’s classical age

eras.name: Early Medieval Kingdoms
eras.desc: Harsha, the Chalukyas, Pallavas, Palas and Cholas vie for power; temple building flourishes and Chola fleets reach Southeast Asia

eras.name: Delhi Sultanate
eras.desc: Turkic Muslim dynasties rule northern India from Delhi, Vijayanagara rises in the south, and Islamic and Indian cultures meet

eras.name: Mughal Empire
eras.desc: Babur founds the Mughal Empire, Akbar rules with tolerance, and monuments such as the Taj Mahal mark its golden age

eras.name: Rise of the Marathas
eras.desc: After Aurangzeb’s death the Mughal Empire declines as the Marathas, Sikhs and provincial governors break away and European companies compete

eras.name: Company Rule
eras.desc: From the Battle of Plassey the British East India Company conquers the subcontinent, bringing both reform and exploitation

eras.name: British Raj
eras.desc: After the great uprising of 1857 the British Crown rules India directly; railways and new schools spread and nationalism awakens

eras.name: Freedom Struggle
eras.desc: Gandhi leads nonviolent mass campaigns as Congress, the Muslim League and revolutionaries seek self-rule, ending in independence and partition

eras.name: Building the Republic
eras.desc: Under Nehru the new republic adopts a constitution, integrates the princely states and pursues planning and non-alignment

eras.name: The Indira Years
eras.desc: Indira Gandhi dominates politics through the Green Revolution, the Bangladesh war, the Emergency and regional conflicts

eras.name: The Reform Era
eras.desc: Economic liberalisation makes India one of the fastest-growing major economies as information technology, spaceflight and democracy advance

events.title: The Hand Axes of Attirampakkam
events.short: Acheulean hand axes from Attirampakkam in Tamil Nadu, about 1.5 million years old, are among the earliest traces of humans in South Asia.
events.detail: Attirampakkam lies about 60 kilometres north-west of Chennai in Tamil Nadu. In 1863 the British geologist Robert Bruce Foote found hand axes in this area, launching the study of Indian prehistory. In 2011 researchers used cosmogenic nuclide dating to show that the Acheulean tools from the site are about 1.5 million years old, far earlier than the Acheulean tradition was once thought to have reached South Asia. The carefully shaped, symmetrical hand axes and cleavers show that early members of the genus Homo left Africa and reached peninsular India very early. The site has also yielded thousands of cores and flakes that record how stone-working changed over the following million years.

events.title: Pebble Tools of the Soan Valley
events.short: Pebble choppers from the Soan valley in the Himalayan foothills represent a Lower Palaeolithic tradition of the north-western subcontinent.
events.detail: The Soanian takes its name from the Soan river in the north of what is now Pakistani Punjab and was defined in the 1930s by scholars such as Helmut de Terra and T. T. Paterson. The river terraces there have produced large numbers of choppers and scrapers made by flaking river pebbles on one side, a simpler technique than the Acheulean hand axe. The Soanian dates roughly from 500,000 to 125,000 years ago and resembles finds from the Siwalik hills of northern India. Scholars once saw it as the work of a different population from the Acheulean, but many now think the two simply reflect people adapting to different raw materials and landscapes.

images.caption: A gorge cut by the Soan River through the Himalayan foothills

images.caption: The Soan River near Chakri, whose terraces yielded many pebble tools

events.title: The Narmada Human
events.short: A skull cap found on the banks of the Narmada is the only archaic human skull yet discovered in India.
events.detail: In 1982 Arun Sonakia of the Geological Survey of India found a fossil human skull cap near the village of Hathnora on the Narmada river in Madhya Pradesh. Known as the Narmada Human, it remains the only archaic human skull yet found in India. Its age is disputed: most estimates are around 250,000 years, though some scholars argue for a younger date. It was first classified as Homo erectus, but later studies found that it combines features of erectus with those of early Homo sapiens and may belong to an archaic form of our own species. The same deposits contained Acheulean tools and fossils of elephants and hippopotamuses, showing that the Narmada valley was an important home for early humans.

images.caption: The Narmada at Narmadapuram, near Hathnora where the fossil was found
images.author: Tanishq pandey

events.title: Stone Tools Beneath the Toba Ash
events.short: At Jwalapuram in Andhra Pradesh, stone tools lie both below and above the ash of the Toba super-eruption, showing that people survived the catastrophe.
events.detail: About 74,000 years ago the Toba volcano on Sumatra produced the largest eruption of the last two million years, and its ash fell thousands of kilometres away across South Asia. At Jwalapuram in the Kurnool district of Andhra Pradesh, archaeologists found similar Middle Palaeolithic stone tools both beneath and above a thick layer of Toba ash. A study published in 2007 argued that the local population carried on living there after the eruption, so that Toba did not cause the near-extinction of humanity that some theories proposed. Whether the toolmakers were early modern humans or another kind of archaic human is still debated.

images.caption: Lake Toba in Sumatra, the caldera of the super-eruption about 74,000 years ago
images.author: NASA Landsat

images.caption: Prehistoric sites of the Krishna and Tungabhadra valleys, including Jwalapuram

events.title: Modern Humans Reach South Asia
events.short: Modern humans who left Africa reached South Asia along the coasts and inland routes, and their descendants form the oldest genetic layer of South Asians today.
events.detail: Genetic and archaeological studies suggest that anatomically modern humans reached the Indian subcontinent soon after leaving Africa, between about 65,000 and 50,000 years ago. They may have moved east along the coasts of Arabia and Iran, or followed inland routes. Geneticists call these first hunter-gatherers the Ancient Ancestral South Indians, and their ancestry is still shared by every population of South Asia, surviving most strongly among the indigenous peoples of the Andaman Islands. Over the following tens of thousands of years people developed microlithic tools, bows and beads, and South Asia became one of the most populous regions of the world.

images.caption: Map of the successive dispersals of early humans out of Africa

events.title: The Rock Shelters of Bhimbetka
events.short: Hundreds of rock shelters in the Vindhya hills of Madhya Pradesh hold paintings spanning tens of thousands of years, among the oldest art in South Asia.
events.detail: The Bhimbetka rock shelters lie at the foot of the Vindhya hills about 45 kilometres south of Bhopal, the capital of Madhya Pradesh, and were discovered by the archaeologist Vishnu Wakankar in 1957. There are more than 700 natural shelters, about 400 of them painted. The oldest paintings may be some 30,000 years old and the latest are medieval. Painted in red and white, they show bison, tigers, deer and elephants as well as people hunting, dancing, riding and fighting, vividly recording the change from foraging to farming life. Traces of habitation in some shelters go back 100,000 years. Bhimbetka became a World Heritage Site in 2003.

events.title: Mehrgarh, South Asia’s First Farming Village
events.short: Mehrgarh in Baluchistan is the earliest known settlement in South Asia where people grew barley and wheat and kept cattle, sheep and goats.
events.detail: Mehrgarh lies at the foot of the Bolan Pass in what is now Balochistan, Pakistan, and was excavated from 1974 by a team led by the French archaeologist Jean-François Jarrige. Its earliest settled layers date to about 7000 BC, when people lived in mud-brick houses, grew barley and wheat and kept sheep, goats and cattle, making it the oldest known farming village in South Asia. The site was occupied for about four thousand years and later saw pottery, copper working and cotton growing. Archaeologists also found teeth drilled with flint tools in burials about 9,000 years old, among the earliest evidence of dentistry in the world. Mehrgarh is seen as a forerunner of the Harappan civilisation.

events.title: The Domestication of the Zebu
events.short: The humped zebu was domesticated in north-western South Asia and became the most important animal in Indian farming and religious life.
events.detail: The zebu is a breed of cattle with a hump over its shoulders, drooping ears and a dewlap, well suited to heat and drought. Archaeological and genetic studies show that people in north-western South Asia domesticated it from the local Indian aurochs around 6500 BC, a process recorded in the cattle bones of Mehrgarh. Unlike the taurine cattle tamed in western Asia, the zebu soon became the mainstay of farming on the subcontinent, pulling ploughs and carts and giving milk. Powerful humped bulls are a favourite motif on Harappan seals. In later Hinduism the cow came to be regarded as sacred, and India still has one of the largest cattle populations in the world.

events.title: The Edakkal Cave Carvings
events.short: The Edakkal caves in the hills of Kerala are covered with carved figures, animals and symbols, the oldest perhaps eight thousand years old.
events.detail: The Edakkal caves sit about 1,200 metres up Ambukuthi hill in the Wayanad district of Kerala and are really a cleft formed when a huge boulder split. In 1890 Fred Fawcett, a local police officer out hunting, noticed the carvings on their walls. They show groups of people, animals, tools and many geometric signs, some of the figures wearing elaborate headdresses. Scholars think the oldest carvings may date from the Neolithic, around 6000 BC, with later peoples adding to them over the ages, including inscriptions in Brahmi and early Tamil. They are an important survival of prehistoric art in southern India.

events.title: The First Cotton
events.short: Cotton fibres from Mehrgarh show that South Asia was one of the first places in the world to grow and use cotton.
events.detail: Cotton was domesticated several times around the world, and the tree cotton of South Asia was among the first. In burials at Mehrgarh dating to about 5500 BC archaeologists found cotton threads preserved inside copper beads, the oldest known evidence of cotton in the Old World. By Harappan times cotton was grown widely in the Indus valley and woven into cloth, and Mesopotamian texts may refer to cotton goods from the east. For thousands of years afterwards Indian cotton cloth was famous for its fine, light weave; the ancient Greeks described it as wool growing on trees. Until the Industrial Revolution India was the world’s largest producer of cotton textiles.

events.title: The Early Harappan Towns
events.short: Walled towns such as Kot Diji spread across the Indus valley, laying the foundations for the great cities that followed.
events.detail: Around 3300 BC the Indus valley and its surroundings entered the Early Harappan phase. Kot Diji in the Sindh province of present-day Pakistan is a typical site of the period: people built mud-brick houses inside stone walls, made wheel-thrown pottery with black painted designs and used copper tools. At the same time settlements at Harappa, Kalibangan and Rakhigarhi were steadily growing. Trade already linked these towns over long distances, and marks scratched on pots may be early forms of the later Indus script. Around 2600 BC many of the early towns were rebuilt and the civilisation entered its mature phase.

images.caption: View from the hilltop fort at Kot Diji, below which lies the Early Harappan site

events.title: Burzahom in Kashmir
events.short: At the Neolithic village of Burzahom in the Kashmir valley, people lived in pit dwellings and sometimes buried dogs with their owners.
events.detail: Burzahom stands on a raised terrace about 16 kilometres north of Srinagar in Kashmir and was settled from about 3000 BC. Its first inhabitants dug deep round or oval pits as dwellings, probably roofed with timber, to shelter from the cold of the highland winters. They used polished stone axes and bone needles, grew wheat and barley and hunted. The site has produced a stone slab engraved with a hunting scene and graves in which dogs and the antlers of wild goats were buried alongside people. Some objects and customs resemble Neolithic cultures in north-western China and Central Asia, pointing to early contacts across the Himalayan region.

events.title: The Ploughed Field of Kalibangan
events.short: Criss-crossing furrows found at Kalibangan in Rajasthan form one of the earliest ploughed fields known anywhere in the world.
events.detail: Kalibangan lies on the dried-up Ghaggar river in northern Rajasthan. It was first recognised by an Italian scholar in 1953 and excavated by the Archaeological Survey of India in the 1960s. In its Early Harappan levels archaeologists found a well-preserved field marked by two sets of furrows at right angles and with different spacing, probably so that two crops could be grown together, a practice still used in the area today. It is one of the oldest ploughed fields known in the world. In its mature phase Kalibangan was divided into a citadel and a lower town, and rows of fire altars were found that may have served religious rites.

events.title: The Indus Civilisation at Its Height
events.short: Towns across the Indus valley adopted planned layouts, standard bricks and common weights, forming one of the world’s earliest urban civilisations.
events.detail: Around 2600 BC the early towns of the Indus valley grew rapidly and the Harappan civilisation entered its mature phase. Spread across what is now Pakistan and north-western India, it covered about a million square kilometres, more than contemporary Egypt or Mesopotamia. Cities shared grid-like streets, houses of fired brick made in a standard 1:2:4 ratio, careful drainage, public wells and a common system of weights. People made fine seals, pottery and jewellery and traded with Mesopotamia and the Persian Gulf. No grand palaces or royal tombs have been found, and how this society was organised remains a mystery.

events.title: The City of Harappa
events.short: Harappa in Punjab was one of the great cities of the Indus civilisation, which is named after it because it was the first site discovered.
events.detail: Harappa lies beside an old bed of the Ravi river in the Punjab province of present-day Pakistan and may have had more than 20,000 inhabitants at its height. In the nineteenth century British engineers building the railway from Lahore to Multan carted away huge quantities of its ancient bricks as ballast, badly damaging the site. In 1921 the Indian archaeologist Daya Ram Sahni began formal excavations and showed that it belonged to a previously unknown ancient civilisation, which is therefore also called the Harappan civilisation. The site includes walled mounds, residential quarters, workshops and cemeteries, and has yielded many seals, pots, beads and weights.

events.title: Mohenjo-daro
events.short: Mohenjo-daro in Sindh was the largest city of the Indus civilisation, with orderly streets and sophisticated drains, and is now a World Heritage Site.
events.detail: Mohenjo-daro stands on the west bank of the Indus in the Sindh province of present-day Pakistan. Built around 2500 BC, it may have housed 40,000 people at its height, making it one of the largest cities in the world at the time. It was divided into a citadel on a raised platform to the west and a lower town to the east, laid out with main streets running north–south and east–west. Most houses were two-storey buildings of fired brick, nearly all with a bathroom and toilet, and waste water ran away through covered brick drains. The city had more than 700 wells. The Indian archaeologist R. D. Banerji first identified its ruins in 1922. Its name means Mound of the Dead in Sindhi, and it became a World Heritage Site in 1980.

events.title: The Great Bath of Mohenjo-daro
events.short: The Great Bath on the citadel, sealed with fitted bricks and bitumen, may have been used for ritual bathing and is one of the earliest public water tanks in the world.
events.detail: The Great Bath lies in the citadel of Mohenjo-daro. It measures about 12 metres by 7 and is about 2.4 metres deep, with a flight of steps at its northern and southern ends. Its walls were built of precisely cut fired bricks set in gypsum plaster, backed by a layer of natural bitumen to keep the water in, and the floor slopes to one corner where a drain could empty it. Around it ran a colonnade with small rooms, and a nearby well supplied the water. Because the Indus script cannot be read, the purpose of the bath can only be guessed, but most scholars connect it with ritual purification, an idea of cleansing by water that remained central to later Indian religions.

events.title: The Undeciphered Indus Script
events.short: The Indus civilisation left more than four hundred different signs on seals and objects, and no one has yet been able to read them.
events.detail: The Indus script is found mainly on thousands of square stone seals and on pottery, copper tablets and ivory objects, and some 400 to 600 different signs have been identified. Most inscriptions are very short, averaging about five signs and never more than about two dozen, which makes decipherment extremely difficult. No bilingual text like the Rosetta Stone has been found, and scholars disagree about the language behind it: Dravidian, Indo-Aryan and other theories have been proposed, and some even doubt that it is a full writing system. At Dholavira a large signboard was found with ten big signs inlaid in gypsum.

events.title: The Port of Lothal
events.short: Lothal in Gujarat had a large brick basin, perhaps a dockyard, and was an important port for the maritime trade of the Indus civilisation.
events.detail: Lothal lies near the Gulf of Khambhat in present-day Gujarat and was discovered by the Indian archaeologist S. R. Rao in 1954. On its eastern side is a brick-lined basin about 220 metres long and 37 metres wide. Rao interpreted it as a dockyard linked by a channel to a river, where boats could berth at high tide, which would make it one of the oldest docks in the world, though some scholars think it was a water reservoir. Lothal was famous for making beads of agate and carnelian, and a seal from the Persian Gulf was found there, showing its place in the sea trade between the Indus civilisation, Oman, Bahrain and Mesopotamia.

events.title: Dholavira, the City of Reservoirs
events.short: Dholavira in the desert of Kutch built huge stone-cut reservoirs, displaying the remarkable water engineering of the Indus civilisation.
events.detail: Dholavira stands on Khadir island in the Great Rann of Kutch in Gujarat. It was discovered in 1967 and excavated on a large scale from 1990 under R. S. Bisht. Rain is scarce there, so its people cut and built more than a dozen great stone reservoirs inside and outside the walls and dammed two seasonal streams to capture their water, a remarkable feat of water management. The city was divided into a citadel, a middle town and a lower town and was built mainly of stone rather than brick, which is unusual among Indus cities. A signboard of ten large characters found near its north gate is one of the longest Indus inscriptions known. Dholavira became a World Heritage Site in 2021.

events.title: The Pashupati Seal
events.short: A seal from Mohenjo-daro shows a seated figure surrounded by animals, which some have seen as an early form of the god Shiva.
events.detail: This steatite seal, about 3.5 centimetres square, was found at Mohenjo-daro in 1928–29. At its centre sits a figure wearing a horned headdress with legs folded beneath it, surrounded by an elephant, a tiger, a rhinoceros and a water buffalo, with two deer below and a line of Indus script above. The excavator John Marshall suggested that the figure was a prototype of the Hindu god Shiva, who is called Pashupati, Lord of Animals, and Lord of Yoga, and the seal is named after this idea. The interpretation has always been disputed, and some scholars see a horned deity of another kind. The seal is now in the National Museum in New Delhi.

events.title: The Dancing Girl
events.short: The small bronze statuette of a girl from Mohenjo-daro, standing with confident poise, is one of the most famous works of Indus art.
events.detail: The Dancing Girl is a bronze figure about 10.5 centimetres tall, found at Mohenjo-daro by the archaeologist Ernest Mackay in 1926 and made by the lost-wax method. She stands naked with her right hand on her hip, her left arm covered in bangles and her head tilted slightly back, natural and self-assured. The archaeologist Mortimer Wheeler described her as a girl perfectly confident of herself and the world. Whether she was really a dancer is uncertain, but the statuette shows how skilled Indus metalworkers had become. After partition it stayed in the National Museum in New Delhi, and Pakistan has repeatedly asked for its return.

events.title: Trade with Mesopotamia
events.short: Mesopotamian cuneiform texts mention ships and goods from Meluhha, which most scholars identify with the Indus valley.
events.detail: Sargon of Akkad, around 2300 BC, boasted in an inscription that ships from Meluhha, Magan and Dilmun moored at the quay of his capital. Later cuneiform texts often mention Meluhha as a source of carnelian, lapis lazuli, gold, ivory, ebony and exotic birds. Most scholars identify Meluhha with the Indus valley. Indus-style seals, etched carnelian beads and weights have been found at Ur and other Mesopotamian cities, while Bahrain and Oman on the Persian Gulf served as staging posts. More than four thousand years ago, then, the Indus civilisation was already part of an international trade network across the sea.

events.title: The Priest-King
events.short: A bearded steatite bust wearing a robe patterned with trefoils, known as the Priest-King, has become an emblem of the Indus civilisation.
events.detail: This steatite figure was found in 1927 in a house in the lower town of Mohenjo-daro and survives to a height of about 17.5 centimetres. The man has a neatly trimmed beard with a shaven upper lip and half-closed eyes, wears a band with a round ornament on his forehead and right arm, and has a robe decorated with trefoils draped over his left shoulder; the trefoils were once filled with red pigment. The excavators named him the Priest-King, but this is only a modern guess, and there is no evidence that the Indus civilisation had priests or kings. Stone sculptures of people are very rare in Indus art, which makes this one especially precious. It is now in the National Museum of Pakistan in Karachi.

events.title: The Bead Workshops of Chanhudaro
events.short: The small town of Chanhudaro in Sindh specialised in making beads, seals and shell ornaments and was a craft centre of the Indus civilisation.
events.detail: Chanhudaro lies about 130 kilometres south of Mohenjo-daro and was excavated by the American archaeologist Ernest Mackay in 1935–36. The town had no citadel but many workshops, which yielded beads at every stage of manufacture together with stone drills and kilns. Its craftsmen could turn hard carnelian into slender beads more than ten centimetres long, boring them through with specially made drills, a technique of great skill; they also made copper tools, shell bangles and seals. Archaeologists even found a brick bearing what may be the paw prints of a cat chasing a bird. Chanhudaro shows that Indus towns had already developed specialised roles.

events.title: The Ochre Coloured Pottery Culture
events.short: Farming villages using ochre-coloured pottery and copper hoards appeared on the Ganges–Yamuna plain, carrying Bronze Age culture eastwards.
events.detail: The Ochre Coloured Pottery culture was spread across the plain between the Ganges and the Yamuna and in north-eastern Rajasthan, from about 2000 to 1500 BC. Its pottery was fired at low temperatures and has an ochre-red slip that rubs off on the fingers. Villagers grew rice, barley and pulses, kept cattle and sheep and used copper axes, swords, harpoons and curious anthropomorphic figures, often buried together in what are called copper hoards. Graves discovered at Sinauli in Uttar Pradesh in 2018 even contained carts decorated with copper, attracting wide attention. The culture is seen as a bridge between the Late Harappan world and later cultures of the Ganges valley.

events.title: The Decline of the Indus Cities
events.short: Weakening monsoons, shifting rivers and declining trade led to the gradual abandonment of the great Indus cities as people moved east towards the Ganges.
events.detail: From about 1900 BC great cities such as Mohenjo-daro and Harappa gradually declined. Town planning, writing, seals and standard weights disappeared, and the population dispersed into smaller villages. An older theory held that invading Aryans destroyed the civilisation, but the archaeological evidence does not support it. Most scholars now think that climate change weakened the monsoon rains, that rivers such as the Ghaggar-Hakra dried up or shifted course, and that the decline of trade with Mesopotamia removed the cities’ economic base. The civilisation did not end suddenly but turned into a number of regional Late Harappan cultures, and many people moved east to the wetter plains of the Ganges and Yamuna.

events.title: The Cemetery H Culture
events.short: In the Punjab the Cemetery H culture, known for painted burial urns, emerged as one of the main Late Harappan cultures.
events.detail: The Cemetery H culture is named after a burial ground in Area H at Harappa, excavated by the archaeologist M. S. Vats in the 1920s. Unlike the people of the mature phase, who buried their dead in the ground, these people also placed bones in large pottery urns. The urns are painted in black with peacocks, stars, cattle and fish, and some scholars read the peacocks carrying small figures as images of souls on their way to the afterlife. The culture spread across the Punjab, Haryana and the western Ganges–Yamuna plain from about 1900 to 1300 BC and marks the change from urban Indus civilisation to rural regional cultures.

events.title: The Daimabad Bronzes
events.short: A hoard of bronzes from Daimabad in Maharashtra, including a man driving an ox chariot, a rhinoceros and an elephant, marks the southernmost reach of Late Harappan culture.
events.detail: Daimabad lies on the Pravara river in the Ahmednagar district of Maharashtra and is a multi-layered site on the Deccan plateau; one of its layers belongs to the Late Harappan culture, the southernmost site of that culture yet known. In 1974 local farmers chanced upon a hoard of bronzes: a chariot drawn by two oxen with a standing driver, together with figures of a rhinoceros, an elephant and a water buffalo, weighing more than 60 kilograms in all. Lively and massive, they are extremely rare in the South Asian Bronze Age. Their date is still debated, but most scholars place them around 1600 BC.

events.title: Indo-Aryans Enter the Subcontinent
events.short: Pastoral tribes speaking Indo-Aryan languages entered the Punjab from Central Asia across the Hindu Kush, bringing horses, chariots and Vedic religion.
events.detail: Linguistic, archaeological and ancient DNA evidence suggests that between about 2000 and 1500 BC groups speaking Indo-Aryan languages moved south from the Central Asian steppe and entered the north-west of the subcontinent in waves. They were herders who bred horses and drove light chariots, worshipped gods such as Indra and Agni, and spoke an ancestor of Sanskrit, a member of the Indo-European family together with Iranian, Greek and Latin. The process was probably a migration and mingling lasting centuries rather than a single conquest. They intermarried with local peoples, including descendants of the Harappans, and together they became the main ancestors of the people of northern India today.

events.title: The Rigveda
events.short: The Rigveda, a collection of over a thousand hymns to the gods, is India’s oldest text and one of the oldest religious scriptures in the world.
events.detail: The Rigveda was compiled roughly between 1500 and 1200 BC. Its ten books contain 1,028 hymns in archaic Vedic Sanskrit, praising above all Indra the thunder god, Agni the god of fire and Soma, the god of a sacred drink, and were chanted at sacrifices. They reflect the life, wars and beliefs of pastoral tribes in the land of seven rivers, roughly today’s Punjab. The Purusha hymn of the tenth book first mentions four social orders, while the Creation hymn asks philosophical questions about the origin of the universe. For more than two thousand years the Rigveda was passed on orally from teacher to pupil with astonishing precision. Rigveda manuscripts were added to UNESCO’s Memory of the World Register in 2007.

events.title: The Battle of the Ten Kings
events.short: The Rigveda tells how King Sudas of the Bharata tribe defeated a confederacy of ten tribes on the banks of the Ravi.
events.detail: The Battle of the Ten Kings is a tribal war described in the seventh book of the Rigveda. King Sudas of the Bharata tribe, supported by the priest Vasishtha, faced an alliance of ten tribes, backed by the rival priest Vishvamitra, on the banks of the Parushni, today’s Ravi. According to the hymns, the allies tried to divert the river to drown Sudas’s army but were swept away themselves. The victory made the Bharatas one of the most powerful tribes of the Vedic age; they later merged with the Purus to form the Kurus. Bharat, the Hindi name of India, comes from the name of this tribe.

events.title: The Vedic Fire Sacrifice
events.short: Vedic religion centred on the fire sacrifice, in which priests offered gifts into the flames and chanted hymns to win the favour of the gods.
events.detail: In Vedic religion the sacrifice was the main way for people to communicate with the gods. Priests lit a sacred fire on an altar built to precise rules and poured offerings of clarified butter, grain, soma juice and animals into the flames, so that Agni, the fire god, would carry them to the other gods in return for rain, cattle, sons and victory. Over time the rituals grew ever more elaborate; great sacrifices needed several priests reciting different Vedas and could last days or even a year, and the horse sacrifice and royal consecration performed by kings became symbols of royal power. The Brahmins’ monopoly on ritual knowledge raised their status. Fire rites remain at the heart of Hindu weddings and other ceremonies today.

events.title: The Coming of Iron
events.short: Iron tools appeared across northern and southern India, and iron axes and ploughshares helped people clear the dense forests of the Ganges valley.
events.detail: When iron-working began in India is still being studied; iron objects from some sites in Uttar Pradesh may date from 1800 to 1200 BC. Vedic texts at first speak only of ayas, copper or metal, and later of black ayas, meaning iron. After about 1200 BC iron was widely used by the Painted Grey Ware culture of the Ganges–Yamuna plain and the megalithic cultures of the south. Iron axes allowed people to clear the monsoon forests of the middle and lower Ganges, and iron ploughshares raised rice yields, laying the material foundations for the rise of cities and states in the Ganges valley in the sixth century BC.

events.title: The Painted Grey Ware Culture
events.short: The Painted Grey Ware culture of the upper Ganges is thought to correspond to the late Vedic tribes such as the Kurus and Panchalas.
events.detail: The Painted Grey Ware culture is named after a fine grey pottery painted in black with dots, lines and swastikas and other geometric designs. It was spread across the upper Ganges–Yamuna plain and the Ghaggar valley from about 1200 to 600 BC. Its people lived in villages of timber posts and mud walls, grew rice and wheat, kept cattle and horses and used iron. Because its area and date match the Kuru and Panchala kingdoms described in the late Vedic texts, many scholars see it as the archaeological trace of Vedic society. Painted Grey Ware has been found at places linked with the Mahabharata such as Hastinapur and Ahichchhatra.

events.title: The Rise of the Kuru Kingdom
events.short: The Kuru kingdom was India’s first state-like power; it codified the Vedic hymns and rituals and later became the setting of the Mahabharata.
events.detail: The Kuru kingdom grew out of a union of tribes including the Bharatas and Purus, with its centre in Kurukshetra in present-day Haryana and around Delhi. Between about 1100 and 900 BC society under the Kuru kings changed from pastoral tribes into a settled agricultural kingdom. The American scholar Michael Witzel argues that the Kurus collected the hymns of the different tribes into the Vedic collections, devised a complex system of rituals and established the four-fold social order, all of which became central to later Indian civilisation. The Kurus were later overshadowed by the Panchalas and others, but their memory survives in the Mahabharata, whose great war takes place at Kurukshetra.

events.title: The Four Vedas and the Brahmanas
events.short: The Samaveda, Yajurveda and Atharvaveda were compiled after the Rigveda, and together the four Vedas became the foundational scriptures of Brahmanism.
events.detail: After the Rigveda the Vedic priests compiled three more collections. The Samaveda consists mainly of hymns set to melodies to be sung at sacrifices; the Yajurveda contains the prayers and formulas recited during rituals; and the Atharvaveda holds many spells for healing, warding off evil, winning love and bringing good fortune, reflecting popular belief. They were followed by the Brahmanas, which explain the meaning of rituals, the Aranyakas, studied in the forest, and the philosophical Upanishads. Together these are called shruti, that which was heard, and are regarded as sacred and eternal knowledge. The tradition of Vedic chanting survives in India today and was recognised by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage in 2003.

events.title: The Four Varnas Take Shape
events.short: Late Vedic society settled into four orders, Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas and Shudras, a hierarchy that shaped Indian society for three thousand years.
events.detail: Varna originally meant colour or class. The Purusha hymn of the Rigveda says that the Brahmin came from the mouth of the cosmic man, the Kshatriya from his arms, the Vaishya from his thighs and the Shudra from his feet. By the late Vedic period these four orders had become fixed: Brahmins performed rituals and taught, Kshatriyas ruled and fought, Vaishyas farmed and traded, and Shudras served the other three. Later still a group of so-called untouchables was placed outside the four orders altogether. In practice the thousands of hereditary occupational groups called jati mattered even more. The caste system had a profound influence on Indian history, and the constitution of independent India outlawed caste discrimination.

events.title: The Gurukula
events.short: In Vedic times pupils lived in their teacher’s household and learned the scriptures by recitation and dialogue, an ancient tradition of Indian education.
events.detail: Gurukula means the family of the guru. In Vedic times boys from Brahmin, Kshatriya and Vaishya families, after the initiation ceremony at which they received the sacred thread, left their parents to live in their teacher’s house, often for more than a decade. Pupils herded the teacher’s cattle, gathered firewood and begged for food, while memorising the Vedas by constant repetition and learning grammar, metre, astronomy and ritual, and discussing philosophy through question and answer; the Upanishads record many such dialogues. This system allowed a vast body of texts to be handed down accurately without writing, and later centres of learning such as Taxila and Nalanda kept its emphasis on the bond between teacher and pupil.

events.title: Videha and the Philosopher King Janaka
events.short: The kingdom of Videha east of the Ganges, famed for King Janaka and the sage Yajnavalkya, was a centre of late Vedic thought.
events.detail: Videha lay in what is now northern Bihar and south-eastern Nepal, east of the Gandak river. According to a Brahmana text, King Videgha Mathava carried the sacred fire eastwards to this land, a story that marks the spread of Vedic culture into the middle Ganges. Videha’s King Janaka was famous for his love of philosophy and often gathered Brahmins at court to debate. The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad tells how the sage Yajnavalkya defeated the other learned men at Janaka’s court and expounded his teaching on the self. In the epic Ramayana, Janaka is the father of Sita, the wife of Rama.

events.title: Geometry in the Shulba Sutras
events.short: To build altars of exact shapes, Brahmins wrote the Shulba Sutras, which already contain the Pythagorean theorem and ways to find square roots.
events.detail: Shulba means cord, and the Shulba Sutras are a group of Vedic auxiliary texts explaining how to measure and build fire altars with cords and pegs. The oldest, by Baudhayana, was composed around 800 to 600 BC, followed by works attributed to Apastamba, Katyayana and others. To make altars of different shapes with equal areas, their authors studied how to convert squares, rectangles and circles into one another. They state clearly that the square on the diagonal of a rectangle equals the sum of the squares on its two sides, list several Pythagorean triples and give an approximation of the square root of two correct to five decimal places. They are the earliest systematic record of Indian mathematics.

events.title: The Upanishads
events.short: The Upanishads taught that the self is one with Brahman, the ultimate reality, and developed the ideas of rebirth and karma that underlie Indian philosophy.
events.detail: Upanishad originally meant sitting down near, referring to teachings passed secretly from teacher to pupil. The oldest, the Brihadaranyaka and Chandogya Upanishads, were composed around 800 to 500 BC, and hundreds more followed, of which a dozen or so are considered principal. Unlike the ritual-centred Brahmanas, the Upanishads turned to philosophical reflection on the universe and human life, teaching that Brahman, the ultimate reality, is in essence the same as atman, the inner self, as in the saying tat tvam asi, you are that. They also set out the ideas of rebirth, karma and liberation. These ideas deeply shaped later Hinduism, Buddhism and Jainism, and when they reached Europe in the nineteenth century they won the admiration of philosophers such as Schopenhauer.

events.title: Megalithic Burials of the South
events.short: Iron Age people in southern India buried their dead in stone circles and huge pottery urns; Adichanallur in Tamil Nadu is a famous urn cemetery.
events.detail: In the first millennium BC megalithic culture flourished across the Deccan and southern India: people built stone circles and dolmens, or placed the dead and their grave goods in huge pottery urns buried in the ground. Adichanallur on the Thamirabarani river in the Thoothukudi district of Tamil Nadu is the most famous urn cemetery. A German scholar dug there as early as 1876, and later excavations produced many skeletons, iron tools, gold diadems and black-and-red ware. Nearby sites such as Keeladi have yielded potsherds inscribed in early Tamil-Brahmi. These finds show that southern India already had an advanced Iron Age culture, the foundation of the later Sangam age.

events.title: The Sixteen Great States
events.short: Sixteen great states such as Magadha, Kosala and Vajji arose across the Ganges basin and beyond, some ruled by kings and others by tribal assemblies.
events.detail: Around 600 BC northern India passed from tribal society into an age of early states. Buddhist and Jain texts list sixteen great states, or mahajanapadas, including Magadha, Kosala, Kashi, Vajji, Malla, Avanti, Kuru, Panchala and Gandhara. Most were centred on cities and had standing armies, taxes and officials. Most were monarchies, but some, such as the Vajjis and Mallas, were ganas or sanghas ruled by assemblies of Kshatriya clan leaders who decided affairs together. The states fought constantly, and by the fourth century BC Magadha, on the middle Ganges with its iron ores and fertile plains, had swallowed up the others.

events.title: Punch-Marked Coins
events.short: Silver pieces stamped with symbols came into use in northern India; they are South Asia’s first coins and among the earliest in the world.
events.detail: Punch-marked coins were pieces of silver, or sometimes copper, cut to a set weight and stamped with separate punches bearing symbols such as the sun, wheels, hills, animals and trees; most are irregular rectangles or rounds. They appeared around the sixth century BC with the rise of cities and trade in the Ganges basin, about the same time as the coins of Lydia in Asia Minor, making them among the earliest coins in the world. Each of the great states first issued its own, and later the coins of Magadha and the Maurya Empire circulated across the subcontinent. The karshapana mentioned in Buddhist texts was probably a coin of this kind.

events.title: Taxila
events.short: Taxila, capital of Gandhara at a crossroads of trade routes, was famed as a seat of learning where many scholars and physicians studied.
events.detail: Taxila, Takshashila in Sanskrit, lies north-west of present-day Islamabad in Pakistan, where trade routes linking India, Central Asia and western Asia met. From the sixth century BC it was the capital of Gandhara, and it was later ruled in turn by the Achaemenid Persians, Alexander, the Mauryas, the Indo-Greeks and the Kushans. According to the Buddhist Jataka tales and later traditions, young men came from far and wide to study the Vedas, medicine, law and the art of war with its teachers, and the grammarian Panini, the Mauryan minister Kautilya and the physician Jivaka are all linked with it by tradition. Its remains include three ancient cities, the Bhir Mound, Sirkap and Sirsukh, and it became a World Heritage Site in 1980.

events.title: Bimbisara and the Rise of Magadha
events.short: King Bimbisara of Magadha expanded his realm through marriage alliances and conquest, ruled from Rajagriha and became a patron of the Buddha.
events.detail: Bimbisara was a king of the Haryanka dynasty who, by traditional reckoning, reigned from about 544 to 492 BC. His capital was Rajagriha, today’s Rajgir in Bihar, ringed by five hills that made it easy to defend. He married princesses of Kosala, Vaishali and Madra and annexed the kingdom of Anga to the east, gaining control of the trade routes and ports of the lower Ganges. He built an orderly administration, with officials to run villages and collect taxes. Both Buddhist and Jain texts claim him as a patron; he is said to have given the Bamboo Grove monastery to the Buddha, one of the first Buddhist monasteries. In old age he was overthrown and imprisoned by his son Ajatashatru.

events.title: Mahavira and Jainism
events.short: Prince Vardhamana renounced the world, became Mahavira, the Great Hero, and established Jainism, a faith centred on non-violence.
events.detail: Mahavira was born Vardhamana into a Kshatriya family near Vaishali. Tradition dates his life to 599–527 BC, though many scholars place him somewhat later. At thirty he gave up his princely life, and after twelve years of severe austerity he attained omniscience and was hailed as a jina, a conqueror, which is why his followers are called Jains. Jains regard him as the twenty-fourth and last tirthankara of the present age. He taught ahimsa, not harming any living being, together with truthfulness, not stealing, chastity and non-attachment, and held that the soul could win liberation from the bonds of karma through austerity. Jainism still has millions of followers in India and influenced Gandhi’s idea of non-violence.

events.title: Persia Conquers the Indus Valley
events.short: The Persian king Darius I conquered Gandhara and the Indus valley and made them provinces of his empire, bringing the Aramaic script and Persian administration.
events.detail: In the late sixth century BC the Achaemenid kings Cyrus the Great and Darius I expanded eastwards, and around 518 BC they conquered Gandhara and the Indus valley, organising them as the satrapies of Gandara and Hindush. Herodotus reports that the Indian province paid 360 talents of gold dust a year, making it the richest in the empire, and Indian soldiers marched with Xerxes against Greece. Persian rule lasted about two centuries and introduced the Aramaic script, from which the Kharosthi script later developed. Some scholars think that the pillars, palaces and edicts of the Maurya Empire were also influenced by Persian models.

events.title: The Buddha’s Enlightenment at Bodh Gaya
events.short: Siddhartha Gautama, a prince of the Shakya clan, attained enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree and founded Buddhism, which later spread across Asia.
events.detail: Siddhartha Gautama was born into the family of a chief of the Shakya clan at Lumbini, in what is now southern Nepal. His dates are much debated, but most modern scholars place his life in about the fifth century BC. Legend tells that at twenty-nine he encountered an old man, a sick man, a corpse and a wandering ascetic, was struck by the suffering of life, and left home. He studied meditation and austerity under several teachers without finding an answer. At Bodh Gaya in Magadha he sat in meditation beneath a pipal tree and at last realised the cause of suffering and the way to freedom from it, becoming the Buddha, the awakened one. The tree became known as the Bodhi tree, and the Mahabodhi Temple at Bodh Gaya is now Buddhism’s holiest site.

events.title: The First Sermon at Sarnath
events.short: Near Varanasi, in the deer park at Sarnath, the Buddha taught the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path to five monks, founding the Buddhist order.
events.detail: After his enlightenment the Buddha went to the deer park at Sarnath near Varanasi, capital of Kashi, and found the five companions with whom he had once practised austerities. To them he explained what he had realised, an event known as the first turning of the wheel of the dharma. He taught the Four Noble Truths: that life is suffering, that suffering has a cause in craving, that it can end, and that the way to end it is the Noble Eightfold Path. He urged a Middle Way between indulgence and self-torment. All five became his disciples, and the Three Jewels of Buddha, dharma and sangha were complete. For more than forty years the Buddha travelled and taught across the Ganges valley, accepting disciples regardless of caste. The Dhamek Stupa at Sarnath is said to mark the site of the first sermon.

events.title: Vaishali and the Vajji Republic
events.short: The Vajji league of clans such as the Licchavis governed from Vaishali through an assembly, and is seen as one of the world’s earliest republics.
events.detail: Vaishali, in what is now northern Bihar, was the capital of the Vajji league. The league was formed by eight clans, among them the Licchavis and Videhas, and had no hereditary king; instead an assembly of thousands of clan heads met to discuss and vote on affairs of state, which is why it is often called one of the first republics in the world. The Buddha taught at Vaishali many times and praised the Vajjis for meeting often, acting in harmony and respecting tradition, saying they would prosper as long as they did so; he also preached his last sermons there, and the Second Buddhist Council was held there about a century after his death. Mahavira, the Jain teacher, was born nearby. Eventually King Ajatashatru of Magadha conquered the league after a long war.

events.title: Ajatashatru Conquers the Vajjis
events.short: King Ajatashatru used catapults and bladed chariots to defeat Kosala and the Vajji league, making Magadha the dominant power of northern India.
events.detail: Ajatashatru, son of Bimbisara, seized the throne around 492 BC. He first fought his uncle’s kingdom of Kosala over the region of Kashi, and then waged a war of more than a decade against the Vajji league of Vaishali. According to Jain texts he used a catapult that hurled large stones and a chariot fitted with whirling maces, the earliest Indian record of such siege and chariot weapons. To attack the Vajjis he built a fortress called Pataligrama on the south bank of the Ganges, which later grew into Pataliputra. After his conquest of the Vajjis, Magadha became the most powerful state in the Ganges valley. Buddhist tradition says that he later repented, turned to the Buddha and sponsored the First Buddhist Council.

events.title: The First Buddhist Council at Rajagriha
events.short: After the Buddha’s death five hundred disciples met at Rajagriha, where Ananda recited his teachings and Upali the monastic rules, forming the core of the Buddhist canon.
events.detail: According to Buddhist tradition the Buddha died at the age of eighty at Kushinagara in the land of the Mallas. To keep his teaching from being lost, his senior disciple Mahakassapa gathered five hundred monks who had become arhats at the Saptaparni cave outside Rajagriha, the capital of Magadha. Ananda, the Buddha’s attendant, who had a remarkable memory, recited the discourses he had heard, which became the Sutta Pitaka; Upali, an expert in discipline, recited the rules of the order, which became the Vinaya Pitaka. Once the assembly had agreed on them, they were passed down orally by generations of monks. This First Council laid the foundation of the Buddhist scriptures, which were not written down until the first century BC in Sri Lanka.

events.title: Pataliputra Becomes the Capital
events.short: Magadha moved its capital to Pataliputra on the Ganges, which remained the foremost political centre of northern India for nearly a thousand years.
events.detail: Pataliputra lies at today’s Patna, capital of Bihar, where the Ganges meets the Son and other rivers, a site that commanded river traffic. Ajatashatru built a fortress there, and his successor Udayin moved the capital of Magadha from Rajagriha to the new city. The Nanda, Maurya and Gupta dynasties all ruled from Pataliputra. In the third century BC the Greek envoy Megasthenes described it as stretching some fifteen kilometres along the river, enclosed by a timber palisade with 570 towers and 64 gates, making it one of the largest cities in the world at the time. Archaeologists have found remains of a Mauryan pillared hall and wooden palisades at Kumhrar and other sites in Patna.

events.title: The Ramayana
events.short: The epic Ramayana, ascribed to Valmiki, tells how Prince Rama rescued his wife Sita, and became a cultural classic across South and Southeast Asia.
events.detail: The Ramayana, the journey of Rama, is traditionally ascribed to the sage Valmiki. Scholars think its core was composed around the fifth or fourth century BC and that it grew until it reached its final form around the third century AD, in seven books of some 24,000 verses. It tells how Rama, prince of Ayodhya, was exiled to the forest for fourteen years, how his wife Sita was carried off by Ravana, the demon king of Lanka, and how Rama, helped by the monkey god Hanuman and his army, crossed the sea, rescued Sita and returned to take the throne. Rama is seen as an incarnation of Vishnu and the model of the ideal king. The epic has been retold in many languages and is popular in Thailand, Cambodia and Indonesia, and it remains a major theme of Indian theatre, dance and festivals.

events.title: The Mahabharata
events.short: The Mahabharata tells of the great war between two branches of the Kuru family over the throne; at about 100,000 verses it is one of the longest epics in the world.
events.detail: The Mahabharata, the great tale of the Bharata dynasty, is traditionally ascribed to the sage Vyasa but in fact took shape over several centuries between the fourth century BC and the fourth century AD. Its main story is the feud between two branches of the Kuru family, the five Pandava brothers and the hundred sons of Dhritarashtra. Duryodhana cheats the Pandavas of their kingdom in a game of dice and humiliates their wife Draupadi; after thirteen years of exile the Pandavas return, and the two sides fight an eighteen-day battle at Kurukshetra which the Pandavas win. The epic is woven through with myths, philosophy, law and moral tales, and includes the Bhagavad Gita, one of Hinduism’s most important scriptures. As an Indian saying goes, what is found here may be found elsewhere, but what is not found here is found nowhere.

events.title: Panini’s Grammar of Sanskrit
events.short: The grammarian Panini described the whole of Sanskrit in nearly four thousand terse rules, regarded as the most remarkable linguistic work of the ancient world.
events.detail: Panini was born in the Gandhara region and lived around the fourth century BC. His Ashtadhyayi, the work in eight chapters, describes the sounds, inflections and word formation of Sanskrit in some 3,959 extremely concise rules, using a metalanguage of special symbols and a carefully ordered arrangement to compress its statements, much like a precise algorithm. It fixed the standard form of the language, known thereafter as Classical Sanskrit. Later grammarians such as Katyayana and Patanjali supplemented it and wrote commentaries. Modern linguists hold it in the highest regard; Saussure and Bloomfield drew on the Indian grammatical tradition, and some computer scientists have compared it to formal grammars.

events.title: The Second Council and the First Schism
events.short: About a century after the Buddha’s death, monks at Vaishali quarrelled over monastic rules, and Buddhism began to split into the Sthavira and Mahasanghika schools.
events.detail: Buddhist sources say that about a hundred years after the Buddha’s death some monks of Vaishali accepted gifts of money from lay followers and relaxed the rules on matters such as the time of meals and storing salt, the so-called ten points. The elder Yasa from the west held that these broke the discipline and gathered seven hundred monks at Vaishali, who ruled the ten points unlawful; this was the Second Council. Afterwards the elders who kept the strict tradition became the Sthavira school, while the larger and more liberal party became the Mahasanghika. Both later split further into eighteen or twenty schools, the period known as sectarian Buddhism, and some ideas of Mahayana Buddhism are linked with the Mahasanghikas.

events.title: The Nanda Empire
events.short: Mahapadma Nanda, a ruler of humble origins, founded the Nanda dynasty, united the Ganges basin and became famous for his vast army and wealth.
events.detail: Around 345 BC Mahapadma Nanda overthrew the Shishunaga dynasty of Magadha and founded the Nanda dynasty. Indian sources say he was born of a Shudra or barber family and call him the destroyer of all Kshatriyas. He annexed Kuru, Panchala, Kashi, Kalinga and other states, stretching Magadha from the Punjab to Bengal and creating India’s first great empire. The Nandas built an effective tax system and amassed enormous wealth. Greek historians record that when Alexander reached the Beas river his soldiers heard that the Nanda king had 200,000 infantry, 20,000 cavalry, 2,000 chariots and 3,000 war elephants, and refused to go further. Unpopular for their harsh rule, the Nandas were later overthrown by Chandragupta Maurya.

events.title: Alexander and Porus at the Hydaspes
events.short: Alexander the Great defeated King Porus of the Punjab on the Jhelum, but his troops then refused to march further east and the army turned back.
events.detail: In 327 BC Alexander of Macedon crossed the Hindu Kush into India, and the king of Taxila submitted to him. In May of the following year he met the army of Porus, king of a realm in the Punjab, at the Hydaspes, today’s Jhelum; Porus had about two hundred war elephants. On a stormy night Alexander crossed the river upstream and attacked the Indian army in the flank, winning after hard fighting. Greek historians say that the badly wounded Porus, asked how he wished to be treated, replied, like a king; Alexander admired his spirit and let him keep his kingdom. But when the army reached the Beas, the exhausted soldiers refused to go any further east, and Alexander had to turn south down the Indus and head home.

events.title: Chandragupta Founds the Maurya Empire
events.short: Guided by his adviser Kautilya, Chandragupta overthrew the Nandas and founded the Maurya Empire, which united most of the subcontinent.
events.detail: Chandragupta Maurya’s origins are obscure; legend says he was discovered and trained as a youth by the Brahmin adviser Kautilya, also called Chanakya. After Alexander withdrew, he drove the Macedonian garrisons out of the Punjab and around 322 BC captured Pataliputra and overthrew the Nandas, founding the Maurya dynasty. He then expanded south and west until his realm reached from Afghanistan to Bengal and from the Himalayas to the Deccan, the first empire to unite almost the whole subcontinent. He built a large central bureaucracy, a standing army and a network of spies. According to Jain tradition he abdicated in favour of his son in old age and became a Jain monk.

events.title: Peace with the Seleucid Empire
events.short: After a failed campaign, Seleucus I made peace with Chandragupta, ceding eastern Afghanistan in return for five hundred war elephants.
events.detail: After Alexander’s death his general Seleucus founded an empire stretching from Syria to Iran and tried to recover the Indus valley. Around 305 BC he crossed the Hindu Kush and fought Chandragupta, without success. In a treaty concluded around 303 BC Seleucus ceded Arachosia, around today’s Kandahar, along with Gedrosia and the Paropamisadae to the Mauryas, and the two dynasties agreed some kind of marriage alliance; Chandragupta in turn gave him five hundred war elephants, which later helped Seleucus defeat his rivals at the Battle of Ipsus. The two empires remained friendly, and Seleucus sent the envoy Megasthenes to live at Pataliputra.

events.title: Megasthenes and the Indica
events.short: Megasthenes, envoy of Seleucus, lived for years at Pataliputra and wrote the Indica, a key source of Greek knowledge about India.
events.detail: Megasthenes was a Greek historian and diplomat who came to the Mauryan court around 302 BC as the envoy of Seleucus I and lived for a long time at Pataliputra. His Indica is lost, but later writers such as Strabo and Arrian quoted it at length. It describes the walls and palaces of Pataliputra, the life of the king, the army and the administration, and divides Indian society into seven classes: philosophers, farmers, herdsmen, artisans, soldiers, overseers and councillors. He also wrote about the Ganges, India’s products and various marvels. Despite its exaggerations and misunderstandings, the Indica remains a precious source for the Maurya Empire.

events.title: Kautilya’s Arthashastra
events.short: The Arthashastra, ascribed to Kautilya, sets out the arts of government, economics, diplomacy and war in detail and has been compared to Machiavelli’s The Prince.
events.detail: The Arthashastra, the science of statecraft, is a Sanskrit manual of government traditionally ascribed to Kautilya, minister of the Mauryas; scholars think it was expanded by several hands over the following centuries and reached its final form between the second century BC and the third century AD. Its fifteen books cover the education and duties of the king, the selection of officials, taxation, mining, agriculture, law, punishment, espionage, diplomacy and war. It sets out the mandala theory, which holds that a neighbouring state is a natural enemy and the neighbour’s neighbour a natural ally, and accepts almost any means in the interest of the state. The work was lost in the Middle Ages, and a manuscript was rediscovered in southern India only in 1905.

events.title: Tamil Sangam Literature
events.short: Tamil poets of the south composed a wealth of poems on love and war, the oldest literature in India outside Sanskrit.
events.detail: Sangam literature is the body of classical Tamil poetry named after the legendary assemblies, or sangams, of poets in Madurai. Composed roughly between the third century BC and the third century AD, it survives in some 2,381 poems by more than four hundred poets, many of them women. The poems fall into two broad classes: akam, the inner poems of love, in which five landscapes, the hills, forest, fields, seashore and wasteland, stand for different moods; and puram, the outer poems of war, heroes, royal generosity and death. They vividly record the life of the three Tamil kingdoms of the Cholas, Cheras and Pandyas and their sea trade with Rome, and are the most important source for the early history of southern India.

events.title: Chandragupta Becomes a Jain Monk
events.short: Jain tradition holds that Chandragupta abdicated, followed the monk Bhadrabahu south and fasted to death at Shravanabelagola in Karnataka.
events.detail: According to Jain tradition a famine lasting twelve years struck northern India at the end of Chandragupta’s reign. He handed the throne to his son Bindusara and followed a band of monks led by the Jain teacher Bhadrabahu south to Shravanabelagola, in what is now Karnataka, where he ended his life by ritual fasting, the Jain practice of sallekhana. A hill there is called Chandragiri after him and has a temple named after him and many later inscriptions. Shravanabelagola became one of the holiest Jain sites, and in 981 a statue of Bahubali about seventeen metres high was carved on the summit of the neighbouring hill; every twelve years it is anointed in a great ceremony.

events.title: King Bindusara
events.short: Chandragupta’s son Bindusara extended the Maurya Empire into the Deccan and kept up contacts with the Greek world.
events.detail: Bindusara reigned from about 297 to 273 BC; Greek writers called him Amitrochates, from the Sanskrit amitraghata, slayer of foes. Later texts say that he continued to expand southwards and conquered the land between the two seas, pushing the empire deep into the Deccan so that only the Tamil kingdoms of the far south and Kalinga on the east coast remained outside it. He kept up friendly relations with the Seleucid king Antiochus I and is said to have asked him to send sweet wine, dried figs and a philosopher; Antiochus replied that Greek law did not allow philosophers to be sold. After his death his sons fought over the throne, and Ashoka emerged the victor.

events.title: Ashoka Takes the Throne
events.short: After years of struggle for the throne Ashoka was crowned, and under him the Maurya Empire reached its height; he is remembered as one of India’s greatest rulers.
events.detail: Ashoka, son of Bindusara, had served as governor of Taxila and Ujjain. After his father’s death he fought for about four years to secure the throne and was crowned around 268 BC. Buddhist legend says he was cruel in his early years, killed his brothers and was called Ashoka the Fierce. Under him the Maurya Empire reached its greatest extent, from Afghanistan to Bengal and south into Karnataka. After the Kalinga war he embraced Buddhism, ruled by dharma, built stupas everywhere and sent out missions that turned Buddhism from a regional faith into a world religion. Until scholars deciphered his edicts in the nineteenth century, Indians had almost forgotten him; today India’s national emblem is his lion capital, and his wheel of dharma sits at the centre of the national flag.

events.title: The Kalinga War
events.short: Ashoka conquered Kalinga on the east coast in a war that killed or captured hundreds of thousands; filled with remorse, he turned to Buddhism and dharma.
events.detail: Kalinga, on the coast of present-day Odisha, controlled the sea routes to Southeast Asia and was the only major power on the edge of the Maurya Empire that had not submitted. Around 261 BC Ashoka conquered it. By his own account in his thirteenth major rock edict, 150,000 people were carried off, 100,000 were killed and many more died of the famine and disease that followed. Seeing the horror of the war, Ashoka was filled with remorse and declared that he would no longer conquer by force but win people over by dharma. The battle may have taken place near Dhauli hill outside Bhubaneswar, where his edicts are carved and a peace pagoda now stands on the summit.

events.title: The Edicts of Ashoka
events.short: Ashoka had his proclamations of dharma carved on rocks and pillars throughout the empire, the oldest legible writings that survive in India.
events.detail: Ashoka had more than thirty edicts carved on cliffs, boulders and pillars across his empire, most in local Prakrit languages in the Brahmi script, those in the north-west in Kharosthi, and some in Afghanistan in Greek and Aramaic. Speaking as Devanampiya Piyadasi, the Beloved of the Gods, the king urged obedience to parents, respect for elders, kindness to servants and compassion for all living things, called for tolerance among religions and banned certain animal sacrifices. He appointed officers of dharma to tour the provinces and had roads, wells, shade trees and hospitals built. Only in 1837, when the British scholar James Prinsep deciphered Brahmi, could the edicts be read again, restoring Ashoka to history.

events.title: The Brahmi Script
events.short: Brahmi, the script of Ashoka’s edicts, is the ancestor of most scripts of South Asia, from Devanagari and Tamil to Tibetan and Thai.
events.detail: Brahmi is an abugida written from left to right: each consonant carries the inherent vowel a, and other vowels are shown by added marks. Some scholars trace it to Semitic alphabets, others regard it as an Indian invention. The oldest surviving examples are mostly Ashoka’s edicts of the third century BC, with inscriptions of similar age in Sri Lanka and Tamil Nadu. Over the following two thousand years Brahmi gave rise to dozens of scripts, including Devanagari, used for Sanskrit and Hindi, Bengali, Gujarati, Tamil and Telugu, as well as Tibetan, Burmese, Thai and Khmer, which together form the Brahmic family of scripts.

events.title: The Third Council and Buddhism’s Spread to Sri Lanka
events.short: Ashoka sponsored a third Buddhist council at Pataliputra and sent missions abroad; his son Mahinda carried Buddhism to Sri Lanka.
events.detail: According to Theravada tradition, around 250 BC Ashoka invited the elder Moggaliputta Tissa to hold a third council of a thousand monks at Pataliputra, which purged dissenters from the order and compiled the Kathavatthu of the Abhidhamma. Afterwards Ashoka sent missions to Kashmir, Gandhara, the Himalayas, the Deccan and Suvarnabhumi, the golden land, perhaps in Myanmar or Thailand. The most famous was led by his son Mahinda to Sri Lanka, where King Devanampiya Tissa converted; Ashoka’s daughter Sanghamitta later brought a cutting of the Bodhi tree, planted at Anuradhapura, where it still grows. Sri Lanka thus became the centre of Theravada Buddhism.

events.title: The Lion Capital of Ashoka
events.short: The superbly carved four-lion capital from the pillar at Sarnath is now the national emblem of the Republic of India.
events.detail: Ashoka raised tall stone pillars across his empire, each shaft carved from a single block of sandstone, polished to a mirror-like sheen and crowned with animal sculptures. The most famous capital, from the pillar at Sarnath, was excavated in 1905. About 2.1 metres high, it has four lions seated back to back facing the four directions; below them a drum is carved with an elephant, a bull, a horse and a lion separated by four wheels, above an inverted lotus. The lions once supported a great wheel of dharma, recalling the Buddha’s first sermon at Sarnath. On 26 January 1950 the Republic of India adopted the capital as its national emblem, and its wheel was placed at the centre of the national flag. The original is in the Sarnath Museum.

events.title: The Great Stupa at Sanchi
events.short: Ashoka built a brick stupa at Sanchi in Madhya Pradesh, later enlarged into the oldest and best-preserved group of stone stupas in India.
events.detail: Sanchi stands on a hill about 46 kilometres north-east of Bhopal in Madhya Pradesh, near the ancient trading city of Vidisha. Ashoka, whose wife is said to have come from a merchant family of Vidisha, built a hemispherical brick stupa here to enshrine relics of the Buddha and erected a stone pillar. In the second century BC the stupa was enlarged in stone to a diameter of about 36 metres and surrounded by a stone railing, and in the first century BC, under the Satavahanas, four tall gateways were added at the cardinal points, densely carved with Jataka tales and scenes from the Buddha’s life, masterpieces of early Indian Buddhist art. Forgotten in the Middle Ages, Sanchi was rediscovered in 1818 and became a World Heritage Site in 1989.

events.title: The Barabar Caves
events.short: Ashoka had caves cut into granite hills in Bihar for Ajivika ascetics; their mirror-smooth walls make them the oldest rock-cut caves in India.
events.detail: The Barabar caves are cut into the Barabar and Nagarjuni hills about 24 kilometres north of Gaya in Bihar. There are seven, four of which bear dedications by Ashoka or his grandson Dasharatha to the Ajivikas, a fatalist sect of ascetics that arose alongside Buddhism and Jainism and later died out. Hollowed out of hard granite, their interiors are polished so smoothly that sounds echo inside for a long time. The entrance of the Lomas Rishi cave is carved in imitation of a wooden arch with a frieze of elephants, the earliest example of the chaitya arch of later Indian rock-cut architecture. The Marabar Caves of E. M. Forster’s novel A Passage to India were modelled on them.

events.title: The Didarganj Yakshi
events.short: The Didarganj Yakshi, a polished statue of a woman holding a fly whisk found near Patna, is a masterpiece of Mauryan-style sculpture.
events.detail: In 1917 villagers at Didarganj near Patna found a sandstone statue of a woman about 1.6 metres tall on the bank of the Ganges. She wears a jewelled headdress, necklaces and a girdle, holds a fly whisk in her right hand and has a full figure, and her surface is polished to a high lustre, a technique typical of Mauryan stone carving. She is therefore usually dated to the Maurya period, though some scholars place her in the first or second century AD. Yakshis are female nature spirits of Indian folk belief, linked with trees and fertility, who also appear in Buddhist and Jain art. The statue is now the prize of the Bihar Museum in Patna.

events.title: The Shungas Replace the Mauryas
events.short: The Mauryan general Pushyamitra assassinated the last emperor at a military review and founded the Shunga dynasty, opening an age of rival kingdoms.
events.detail: After Ashoka’s death the Maurya Empire declined rapidly as province after province broke away. Around 185 BC Pushyamitra Shunga, a general of Brahmin birth, assassinated Brihadratha, the last Mauryan king, while reviewing the army, and founded the Shunga dynasty, still ruling from Pataliputra. The Shungas held the Ganges valley and central India and repeatedly fought off Indo-Greeks invading from the north-west, and Pushyamitra performed the Vedic horse sacrifice to proclaim his sovereignty. Buddhist texts accuse him of persecuting Buddhism, yet the railings of the stupas at Bharhut and Sanchi, built in his time, show that Buddhism still flourished. The dynasty lasted about 110 years before it was replaced by the Kanvas.

events.title: Menander, the Indo-Greek King
events.short: Menander, an Indo-Greek king who ruled the Punjab, appears in the Buddhist text Milinda Panha, which records his dialogues with the monk Nagasena.
events.detail: Early in the second century BC Greeks from Bactria in northern Afghanistan crossed the Hindu Kush into India and founded a series of Indo-Greek kingdoms. The most famous king was Menander I, who reigned from about 155 to 130 BC from Sagala, today’s Sialkot in Pakistan, over the Punjab and Gandhara and is said to have campaigned deep into the Ganges valley. He issued many coins with bilingual legends in Greek and Kharosthi. The Pali Buddhist text Milinda Panha, the Questions of Milinda, records his debates with the monk Nagasena on the soul, rebirth and nirvana, at the end of which Milinda is won over. Plutarch writes that after his death the cities quarrelled over his ashes, dividing them to enshrine in monuments.

events.title: Kharavela of Kalinga
events.short: King Kharavela of Kalinga recorded his campaigns and good works in the Hathigumpha inscription; he was a celebrated Jain ruler.
events.detail: After the Mauryas declined, Kalinga regained its independence. Kharavela was a king of its Chedi dynasty who probably lived in the second or first century BC. What we know of him comes mainly from the Hathigumpha, or Elephant Cave, inscription on Udayagiri hill near Bhubaneswar. Its seventeen lines record his deeds year by year: he repaired the gates and reservoirs of his capital, held festivals, built canals and sent armies against the Satavahanas to the west, Magadha to the north and the Pandyas to the south, reportedly recovering a Jain image that the Nandas had carried off from Kalinga. A devout Jain, Kharavela had many caves cut for Jain monks in the twin hills of Udayagiri and Khandagiri.

events.title: The Carvings of Bharhut
events.short: The stone railing of the stupa at Bharhut in Madhya Pradesh is carved with Jataka tales, each labelled with an inscription, a treasury of early Buddhist narrative art.
events.detail: Bharhut, in the Satna district of Madhya Pradesh, was discovered by the British archaeologist Alexander Cunningham in 1873. The stupa itself has been destroyed, but much of the stone railing and gateway that surrounded it survives, dating from around the second century BC under the Shungas. The railing is carved with Jataka stories of the Buddha’s previous lives, scenes from his life, and yakshas, yakshis and animals. Unlike later Buddhist art, the Buddha never appears in human form here; he is shown by symbols such as the Bodhi tree, the wheel, footprints or an empty throne. Many reliefs carry Brahmi inscriptions naming the story and the donor. Most of the carvings are now in the Indian Museum in Kolkata.

events.title: The Bhagavad Gita
events.short: Krishna’s teaching to Arjuna in the Mahabharata, urging duty without attachment to results and devotion to God, became Hinduism’s most revered scripture.
events.detail: The Bhagavad Gita, the Song of the Lord, is a passage of eighteen chapters and seven hundred verses in the sixth book of the Mahabharata, composed according to most scholars around the second century BC. On the eve of the battle of Kurukshetra the Pandava warrior Arjuna sees his kinsmen and teachers on the opposing side and refuses to fight. Krishna, his charioteer, then teaches him that the soul is neither born nor dies, that a person must do his duty without attachment to the fruits of action, and that there are paths to liberation through knowledge, action and devotion. Finally Krishna reveals his cosmic form as Vishnu. The Gita has had an immense influence on Indian thought; Gandhi called it his spiritual dictionary.

events.title: The Heliodorus Pillar
events.short: Heliodorus, an Indo-Greek envoy, set up a pillar at Vidisha calling himself a devotee of Vishnu, the earliest record of a foreigner embracing Hinduism.
events.detail: The pillar stands at Besnagar near Vidisha in Madhya Pradesh, where locals call it Khamba Baba. Alexander Cunningham noticed its inscription in 1901, and it was deciphered in 1909. Written in Brahmi, it records that this pillar, once topped by a figure of Garuda, was set up in honour of Vasudeva, god of gods, by Heliodorus, son of Dion, a Greek from Taxila, who had come as ambassador from the Indo-Greek king Antialcidas to the local king and called himself a Bhagavata, a devotee. It adds that three immortal steps, self-restraint, generosity and vigilance, lead to heaven. It is the earliest evidence of a foreigner worshipping Vishnu and an important early monument of the cult of Krishna.

events.title: The Great Chaitya of Karla
events.short: The great chaitya hall at Karla in the Western Ghats is the largest and finest of India’s early Buddhist rock-cut prayer halls.
events.detail: The Karla caves lie in the Western Ghats between Pune and Mumbai in Maharashtra, close to an ancient trade route linking the Deccan with the ports of the west coast. Their main cave is a chaitya hall cut around the first century BC to the first century AD, about 45 metres deep and 14 metres high, the largest early Buddhist cave in India. Two rows of pillars, crowned with carvings of couples riding elephants, divide it into a nave and aisles leading to a rock-cut stupa, and the vaulted ceiling still has teak ribs two thousand years old. A huge horseshoe-shaped window above the entrance lets in the light. Inscriptions show that merchants, monks and even Greek donors paid for the work.
