events.title: The Satavahanas of the Deccan
events.short: The Satavahanas ruled the Deccan for about three centuries, controlled trade through ports on both coasts and patronised Buddhist art.
events.detail: The Satavahanas were a powerful dynasty that rose in the Deccan after the Mauryas and lasted from about the first century BC to the early third century AD, with capitals at Pratishthana in Maharashtra and near Amaravati in Andhra Pradesh. Their most famous king, Gautamiputra Satakarni, defeated the Western Satraps, Shaka rulers from the north-west, early in the second century AD and restored the dynasty’s power. The Satavahanas controlled the routes linking the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal and traded busily with the Roman Empire. They were among the first Indian dynasties to issue coins bearing the king’s portrait, and they granted land to Buddhist monks and paid for the gateways at Sanchi, the stupa at Amaravati and many cave temples.

events.title: The Laws of Manu
events.short: The Manusmriti set out the duties of each class, marriage, inheritance and punishment; it is Hinduism’s most influential law book and is criticised for its treatment of women and lower castes.
events.detail: The Manusmriti is attributed to Manu, the first man, but was actually composed between the second century BC and the third century AD, in twelve chapters of some 2,700 verses. It sets out dharma in all its aspects: the creation of the world, the duties of the four varnas, the four stages of life as student, householder, forest-dweller and renouncer, marriage and family, the duties of the king, civil and criminal law, and penance and rebirth. It upholds the privileges of Brahmins, says that a woman should be protected by her father, husband and son throughout her life, and lays harsh rules on Shudras and lower castes. Under British rule it was treated as the law of Hindus, raising its status further. In 1927 B. R. Ambedkar publicly burned a copy in protest against caste oppression.

events.title: The Shakas Arrive
events.short: Driven from Central Asia by the Yuezhi, the Shakas moved south into India, replaced the Indo-Greeks in the north-west and later founded lasting satrapies in western India.
events.detail: The Shakas were nomads of Central Asia, known to Chinese chroniclers as the Sai. In the second century BC the Yuezhi, defeated by the Xiongnu, migrated west and drove the Shakas from the Ili valley, and the Shakas moved on through eastern Iran into India. In the first century BC the Shaka king Maues established his rule in Gandhara and Taxila, gradually replacing the Indo-Greeks. Later Shaka governors founded the Western Satraps in western India, centred on Ujjain, who ruled Gujarat, Rajasthan and Malwa for more than three hundred years until the Guptas destroyed them. The Shakas soon adopted Indian languages and religions, and the Shaka era used in today’s Indian national calendar is linked with them.

events.title: The Vikram Samvat Calendar
events.short: Legend says King Vikramaditya of Ujjain founded the Vikram Samvat era after defeating the Shakas; the calendar is still used in India and Nepal.
events.detail: The Vikram Samvat takes 57 BC as its first year and is one of the most widely used traditional calendars of India. Legend says that in that year King Vikramaditya of Ujjain defeated the invading Shakas and founded the era, but historians have found no contemporary evidence for such a king; the era was first called the Krita or Malava era and was linked with Vikramaditya’s name only in the ninth century. It is a lunisolar calendar whose months follow the phases of the moon, with an extra month inserted from time to time to keep in step with the solar year. Today it is Nepal’s official calendar, and many festivals of northern and western India, such as Diwali and Holi, are dated by it.

events.title: Muziris and the Roman Trade
events.short: Roman ships used the monsoon winds to cross the Arabian Sea to Muziris and other Kerala ports for pepper, gems and silk, and Roman gold poured into India.
events.detail: After Rome annexed Egypt in the late first century BC, Greek and Roman merchants mastered the route across the Arabian Sea using the monsoon winds; sailing from Red Sea ports each summer, they could reach India’s west coast in about forty days. Muziris, near today’s Kochi in Kerala, was the chief port of the Chera kingdom and famous for black pepper. The first-century Periplus of the Erythraean Sea and the Tamil Sangam poems both describe the ships of the Yavanas, Greeks and Romans, arriving laden with gold and leaving laden with pepper. The Roman writer Pliny the Elder complained of the huge sums of gold and silver flowing to India every year. Thousands of Roman gold coins have been found in southern India, and Roman pottery has been excavated at Arikamedu near Puducherry.

events.title: The Saint Thomas Christians
events.short: Tradition says that Thomas, an apostle of Jesus, came to Kerala in AD 52; the Christian community there is one of the oldest in the world.
events.detail: According to the tradition of Kerala’s Christians, the apostle Thomas, one of the twelve disciples of Jesus, landed near Muziris in AD 52, founded seven churches on the Malabar coast and was later martyred at Mylapore near present-day Chennai, where the San Thome Basilica is said to stand over his tomb. Historians cannot confirm the story, but it is certain that by the fourth to sixth centuries at the latest Kerala had a Christian community linked with the Church of the East in Persia. Known as Saint Thomas or Syrian Christians, they long used the Syriac liturgy, shared many customs with their Hindu neighbours and lived by trade and farming. Today they belong to several churches with millions of members.

events.title: Buddhism Reaches China
events.short: Legend says the Indian monks Kashyapa Matanga and Dharmaratna brought scriptures to Luoyang on white horses, and Emperor Ming of Han built the White Horse Temple for them.
events.detail: According to Chinese tradition, Emperor Ming of the Eastern Han dreamed one night of a golden man with a halo, whom his ministers identified as the Buddha, a god of the west, and he sent envoys to seek the teaching. In the land of the Yuezhi they met the Indian monks Kashyapa Matanga and Dharmaratna, who around AD 67 came to Luoyang with scriptures and images carried on white horses. The emperor had a monastery built for them west of the city, where they lived and translated texts; this was the White Horse Temple, called the first temple of China, and the Sutra of Forty-two Sections they are said to have translated is held to be the earliest Chinese Buddhist scripture. Buddhism had probably reached China along the Silk Road before then, but the story marks the start of a Buddhist exchange between the two civilisations that lasted a thousand years.

events.title: The Shaka Era
events.short: The Shaka era, beginning in AD 78, was widely used in India for nearly two thousand years and was adopted for India’s national calendar in 1957.
events.detail: The Shaka era begins in AD 78, and its origin is disputed: some link it with the accession of the Kushan king Kanishka, others with the founding of the Shaka dynasty of the Western Satraps, or with a Satavahana victory over the Shakas. It was widely used in the inscriptions of medieval India, especially in the south and in Southeast Asia, and Indian astronomers such as Varahamihira and Bhaskara used it to reckon dates. After independence the Calendar Reform Committee based the Indian national calendar on the Shaka era, and from 22 March 1957 it has been used officially alongside the Gregorian calendar; government gazettes and All India Radio give the national calendar date.

events.title: The Art of Gandhara
events.short: Blending Greco-Roman and Indian styles, sculptors in Gandhara carved some of the first images of the Buddha in human form, influencing Buddhist art in Central Asia, China and Japan.
events.detail: Gandhara, the Peshawar valley of north-western Pakistan and eastern Afghanistan, was long a meeting place of Greek, Persian, Indian and Central Asian cultures. Under the Kushan Empire its craftsmen began to carve the Buddha and bodhisattvas in grey schist and stucco. Gandharan Buddhas have high noses, deep-set eyes and wavy hair, and wear heavy robes with deep folds, showing the clear influence of Greco-Roman realism, in contrast with the native style of contemporary Mathura. The style travelled with Buddhism along the Silk Road and influenced Buddhist sculpture from Xinjiang, Dunhuang and Yungang to Korea and Japan. The Bamiyan Buddhas destroyed by the Taliban in 2001 also showed Gandharan influence.

events.title: The Buddhas of Mathura
events.short: Craftsmen at Mathura carved robust, lively figures of the Buddha and Jain teachers in red sandstone, representing the native Indian style of sculpture.
events.detail: Mathura, on the Yamuna in present-day Uttar Pradesh, was sacred to Krishna and served as the southern centre of the Kushan Empire. Between the first and third centuries AD its workshops carved many figures of the Buddha, bodhisattvas, Jain tirthankaras, Hindu gods and yakshas in the spotted red sandstone of the region. Compared with Gandharan images, Mathura Buddhas have round faces and sturdy bodies, wear thin robes that cling to the body, often leaving the right shoulder bare, and smile with joy, continuing the tradition of early Indian yaksha statues. Scholars still debate whether the Buddha was first shown in human form at Gandhara or at Mathura. A headless standing statue of the Kushan king Kanishka was also found there. The Mathura style later developed into the classical Buddha images of the Gupta age.

events.title: The Classics of Ayurveda
events.short: The Charaka Samhita and the Sushruta Samhita systematised medical and surgical knowledge and laid the foundations of Ayurveda, India’s traditional medicine.
events.detail: Ayurveda means the knowledge of life. The Charaka Samhita, the classic of internal medicine, is ascribed to Charaka and was composed between about the second century BC and the second century AD. It explains health in terms of three bodily humours, vata, pitta and kapha, and sets out methods of diagnosis, diet, herbal remedies and healthy living, stressing the ethics of the physician. The Sushruta Samhita, ascribed to Sushruta, is the classic of surgery; it describes more than a hundred surgical instruments and three hundred operations, including cataract couching, removal of bladder stones and the reconstruction of the nose with skin from the cheek, regarded as the earliest record of rhinoplasty. Both works later reached China, the Arab world and Southeast Asia, and they remain the core texts of Ayurveda today.

events.title: Kanishka of the Kushan Empire
events.short: The Kushan king Kanishka ruled a great empire from Central Asia to the Ganges, championed Buddhism and is said to have convened the Fourth Buddhist Council.
events.detail: The Kushans descended from the people Chinese chroniclers called the Yuezhi. They founded a kingdom in Bactria and crossed the Hindu Kush into India in the first century AD. Kanishka came to the throne around 127 and ruled from Purushapura, today’s Peshawar, and Mathura over an empire reaching from what is now Uzbekistan and Afghanistan to the middle Ganges. He controlled a key stretch of the Silk Road and had contacts with Rome, Parthia and Han China. His coins show Greek, Iranian and Indian gods, a sign of religious tolerance. Buddhist tradition ranks him with Ashoka and says he convened the Fourth Council in Kashmir and built a towering stupa at Peshawar, which the Chinese pilgrims Faxian and Xuanzang later visited.

events.title: Nagarjuna and Mahayana Buddhism
events.short: Mahayana Buddhism taught the path of the bodhisattva who saves all beings, and Nagarjuna of southern India developed the Madhyamaka philosophy of emptiness.
events.detail: Around the beginning of the common era a new current arose in Indian Buddhism that called itself Mahayana, the great vehicle able to carry all beings to the far shore, and labelled earlier schools focused on individual liberation the Hinayana. Mahayana Buddhists worshipped buddhas and bodhisattvas such as Amitabha and Avalokiteshvara, taught the bodhisattva path of vowing to save all beings, and produced new scriptures such as the Perfection of Wisdom and Lotus sutras. In the second century Nagarjuna of southern India wrote the Mulamadhyamakakarika and other works expounding the idea that all things are empty: everything arises from causes and conditions and has no independent, unchanging nature. His Madhyamaka school profoundly shaped later Buddhism. Mahayana then spread along the Silk Road to China, Korea and Japan and became the main form of Buddhism in East Asia.

events.title: Rudradaman’s Junagadh Inscription
events.short: Rudradaman, a Western Satrap, carved an inscription in Gujarat recording the repair of a reservoir, the earliest surviving long inscription in Sanskrit.
events.detail: Rudradaman I, who reigned from about 130 to 150, was the best known of the Shaka Western Satraps who ruled western India. His inscription is carved on a great boulder near Junagadh in Gujarat that also bears edicts of Ashoka. It records that a storm had breached the dam of the Sudarshana lake, built in the time of Chandragupta Maurya and enlarged under Ashoka, and that Rudradaman repaired it from his own treasury without levying new taxes on his subjects. It also boasts that he twice defeated the Satavahanas and was learned in grammar, music and logic. Written in elegant Sanskrit prose, it is the earliest surviving long Sanskrit inscription and shows that the foreign Shaka rulers had embraced Indian cultural traditions.

events.title: The Amaravati Stupa
events.short: The stupa at Amaravati on the Krishna river in Andhra Pradesh was famed for its fine white limestone reliefs, the peak of Buddhist art in southern India.
events.detail: The Amaravati stupa stands on the Krishna river in present-day Andhra Pradesh. First built perhaps in the time of Ashoka, it was greatly enlarged around the second century AD under the Satavahanas into the largest stupa of southern India, about fifty metres across. Its surface and railings were covered with reliefs in pale limestone showing the life of the Buddha, Jataka tales and images of the stupa itself, with slender figures in rhythmic movement and crowded, lively compositions. This Amaravati style strongly influenced Buddhist art in Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia. In the nineteenth century locals dismantled the ruins to burn the stone for lime, and many reliefs were taken to Madras and London; they are now in the Government Museum in Chennai and the British Museum.

events.title: The Tirukkural
events.short: The Tirukkural of the Tamil poet Valluvar discusses virtue, wealth and love in 1,330 couplets and is hailed as a universal scripture of the Tamils.
events.detail: The Tirukkural is a collection of aphoristic couplets in classical Tamil. Almost nothing is known of its author Valluvar, and it was composed sometime between the third and fifth centuries AD. Its 133 chapters of ten couplets each fall into three books, on virtue, wealth and love, covering personal character, family ethics, statecraft, friendship and the love between man and woman. It favours no religion or caste, and its language is terse and memorable, as in the saying that learning is the only wealth that cannot be destroyed. Tamils revere it as their greatest classic; it has been translated into dozens of languages and inspired Tolstoy and Gandhi. A statue of Valluvar about 41 metres high stands in the sea at Kanyakumari, the southern tip of Tamil Nadu.

events.title: The Panchatantra
events.short: The Panchatantra teaches worldly and political wisdom through animal fables; through Persian and Arabic versions it spread around the world as one of India’s most widely read works.
events.detail: The Panchatantra, the five treatises, is a Sanskrit collection of fables said to have been compiled by the Brahmin Vishnu Sharma to educate three dull princes, and was composed sometime between the third century BC and the third century AD. Its five books use a frame structure of stories within stories, told about lions, bulls, jackals, crows, monkeys and crocodiles, to teach lessons about friendship, worldly prudence, strategy and government. Around the sixth century it was translated into Middle Persian, and through the Arabic Kalila wa-Dimna it passed into Hebrew, Latin and the languages of Europe; its influence is said to be visible even in La Fontaine’s fables. It is regarded as one of the most translated books in the world.

events.title: The Gupta Dynasty Is Founded
events.short: Chandragupta I married a Licchavi princess, took the title King of Kings in Magadha and founded the Gupta dynasty.
events.detail: The Gupta family were originally minor chiefs in the Magadha region. Around 320 Chandragupta I came to the throne and adopted the title Maharajadhiraja, King of Kings; the year was later taken as the start of the Gupta era. He married Kumaradevi, a princess of the ancient and prestigious Licchavi clan, raising his family’s standing and enlarging its lands; later gold coins show the king and queen standing side by side. His realm covered Magadha and the middle Ganges, centred on Pataliputra. Under his son Samudragupta and grandson Chandragupta II, the Guptas united northern India and ushered in a prosperous age often called India’s golden age.

events.title: The Campaigns of Samudragupta
events.short: Samudragupta conquered the kingdoms of the north and campaigned far to the south, and his deeds were inscribed on an Ashokan pillar at Allahabad.
events.detail: Samudragupta reigned from about 335 to 375. A eulogy composed by his court poet Harishena was carved on an Ashokan pillar now at Prayagraj, formerly Allahabad. It records that he uprooted nine kings of the north and annexed their lands, then led an army down the east coast and defeated twelve southern kings, allowing them to keep their thrones on payment of tribute, while frontier tribes and chiefs and neighbours such as Sri Lanka sent missions with gifts. He performed the horse sacrifice and issued gold coins showing him on horseback, slaying a tiger and playing the veena, presenting him as warrior, musician and poet alike. The British historian Vincent Smith called him the Napoleon of India.

events.title: Chandragupta II Vikramaditya
events.short: Chandragupta II destroyed the Western Satraps and won the ports of the west coast, bringing the Gupta Empire to its height; he took the title Vikramaditya.
events.detail: Chandragupta II reigned from about 380 to 415 and took the title Vikramaditya, sun of valour. He married his daughter to the Vakataka king of the Deccan, securing a dependable ally in the south, and then destroyed the Shaka Western Satraps who had ruled Gujarat and Malwa for three centuries, extending the empire to the Arabian Sea and its ports for trade with Rome and western Asia. He made Ujjain a second capital, and his court attracted many poets and scholars; the nine gems of later legend include the poet Kalidasa. During his reign the Chinese monk Faxian came to India and described a peaceful and prosperous land.

events.title: Kalidasa and Shakuntala
events.short: Kalidasa was the greatest poet and playwright of Sanskrit; his play Shakuntala and his poem The Cloud Messenger are still loved today.
events.detail: Almost nothing reliable is known of Kalidasa’s life; most scholars place him in the Gupta period of the fourth and fifth centuries, perhaps as a poet at the court of Chandragupta II. He left three plays and four poems. The play Abhijnanashakuntalam tells how King Dushyanta falls in love with Shakuntala, a girl of a forest hermitage, forgets her under a curse and is at last reunited with her; the lyric poem Meghaduta has an exiled yaksha send a rain cloud with a message to his distant wife; the epic Raghuvamsha recounts the dynasty of Rama. William Jones translated Shakuntala into English in 1789, causing a sensation in Europe, and Goethe wrote a poem in its praise.

events.title: The Puranas and the Shaping of Hinduism
events.short: The Puranas gathered myths, genealogies and rites of worship, and devotion to Shiva, Vishnu and the Goddess replaced Vedic sacrifice, shaping Hinduism as it is known today.
events.detail: Purana means ancient tale, and the Puranas are a large class of Sanskrit religious texts; the eighteen principal ones include the Vishnu, Bhagavata, Shiva and Markandeya Puranas, most composed during the Gupta age and the centuries after. They tell of the creation and destruction of the universe, the deeds of the gods, the ten avatars of Vishnu, the genealogies of dynasties and the legends of holy places, and prescribe rites of image worship, pilgrimage and festivals. In this period worship centred on temples and images and on devotion to a chosen god gradually replaced the fire sacrifices of Vedic religion, and the Shaiva, Vaishnava and Shakta traditions became the main branches of Hinduism.

events.title: The Boar Avatar at Udayagiri
events.short: The Udayagiri caves near Vidisha hold a colossal relief of Vishnu’s boar avatar and are among the earliest surviving Hindu cave temples.
events.detail: The Udayagiri caves near Vidisha in Madhya Pradesh number about twenty, and an inscription dates one of them to 401, in the reign of Chandragupta II. The most famous is the colossal relief in Cave 5 showing Vishnu as Varaha, the boar-headed man, raising the earth goddess from the cosmic ocean as she clings to his tusk, surrounded by rows of gods and sages, an image of the king as saviour of the world. The caves also contain a Shiva linga, the goddess Durga and the river goddesses Ganga and Yamuna, showing the maturity of early Hindu iconography. Scholars see the site as important evidence of how the Guptas linked their kingship with the Hindu gods.

events.title: The Iron Pillar of Delhi
events.short: The iron pillar in Delhi’s Qutb complex, over seven metres tall, has hardly rusted in sixteen hundred years, a tribute to ancient Indian metallurgy.
events.detail: The iron pillar of Delhi is about 7.2 metres tall and weighs some six tonnes. A Sanskrit inscription on it says that it was raised in honour of Vishnu in memory of a king named Chandra, whom most scholars identify with Chandragupta II. It probably stood elsewhere originally and was brought to Delhi around the eleventh century; it now stands in the mosque courtyard beside the Qutb Minar. Remarkably, it has barely corroded after sixteen centuries in the open air. Materials scientists have found that its high phosphorus content helped form a dense protective film on the surface that stops further rusting. It is regarded as a masterpiece of ancient Indian wrought-iron technology.

events.title: Faxian’s Pilgrimage
events.short: The Chinese monk Faxian travelled from Chang’an through Central Asia to India in search of monastic rules and described Gupta India in his Record of Buddhist Kingdoms.
events.detail: Faxian was an eminent monk of the Eastern Jin dynasty. Feeling that Chinese Buddhism lacked a complete code of monastic discipline, he set out from Chang’an in 399, already in his sixties, crossing the Hexi Corridor, the Taklamakan desert and the Pamirs to reach India. He studied Sanskrit and copied scriptures at Pataliputra and elsewhere and visited the holy sites of Lumbini, Bodh Gaya and Sarnath, then sailed from the mouth of the Ganges to Sri Lanka and returned by sea via Sumatra or Java, landing in 412 on the Laoshan coast near present-day Qingdao. His Record of Buddhist Kingdoms describes central India as peaceful, with light punishments, people who neither killed animals nor drank wine, and free hospitals in the cities. It is an important source for the Gupta age and has been translated into many languages.

events.title: Nalanda
events.short: Gupta kings founded Nalanda in Bihar, which grew into a Buddhist centre of learning with thousands of teachers and students, often called one of the world’s first universities.
events.detail: Nalanda lies near Rajgir in present-day Bihar. It was founded in the fifth century by the Gupta king Kumaragupta I and enlarged and endowed by later kings, and at its height housed thousands of monks and students and a great library. It taught not only Mahayana Buddhism but also the Vedas, logic, grammar, medicine and astronomy, and admission required a demanding examination. The Chinese monks Xuanzang and Yijing both studied there for years, and Xuanzang’s teacher Shilabhadra was its abbot. Around 1200 Nalanda was destroyed by Turkic troops under Bakhtiyar Khalji and abandoned. The ruins became a World Heritage Site in 2016, and a modern Nalanda University opened nearby in 2014.

events.title: Skandagupta Repels the Huns
events.short: The Gupta king Skandagupta drove back the Huns invading from Central Asia, saving the empire for a time.
events.detail: Skandagupta reigned from about 455 to 467. Around the time of his accession a nomadic people from Central Asia, whom Indians called the Hunas and Western sources the White Huns, crossed the Hindu Kush and attacked the north-western frontier of the Gupta Empire. According to his Bhitari pillar and Junagadh inscriptions, Skandagupta defeated the invaders after fierce fighting, so that even the earth shook. He also repaired the Sudarshana lake at Junagadh, whose dam had burst once again. But years of war emptied the treasury, and his later gold coins contain markedly less gold. After his death the dynasty fell into internal strife and could no longer withstand new invasions.

events.title: The Paintings of Ajanta
events.short: Under the Vakataka dynasty the Ajanta caves of Maharashtra were covered with superb Buddhist murals, the supreme achievement of ancient Indian painting.
events.detail: The Ajanta caves near Aurangabad in Maharashtra are cut into the cliff of a horseshoe-shaped gorge above the Waghur river and number about thirty. The first group was excavated in the second and first centuries BC, and a second group around 460 to 480 under the Vakataka king Harishena. Their murals, painted with mineral pigments on plaster, show Jataka tales and the life of the Buddha; the bodhisattva Padmapani holding a lotus in Cave 1 is especially famous for its serene expression and flowing line, and the paintings vividly portray palaces, streets and landscapes. The caves were later swallowed by jungle and found by chance in 1819 by a British officer out hunting, and they became a World Heritage Site in 1983.

events.title: Aryabhata’s Astronomy
events.short: In the Aryabhatiya the mathematician Aryabhata proposed that the earth rotates, gave pi as about 3.1416 and set out a table of sines.
events.detail: Aryabhata was born in 476 and worked at Kusumapura near Pataliputra. In 499, at the age of twenty-three, he wrote the Aryabhatiya, 121 verses covering arithmetic, algebra, trigonometry and astronomy. He proposed that the daily rising and setting of the stars is caused by the earth’s rotation, just as a man in a boat sees trees on the shore moving backwards. He correctly explained solar and lunar eclipses as caused by the shadows of the earth and moon, not by the demon Rahu swallowing them; he gave pi as about 3.1416 and compiled a table of sines. His work was later translated into Arabic and influenced astronomy in the Islamic world. In 1975 India’s first satellite was named after him.

events.title: Place-Value Numerals and Zero
events.short: Indian mathematicians wrote numbers with ten digits in a place-value system and treated zero as a number, a method later spread worldwide by the Arabs.
events.detail: India had early Brahmi numerals for one to nine, and around the fifth century mathematicians began to write numbers of any size using these nine digits plus a symbol for an empty place, arranged by place value. The Jain cosmological work Lokavibhaga of 458 already uses place value, and the Bakhshali manuscript in Oxford uses a dot for zero; radiocarbon dating suggests some of its pages may go back to the third or fourth century. In 628 Brahmagupta first treated zero as a number in its own right and gave rules for calculating with it. In the ninth century the Arab mathematician al-Khwarizmi described this Indian reckoning, which reached Europe in the twelfth century and became known as Arabic numerals.

events.title: The Dashavatara Temple at Deogarh
events.short: The Dashavatara Temple at Deogarh in Uttar Pradesh is one of the earliest surviving stone Hindu temples, famous for its relief of Vishnu reclining on the cosmic serpent.
events.detail: The Dashavatara Temple stands by the Betwa river in the Lalitpur district of Uttar Pradesh and was built for Vishnu around 500 to 550, in the late Gupta period. It rises on a raised platform, and its square sanctum was once crowned by a pyramidal tower, an early form of the spire of the northern Nagara style of temple. Each of three outer walls bears a large relief panel: Vishnu asleep on the cosmic serpent Shesha, with Brahma emerging from the lotus that grows from his navel; Vishnu rescuing the king of elephants; and the sages Nara and Narayana in meditation. Gracefully composed and serene, these reliefs are regarded as masterpieces of Gupta sculpture.

events.title: The Hun Invasions
events.short: Led by Toramana and Mihirakula, the Alchon Huns swept into northern India, destroying cities and monasteries and hastening the collapse of the Gupta Empire.
events.detail: Late in the fifth century the Alchon Huns of Central Asia, led by their king Toramana, invaded the Punjab and central India and seized the western lands of the Guptas. Around 515 his son Mihirakula succeeded him, ruling Gandhara, Kashmir and the Punjab from Sagala. According to Xuanzang’s Great Tang Records on the Western Regions and other sources, Mihirakula cruelly persecuted Buddhism and destroyed many monasteries and stupas in Gandhara, whose Buddhist culture never recovered. Around 528 Yashodharman, king of Malwa, together with the Gupta king, defeated Mihirakula and drove him back to Kashmir. The Hun invasions badly damaged the cities and trade routes of northern India, and under their impact the Gupta Empire finally fell apart.

events.title: Bodhidharma Goes East
events.short: Legend says that the south Indian monk Bodhidharma sailed to China, meditated facing a wall for nine years at Shaolin and became the first patriarch of Chan Buddhism.
events.detail: Bodhidharma was a monk who came to China in the period of the Northern and Southern Dynasties. Chinese sources say he came from southern India, and some call him a prince of a south Indian kingdom. Tradition says that he arrived by sea at Guangzhou, met Emperor Wu of Liang, and when their conversation went nowhere crossed the Yangtze northwards, according to legend on a single reed. In the Northern Wei he is said to have sat facing a cave wall near the Shaolin monastery on Mount Song for nine years and passed his teaching to his disciple Huike. He stressed pointing directly to the mind and seeing one’s true nature, without relying on words and scriptures. The Chan, or Zen, school reveres him as its first patriarch in China, and Chinese and Japanese painters depict him as a foreign monk with a bushy beard and wide eyes. His link with Shaolin martial arts is a later legend.

events.title: The Gupta Empire Breaks Up
events.short: After the Guptas faded, northern India split into regional kingdoms such as the Maukharis, the Later Guptas and Valabhi, and the subcontinent entered an age of rival powers.
events.detail: By the middle of the sixth century, under the combined pressure of the Hun invasions, an exhausted treasury and the rise of regional powers, the Gupta Empire had fallen apart; the last known Gupta king ruled only a small territory around 550. Northern India split into regional kingdoms such as the Maukharis of Kannauj, the Later Guptas of Magadha, the Maitrakas of Valabhi in Gujarat and the Pushyabhutis of Thanesar, while in the south the Chalukyas and Pallavas rose to power. Grants of land to Brahmins and temples became ever more common and local lords grew stronger, and historians often see this as the turning point from ancient to medieval India.

events.title: Varahamihira’s Five Treatises
events.short: Varahamihira, an astronomer of Ujjain, summarised five astronomical systems of his day and wrote an encyclopaedia covering weather, architecture and gems.
events.detail: Varahamihira lived from about 505 to 587 and worked for many years at Ujjain; legend counts him among the nine gems of the court. Around 575 he wrote the Pancha-Siddhantika, which brought together and compared the five astronomical systems current in his day, including the Romaka and Paulisha Siddhantas influenced by Greek astronomy, preserving much knowledge that would otherwise have been lost. His Brihat Samhita ranges extremely widely, covering astronomy, weather forecasting, earthquakes, agriculture, architecture, gems, perfumes and animals as well as omens, and is regarded as an encyclopaedia of ancient India. He also wrote several works on astrology that shaped the Indian astrological tradition.

events.title: The Chalukya Caves of Badami
events.short: The Chalukyas carved Hindu and Jain cave temples into the red sandstone cliffs of their capital Badami, founding the temple-building tradition of the Deccan.
events.detail: The Chalukya dynasty rose in the western Deccan in the mid-sixth century with its capital at Badami, ancient Vatapi, in present-day Karnataka. The town lies between two hills of red sandstone beside an artificial lake. Its four cave temples were cut in the sixth and seventh centuries; an inscription in Cave 3 dates its completion to 578, making it one of the earliest securely dated Hindu cave temples. The caves contain fine reliefs of an eighteen-armed dancing Shiva, Vishnu seated on the cosmic serpent, the man-lion avatar and the dwarf avatar striding across the worlds, while Cave 4 is Jain. The Chalukyas also built more than a hundred stone temples nearby at Aihole and Pattadakal, the latter now a World Heritage Site.

events.title: Chaturanga, the Ancestor of Chess
events.short: Chaturanga, which appeared in northern India around the sixth century and pitted infantry, cavalry, elephants and chariots against each other, is the ancestor of chess.
events.detail: Chaturanga means four parts in Sanskrit, referring to the four divisions of an ancient Indian army: infantry, cavalry, elephants and chariots. The game was played on an eight-by-eight board, with each side having a king, a minister, elephants, horses, chariots and foot soldiers, and its earliest reliable mention is in Bana’s biography of King Harsha, written early in the seventh century. Around the sixth century it reached Sasanian Persia as chatrang, and the Persian epic Shahnameh tells how an Indian king sent the game to the Persian king to test his wisdom. After the Arab conquest of Persia it passed through the Islamic world to Europe and developed into modern chess. Scholars think Chinese xiangqi and Japanese shogi may share the same ancestry.

events.title: Harsha Unites Northern India
events.short: Harshavardhana of the Pushyabhuti dynasty made Kannauj his capital and reunited most of northern India.
events.detail: Harshavardhana, prince of the Pushyabhuti dynasty of Thanesar, came to the throne in 606 at the age of sixteen after his elder brother was murdered. He avenged his brother, rescued his imprisoned sister and moved his capital to Kannauj on the Ganges, and after years of campaigning ruled most of northern India from the Punjab to Bengal, though he was defeated by the Chalukya king Pulakeshin II when he tried to push south into the Deccan. Harsha was himself a poet and wrote three Sanskrit plays, and his court poet Bana wrote his biography, the Harshacharita. In later life he favoured Buddhism and every five years held a great assembly at Prayaga where he gave away the treasury to followers of all faiths. He exchanged envoys with Tang China, and his empire quickly fell apart after his death in 647.

events.title: Pulakeshin II Halts Harsha
events.short: The Chalukya king Pulakeshin II defeated Harsha on the Narmada, stopping the northern power’s advance south and making himself master of the Deccan.
events.detail: Pulakeshin II, the most famous king of the Chalukyas of Badami, reigned from about 610 to 642. He crushed a civil war on his accession and expanded in every direction until he controlled most of the Deccan. Around 618–619 Harsha marched south, and Pulakeshin defeated him on the banks of the Narmada, which thereafter became the frontier between the two great powers of north and south. An inscription at the Meguti temple in Aihole records his victories. When Xuanzang visited his kingdom he praised its brave soldiers and simple people. Pulakeshin also fought long wars with the Pallavas to the south, and in 642 the Pallava king Narasimhavarman I captured Badami; Pulakeshin probably died in the fighting.

events.title: Brahmagupta and the Arithmetic of Zero
events.short: In the Brahmasphutasiddhanta Brahmagupta first gave rules for calculating with zero and negative numbers and studied quadratic and indeterminate equations.
events.detail: Brahmagupta was born in 598 and worked at Bhinmal in present-day Rajasthan. In 628 he wrote the Brahmasphutasiddhanta, a treatise on astronomy and mathematics. It is the first work to treat zero as a number in its own right, giving rules for adding, subtracting and multiplying it with positive and negative numbers, for instance that a number minus itself is zero and that any number times zero is zero; he called positive numbers fortunes and negative numbers debts. He also gave a method for solving quadratic equations, a composition method for indeterminate equations such as Pell’s equation, and a formula for the area of a cyclic quadrilateral. In the eighth century the book was translated into Arabic and had an important influence on mathematics and astronomy in the Islamic world.

events.title: Xuanzang in India
events.short: The Tang monk Xuanzang spent over a decade in India, studying at Nalanda, and his Great Tang Records on the Western Regions became a priceless source for medieval India.
events.detail: Xuanzang left Chang’an in 629, slipping across the frontier against imperial orders, and travelled through Turfan, the states of Central Asia and the Hindu Kush, entering India around 630. He studied Yogacara teachings under Shilabhadra at Nalanda for five years and travelled all over India visiting Buddhist holy places. In 642 King Harsha held a great assembly for him at Kannauj, where he expounded Mahayana doctrine and, it is said, no one could refute him for eighteen days, making him famous. In 645 he returned to Chang’an with 657 scriptures and spent nearly twenty years translating them. His Great Tang Records on the Western Regions, dictated to his disciple Bianji, describes the geography, customs, religions and history of 138 countries and regions, and since the nineteenth century it has guided archaeologists to sites such as Nalanda.

events.title: Wang Xuance’s Mission to India
events.short: When the Tang envoy Wang Xuance was attacked in India by a usurper, he raised troops from Tibet and Nepal, defeated him and took him captive to Chang’an.
events.detail: Wang Xuance was a Tang official who travelled to India on several missions. On his second mission, in 648, Harsha had just died and his minister Arunashva had seized the throne; Arunashva’s troops attacked the Chinese mission and plundered its gifts, but Wang and his deputy Jiang Shiren escaped. They went to Tibet and Nepal, raised about 1,200 Tibetan and more than 7,000 Nepalese horsemen, returned to defeat Arunashva and carried him captive to Chang’an to present to Emperor Taizong. The episode is recorded in Chinese histories but not in Indian sources. Wang also brought back Indian techniques of sugar-making; his account of his travels in central India is lost apart from fragments quoted in other books.

events.title: The Pallava Monuments of Mamallapuram
events.short: At the port of Mamallapuram the Pallavas carved a giant rock relief, monolithic temples and the Shore Temple, treasures of south Indian stone art.
events.detail: The Pallavas were a powerful dynasty that ruled northern Tamil Nadu from the sixth to the ninth century, with their capital at Kanchipuram. The port of Mamallapuram takes its name from Mamalla, great wrestler, a title of King Narasimhavarman I. In the seventh and eighth centuries the Pallavas left a wealth of carving there: the giant relief known as the Descent of the Ganges, about 29 metres long and 13 high, with more than a hundred gods, people and animals; five rathas, temples carved each from a single boulder; and the Shore Temple, built by the sea in the early eighth century and one of the earliest structural stone temples in the south. These monuments pioneered the Dravidian temple style of southern India and became a World Heritage Site in 1984.

events.title: The Tamil Bhakti Saints
events.short: In the Tamil country Shaiva and Vaishnava poet-saints sang of their love for God in the language of the people, starting the bhakti movement that swept India.
events.detail: Between the sixth and ninth centuries the Tamil country produced sixty-three Nayanars devoted to Shiva and twelve Alvars devoted to Vishnu. They came from many castes, kings, Brahmins, farmers and potters among them, and included women such as the poet Andal. Composing hymns in Tamil rather than Sanskrit, they wandered from temple to temple singing of their passionate love and longing for God and taught that sincere devotion, whatever one’s birth, wins divine grace. Their poems were later collected in the Shaiva Tirumurai and the Vaishnava Four Thousand Divine Hymns, which are still sung in temples today. This bhakti movement later spread north and profoundly changed the face of Hinduism.

events.title: The Kailasanatha Temple at Kanchipuram
events.short: The Pallava king Narasimhavarman II built the Kailasanatha Temple in his capital Kanchipuram, one of the earliest large stone temples of southern India.
events.detail: Kanchipuram was the Pallava capital and a centre of religion and learning in the south; Xuanzang visited it and called it the capital of the Dravida country, with more than a hundred monasteries. Around 700 the Pallava king Narasimhavarman II, also called Rajasimha, built the Kailasanatha Temple there in honour of Shiva. Built of sandstone, its main shrine is crowned by a pyramidal tower of several storeys and surrounded by fifty-eight small shrines, and its walls are covered with images of Shiva and Parvati and rearing lions. It is an early example of the Dravidian temple style, and later the great Chola temple at Thanjavur drew on it.

events.title: The Arab Conquest of Sindh
events.short: The Umayyad general Muhammad ibn Qasim conquered Sindh, giving Islam its first foothold in South Asia.
events.detail: By the early eighth century the Umayyad Caliphate stretched from Spain to Central Asia. Citing attacks by Sindhi pirates on Arab ships, al-Hajjaj, governor of Iraq, sent his young nephew Muhammad ibn Qasim, aged about seventeen, to invade Sindh by land and sea. In 712 he took the port of Debal, defeated and killed King Dahir of Sindh near Aror and then marched north to capture Multan. He treated local Hindus and Buddhists with relative tolerance, letting them keep their faith and temples on payment of the jizya tax. Soon afterwards he was recalled to Iraq and died in prison. Sindh became part of the Islamic world, and for centuries Indian mathematics, astronomy and medicine travelled through it to Baghdad.

events.title: Lalitaditya of Kashmir
events.short: Lalitaditya of Kashmir’s Karkota dynasty campaigned widely, built the magnificent Martand Sun Temple and exchanged envoys with Tang China.
events.detail: Lalitaditya Muktapida, who reigned from about 724 to 760, was the most powerful king of Kashmir’s Karkota dynasty. According to the twelfth-century Rajatarangini he defeated Yashovarman of Kannauj and campaigned across northern India, Central Asia and the Tibetan borderlands; the account is exaggerated, but he did make Kashmir for a time a leading power in the north. Chinese histories record that a king of Kashmir named Muduobi sent envoys to the Tang court seeking an alliance against Tibet. He built many towns, temples and monasteries, the most famous being the Martand Sun Temple on a plateau overlooking the Kashmir valley, surrounded by a colonnade; it was destroyed in the fifteenth century, but its majestic ruins still stand.

events.title: The Rajput Kings Turn Back the Arabs
events.short: Indian kings such as Nagabhata I of the Gurjara-Pratiharas defeated Arab armies advancing east from Sindh, halting Islamic expansion into India’s heartland for centuries.
events.detail: After conquering Sindh, the Umayyad governors there repeatedly raided east into Rajasthan, Gujarat and Malwa. In the 730s Indian kings including Nagabhata I of the Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty, Bappa Rawal of Mewar and a Gujarat branch of the Chalukyas defeated the Arab armies one after another; a Chalukya inscription records an Arab defeat at Navsari. These campaigns confined Arab power to Sindh and Multan. The Gurjara-Pratiharas went on to become the leading power of northern India, whose king Arab travellers called the greatest enemy of Islam, and for nearly three centuries Islamic power made no deep inroads into the Indian heartland.

events.title: The Pala Empire of Bengal
events.short: Bengal’s nobles chose Gopala as king, founding the Pala dynasty, the last great royal patron of Buddhism, which ruled eastern India for four centuries.
events.detail: In the mid-eighth century Bengal fell into prolonged chaos, described as the law of the fishes, in which the big fish eat the small. Around 750 the local chiefs chose Gopala as their king, founding the Pala dynasty, a rare event in Indian history. Under his son Dharmapala and grandson Devapala the Palas fought the Gurjara-Pratiharas and the Rashtrakutas for Kannauj and for a time controlled most of northern India. The Pala kings were Buddhists who supported Nalanda and founded new great monasteries such as Vikramashila and Odantapuri, where Tantric Buddhism developed. Pala bronzes and black stone sculptures have a distinctive style that influenced Buddhist art in Nepal, Tibet and Southeast Asia.

events.title: The Kailasa Temple at Ellora
events.short: The Rashtrakuta king Krishna I had the Kailasa Temple carved from the top down out of a single cliff, the largest monolithic rock-cut structure in the world.
events.detail: The Ellora caves near Aurangabad in Maharashtra comprise thirty-four Buddhist, Hindu and Jain caves cut between the sixth and tenth centuries, a testament to the coexistence of three faiths. Cave 16, the Kailasa Temple, was commissioned around the 760s by the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I to represent Mount Kailash, the abode of Shiva. Working downwards from the top of a basalt hill, the masons first cut three deep trenches and then carved the huge block left in the middle into a complete temple with a main shrine, gateway, hall, stone elephants and tall pillars, removing an estimated 200,000 tonnes of rock. The temple is about sixty metres long and thirty wide, and its walls are covered with fine carving. Ellora became a World Heritage Site in 1983.

events.title: Adi Shankara and Advaita Vedanta
events.short: The Kerala-born philosopher Shankara expounded Advaita Vedanta, the non-duality of self and Brahman, and founded monasteries across India, reviving Brahmanical thought.
events.detail: Shankara was born at Kaladi in present-day Kerala; tradition dates his life to 788–820, and scholars generally place him around the eighth century. Legend says he renounced the world as a boy, travelled the length of India and debated Buddhists, Mimamsakas and scholars of other schools. In commentaries on the Upanishads, the Bhagavad Gita and the Brahma Sutras he set out Advaita, non-dual, Vedanta: the only reality is undifferentiated Brahman, the individual self is in truth identical with it, and the world of appearances is an illusion produced by maya; realising this brings liberation. He is said to have founded four monasteries at the four corners of India, at Sringeri, Dwarka, Puri and Jyotirmath, a system that survives today. He is regarded as a key figure in the revival of Hinduism.

events.title: The Parsis Arrive in Gujarat
events.short: Escaping pressure under Arab rule, a group of Zoroastrians sailed from Iran to Gujarat; their descendants are India’s Parsis.
events.detail: After the Arab conquest of Sasanian Persia, Iran’s Zoroastrians came under growing pressure. According to the Qissa-i Sanjan, a sixteenth-century narrative poem, a group of believers set out from Khorasan in north-eastern Iran, sailed by way of Hormuz and landed on the coast of Gujarat, where the local ruler Jadi Rana let them settle at Sanjan on condition that they adopt the local language and dress. Legend says their priest answered the king with the image of sugar dissolved in milk: they would blend into society and sweeten it. Accounts of the date vary from the eighth to the tenth century. The Parsis still keep a sacred fire brought from Iran. They later played a major part in the commerce and industry of Bombay; the Tata family are Parsis.

events.title: Vikramashila
events.short: The Pala king Dharmapala founded Vikramashila, which with Nalanda was the foremost Buddhist university of medieval India and trained Atisha, who took Buddhism to Tibet.
events.detail: Vikramashila stood on the Ganges in the Bhagalpur district of present-day Bihar and was founded by the Pala king Dharmapala around the late eighth or early ninth century. Its centre was a great cruciform stupa surrounded by more than two hundred monks’ cells; at its height it had over a hundred teachers and a thousand students in six colleges and was famous for Tantric studies. Its abbots were appointed by the king, and its best scholars earned the title of pandita. In the eleventh century the great teacher Atisha was a senior monk there; in 1042 he accepted an invitation to Tibet, where he did much to revive Tibetan Buddhism. Around 1203 Vikramashila was destroyed by the army of Bakhtiyar Khalji. The Archaeological Survey of India began excavating the site in the 1960s.

events.title: Amoghavarsha of the Rashtrakutas
events.short: The Rashtrakuta king Amoghavarsha ruled the Deccan for over sixty years, patronised literature and Jainism, and was counted by an Arab traveller among the four great kings of the world.
events.detail: The Rashtrakutas overthrew the Chalukyas of Badami in 753, became masters of the Deccan and repeatedly marched north to fight for Kannauj. Amoghavarsha I came to the throne in 814 while still a youth and reigned for more than sixty years, moving the capital to Manyakheta, today’s Malkhed in Karnataka. A lover of literature, he gathered Sanskrit and Kannada writers at his court and is traditionally credited with the Kavirajamarga, the oldest surviving work on poetics in Kannada. In later life he followed Jainism and is said to have withdrawn from the throne several times for religious practice. In 851 the Arab merchant Sulaiman listed the Rashtrakuta king with the Abbasid caliph, the Byzantine emperor and the emperor of China as the four great sovereigns of the world.

events.title: Mihira Bhoja of the Gurjara-Pratiharas
events.short: Mihira Bhoja ruled most of northern India from Kannauj and was the most powerful king of the early medieval north.
events.detail: The Gurjara-Pratiharas rose to power after resisting the Arabs in the eighth century and captured Kannauj early in the ninth. Mihira Bhoja, who reigned from about 836 to 885, was the dynasty’s strongest king, ruling from the Punjab and Rajasthan to the middle Ganges and contending with the Palas in the east and the Rashtrakutas in the south in what historians call the tripartite struggle. A devotee of Vishnu, he styled himself Adivaraha, the primeval boar, on his coins, after Vishnu’s boar avatar. The Arab merchant Sulaiman, who visited in 851, wrote that this king had a vast cavalry, that his lands were rich and safe, and that he was the greatest enemy of Islam.

events.title: Vijayalaya Revives the Cholas
events.short: The Chola chief Vijayalaya captured Thanjavur and revived the ancient Tamil dynasty, which went on to dominate southern India.
events.detail: The Cholas were one of the three Tamil dynasties of the Sangam age, centred on the Kaveri delta, but between the sixth and ninth centuries they declined into vassals of the Pallavas and Pandyas. Around 848 the Chola chief Vijayalaya seized Thanjavur from a Pandya feudatory, made it his capital and built a temple to the goddess Durga there, marking the revival of the dynasty, known as the medieval or Imperial Cholas. His son Aditya I defeated the Pallavas and won northern Tamil country. Later Chola kings expanded steadily through war and marriage, and by the time of Rajaraja I in the late tenth century the Cholas had become the strongest empire in southern India, with a powerful navy.

events.title: The Temples of Khajuraho
events.short: The Chandela dynasty built more than eighty Hindu and Jain temples at Khajuraho in Madhya Pradesh, famous for their soaring spires and profuse sculpture.
events.detail: Khajuraho in northern Madhya Pradesh was the religious centre of the Chandela dynasty. Between about 950 and 1050 the Chandela kings built some eighty-five temples there, of which about twenty-five survive. Most stand on high platforms, and their clustered, rising spires imitate the peaks of the Himalayas, the mountain home of the gods; they represent the summit of the northern Nagara style, the grandest being the Kandariya Mahadeva Temple dedicated to Shiva. Their walls inside and out teem with gods, celestial women, musicians, warriors and scenes of daily life, and a small number of carvings of lovers are especially famous. Khajuraho was later forgotten, rediscovered by a British officer in 1838 and made a World Heritage Site in 1986.

events.title: Rajaraja I and the Chola Empire
events.short: Rajaraja I conquered southern India and northern Sri Lanka and built a well-organised administration and land survey, opening the Chola golden age.
events.detail: Rajaraja I came to the throne in 985 and reigned for about thirty years. He defeated the Pandya and Chera kingdoms of the south, destroying the Chera fleet, crossed the sea to take northern Sri Lanka, where he burned the old capital Anuradhapura, beat the Western Chalukyas to the north and conquered the Maldives. He built a centralised administration that divided the realm into provinces, districts and villages and carried out a full land survey to fix taxes, while village assemblies governed themselves through elected committees, whose procedures are recorded in detail in the inscriptions of Uthiramerur. He also built the majestic Brihadisvara Temple at Thanjavur. His reign laid the foundations of the Chola Empire’s expansion overseas.

events.title: The Raids of Mahmud of Ghazni
events.short: Sultan Mahmud of the Ghaznavid dynasty of Afghanistan invaded northern India seventeen times, plundering cities and temples and annexing the Punjab.
events.detail: Mahmud was sultan of the Ghaznavid dynasty of Afghanistan from 998 to 1030. Beginning with his defeat of Jayapala of the Hindu Shahi dynasty near Peshawar in 1001, he led an army into India almost every winter, raiding Multan, Thanesar, Mathura, Kannauj, Kalinjar, Somnath and other places seventeen times and carrying off vast amounts of gold, silver, jewels and slaves. The loot paid for palaces, mosques and colleges in his capital Ghazni, which became one of the cultural centres of the Islamic world. He destroyed many Hindu temples, leaving a deep wound in Indian historical memory. His annexation of the Punjab opened the door for later Muslim dynasties to enter India.

events.title: The Great Temple of Thanjavur
events.short: Rajaraja I completed the Brihadisvara Temple at Thanjavur, whose tower, about 66 metres high, was the tallest building in India at the time.
events.detail: The Brihadisvara Temple, dedicated to Shiva, was commissioned by Rajaraja I and completed in 1010, and is also called the Rajarajeshwaram. The pyramidal tower over its main shrine rises some 66 metres in thirteen storeys of granite, and the capstone at its summit is said to weigh about eighty tonnes. In the courtyard stands a monolithic statue of the bull Nandi, and the walls preserve Chola-era paintings. The temple’s inscriptions record in detail the gifts of the king and queen, the lands and villages it owned, and the names and pay of hundreds of dancers, musicians, priests and craftsmen, showing that the great temple was also an economic and social centre. Together with two later Chola temples it is a World Heritage Site.

events.title: Bhoja, the Scholar King of Malwa
events.short: Bhoja of the Paramara dynasty was famed for his learning, credited with more than eighty books, and built a great lake and the unfinished Bhojpur temple.
events.detail: Bhoja ruled the Paramara kingdom of Malwa from Dhar from about 1010 to 1055. He was the most celebrated scholar king of medieval India; tradition credits him with more than eighty works on poetics, grammar, astronomy, medicine, architecture and yoga, among them the Samarangana Sutradhara, an important treatise on architecture. At Dhar he founded the Bhoja Shala, a college dedicated to Saraswati, goddess of learning. The city of Bhopal is said to take its name from a great artificial lake he built. Near Bhopal he began the Bhojeshwar temple to Shiva, which houses a huge linga about 2.3 metres high, but the temple was never finished; construction drawings carved on nearby rocks still show how ancient temples were built.

events.title: The Sack of Somnath
events.short: Mahmud of Ghazni stormed the Shiva temple of Somnath on the Gujarat coast and carried off great riches; the temple was destroyed and rebuilt many times in later centuries.
events.detail: The Somnath temple on the south-western coast of Gujarat is one of the twelve jyotirlinga shrines of Shiva and was famous for its wealth. In the winter of 1025–26 Mahmud marched across the Thar desert, stormed the temple after fierce fighting, killed many of its defenders, broke the linga and carried off treasure said to be worth twenty million dinars. Persian historians celebrated the raid as a great victory for Islam, while in Hindu memory it became a symbol of foreign aggression. The temple was rebuilt and destroyed again several times. After independence, Deputy Prime Minister Vallabhbhai Patel led its reconstruction, and President Rajendra Prasad consecrated the new temple in 1951.

events.title: The Chola Expedition to Srivijaya
events.short: Rajendra I sent a fleet across the Bay of Bengal to attack Srivijaya, the maritime power of Southeast Asia, gaining control of the sea routes to China.
events.detail: Rajendra I, son of Rajaraja I, reigned from 1014 to 1044 and expanded the Chola Empire further, completing the conquest of Sri Lanka. At the time Srivijaya, based on Sumatra, controlled the Strait of Malacca and taxed the ships trading between India and China. Around 1025 Rajendra sent a fleet across the Bay of Bengal against Srivijaya and a dozen of its ports in the Malay peninsula and Sumatra, and captured the Srivijayan king. It was one of the few great overseas expeditions in Indian history, and inscriptions at Thanjavur list the ports that were taken. Afterwards Chola merchants gained influence in Southeast Asia, and the Cholas sent several missions to Song China, whose histories call their country Zhunian.

events.title: The Sun Temple at Modhera
events.short: The Solanki dynasty of Gujarat built the Sun Temple at Modhera, fronted by a stepped tank lined with more than a hundred small shrines.
events.detail: The Sun Temple at Modhera in the Mehsana district of Gujarat is dedicated to Surya, the sun god, and was built in 1026–27 by the Solanki king Bhima I, shortly after Mahmud’s sack of Somnath. It has three parts: the shrine, a pillared assembly hall and, in front, the great stepped tank called Surya Kund. The rectangular tank is lined with terraces of steps descending in tiers, among which stand 108 small shrines. The temple is aligned so that at the equinoxes the first rays of the rising sun fall on the image in the shrine. Its pillars and walls are densely carved with gods, dancers and ornament. The shrine’s superstructure has collapsed, but a dance festival is still held there every year.

events.title: Al-Biruni’s Book on India
events.short: The Central Asian scholar al-Biruni came to India with Mahmud, learned Sanskrit and wrote a remarkably objective book on Indian religion, science and customs.
events.detail: Al-Biruni, born in 973 in Khwarazm, was one of the most brilliant scholars of the Islamic world, master of astronomy, mathematics, geography and pharmacology. When Mahmud of Ghazni conquered Khwarazm he took al-Biruni to Ghazni, and the scholar travelled several times with the army to the Punjab, where he learned Sanskrit and studied Indian texts. Around 1030 he completed his Kitab ta’rikh al-Hind, a systematic account of Indian philosophy, religion, caste, calendars, astronomy, geography, literature and festivals. He strove for objectivity, often comparing Indian ideas with Greek philosophy, and frankly noted that the Muslim invasions had made Indians hostile to foreigners. The book is hailed as one of the first works of anthropology and is a precious source for eleventh-century India.

events.title: The Dilwara Temples of Mount Abu
events.short: The Jain temples at Dilwara on Mount Abu in Rajasthan are carved from white marble, with ceilings and pillars as delicate as lace.
events.detail: The Dilwara temples on Mount Abu in south-western Rajasthan are a group of five Jain temples built between the eleventh and thirteenth centuries. The oldest, the Vimal Vasahi, was built in 1031 by Vimal, a minister of the Solanki dynasty, and is dedicated to Adinatha, the first tirthankara. Another, the Luna Vasahi, was built in 1230 by the brother ministers Vastupala and Tejapala. Plain outside, the temples are carved throughout in white marble inside; their domes, ringed with lotuses, dancers and musicians, are so finely worked that the marble is almost translucent. Legend says the craftsmen were paid by the weight of the marble dust they chiselled away, which is why the carving is so delicate.

events.title: The City of the Chola Who Took the Ganges
events.short: After his army reached the Ganges, Rajendra I built a new capital named for the Chola who conquered the Ganges, with a grand temple and an artificial lake.
events.detail: Between about 1019 and 1021 Rajendra I’s army marched north along the east coast through Kalinga as far as the Pala kingdom of Bengal and reached the Ganges. Defeated kings, it is said, were made to carry pots of Ganges water on their heads back to the south, where it was poured into a great lake near his new capital, the Cholagangam, symbolising the Ganges flowing south. To celebrate the expedition he took the title Gangaikonda, he who took the Ganges, and founded a new capital, Gangaikonda Cholapuram, in what is now the Ariyalur district of Tamil Nadu, which remained the Chola capital for more than two centuries. Its Brihadisvara Temple, modelled on the great temple of Thanjavur, is slightly lower but more graceful, and forms part of a World Heritage Site.

events.title: Ramanuja and Qualified Non-Dualism
events.short: The Tamil philosopher Ramanuja taught qualified non-dualism, joining Vedanta philosophy with devotion to Vishnu and inspiring later bhakti movements.
events.detail: Ramanuja was born at Sriperumbudur near present-day Chennai and, according to tradition, lived from 1017 to 1137. For many years he directed the great Vishnu temple at Srirangam and organised its rituals. Unlike Shankara, who held the world to be illusion, Ramanuja taught Vishishtadvaita, qualified non-dualism: Brahman, identified with Vishnu, is the sole reality, but individual souls and the material world truly exist as his body and attributes, and the soul can win liberation through devotion and surrender to God, who grants his grace. He carried on the tradition of the Tamil Alvars and is said to have revealed a sacred mantra openly to people of all castes. His ideas deeply influenced the later Rama and Krishna devotional movements of northern India.

events.title: The Hoysala Temple at Belur
events.short: The Hoysala king Vishnuvardhana built the Chennakeshava Temple at Belur in Karnataka, famous for its star-shaped plan and intricate soapstone carving.
events.detail: The Hoysala dynasty ruled southern Karnataka from the eleventh to the fourteenth century. In 1117 King Vishnuvardhana built the Chennakeshava Temple to Vishnu at his capital Belur to celebrate a victory over the Cholas; its construction is said to have continued for more than a century. Raised on a star-shaped platform and carved from fine, soft chloritic schist, its outer walls are banded with friezes of elephants, lions, horsemen, scrolls and scenes from the epics, and its pillars look as if turned on a lathe. Most famous are the forty-two madanika figures of celestial dancers beneath the eaves, with graceful poses and hair-fine jewellery. The equally exquisite Hoysaleswara Temple at nearby Halebidu was inscribed with Belur as a World Heritage Site in 2023.

events.title: The Jagannath Temple at Puri
events.short: The Eastern Ganga dynasty built the Jagannath Temple at Puri in Odisha, where each year hundreds of thousands of devotees haul giant wooden chariots in the Ratha Yatra.
events.detail: Jagannath, Lord of the Universe, is worshipped as a form of Vishnu or Krishna; his wooden image has huge round eyes and stumps instead of full arms and legs. The Jagannath Temple at Puri was begun in the twelfth century by the Eastern Ganga king Anantavarman Chodaganga, and its main tower rises about 65 metres; Puri is one of the four great pilgrimage sites of Hinduism. In the Ratha Yatra held at the start of the monsoon each year, the images of Jagannath and his brother and sister are placed on three towering wooden chariots that devotees pull through the streets. The English word juggernaut, meaning an unstoppable force, comes from the impression the festival made on European travellers.

events.title: Kalhana’s River of Kings
events.short: The Kashmiri poet Kalhana wrote the chronicle Rajatarangini, hailed as India’s first true work of history.
events.detail: Kalhana, son of a Kashmiri minister, wrote the Rajatarangini, the River of Kings, in 1148–49: eight books of Sanskrit verse, about 7,800 stanzas in all, recounting the kings of Kashmir from legendary times to the twelfth century. Unlike most ancient Indian texts, it states plainly that the historian must be impartial like a judge; Kalhana consulted older chronicles, inscriptions, coins and buildings and tried to separate legend from fact. The closer he comes to his own time, the fuller and more reliable his account becomes, vividly describing court intrigues, famines, floods and the sufferings of the people. The Rajatarangini is considered the only work of ancient India that can be compared with Western historiography, and later writers added continuations to it.

events.title: Bhaskara II and the Lilavati
events.short: The mathematician Bhaskara II wrote the Siddhanta Shiromani, whose arithmetic book Lilavati poses problems in graceful verse and was studied for centuries.
events.detail: Bhaskara II, born in 1114, headed the observatory at Ujjain and was the greatest mathematician and astronomer of medieval India. In 1150 he completed the Siddhanta Shiromani, in four parts: the arithmetic Lilavati, the algebra Bijaganita and two books on astronomy. Legend says the Lilavati is named after his daughter; it poses problems in verse, such as finding the height of a lotus or the number of bees in a swarm. He gave the chakravala, or cyclic, method for solving Pell’s equation, discussed division by zero as yielding infinity, and in astronomy came close to the idea of the derivative. In the sixteenth century a poet at Akbar’s court translated the Lilavati into Persian. India’s second satellite, launched in 1979, was named after him.

events.title: Basava and the Lingayats
events.short: Basava, a reformer of Karnataka, rejected caste hierarchy and elaborate ritual, taught that all could worship Shiva as equals and founded the Lingayat tradition.
events.detail: Basava, born around 1105, was a minister of King Bijjala of the Kalachuri dynasty, whose capital was Kalyana in present-day Karnataka. He wrote many vachanas, prose poems in simple Kannada, criticising caste discrimination, idol worship, elaborate ritual and the oppression of women, and teaching that work is sacred and that everyone could wear a small linga as a sign of Shiva and commune with God directly. He founded the Anubhava Mantapa, a hall of experience, where people of all castes and both sexes discussed faith together. A marriage he sanctioned between a Brahmin and a low-caste family is said to have caused social upheaval. The Lingayat tradition he founded still has many followers in Karnataka.

events.title: Jayadeva’s Gita Govinda
events.short: The Gita Govinda of the poet Jayadeva celebrates the love of Krishna and the cowherd girl Radha and became a major theme of Indian music, dance and painting.
events.detail: Jayadeva was a twelfth-century Sanskrit poet who lived in Bengal under the Sena dynasty or in Odisha. His lyric poem the Gita Govinda, in twelve chapters, tells of the love, separation, longing and reunion of the cowherd Krishna and the cowherd girl Radha, an allegory of the soul’s yearning for God. Each song is marked with the raga and rhythm in which it is to be sung, so it could be performed directly to music. The poem spread quickly across India; it became a daily hymn in the Jagannath temple at Puri and central to classical dances such as Odissi, and later Rajasthani and Pahari miniatures illustrated its story again and again. It is one of the most influential works of the bhakti movement.

events.title: The First Battle of Tarain
events.short: The Rajput king Prithviraj Chauhan defeated Muhammad of Ghor at Tarain, forcing the invader to retreat.
events.detail: In the late twelfth century the Ghurid dynasty of Afghanistan replaced the Ghaznavids, and its ruler Muhammad of Ghor seized the Punjab and began to push towards Delhi. Delhi and Ajmer were then ruled by the young Chauhan king Prithviraj III. In 1191 the two armies met at Tarain near Thanesar in present-day Haryana, and Prithviraj, leading a confederacy of Rajputs with war elephants, defeated the Ghurid army; Muhammad himself was wounded and carried from the field by his men and retreated to Afghanistan. The victory made Prithviraj famous, and the later epic Prithviraj Raso portrays him as a hero, including the romantic tale of how he carried off Princess Samyukta of Kannauj.

events.title: The Second Battle of Tarain
events.short: Muhammad of Ghor returned and defeated Prithviraj at Tarain, opening the way to Delhi and the Ganges valley.
events.detail: After his defeat Muhammad of Ghor spent a year rebuilding his army and in 1192 returned to Tarain with some 120,000 picked horsemen. Prithviraj gathered an even larger Rajput confederacy to meet him. The Ghurids used the mounted archery of Central Asia, sending light cavalry to harass the Rajputs from all sides and feign retreats to wear them down, and then launched a general assault with heavy cavalry at dusk, routing the Rajput army. Prithviraj was captured as he fled and later executed. The battle was a turning point in Indian history: the Ghurids went on to take Delhi, Ajmer and Kannauj, and Muslim rule began its long period in northern India.

events.title: The Qutb Minar
events.short: Qutb ud-Din Aibak, a general of the Ghurids, began the Qutb Minar in Delhi; about 73 metres tall, it is the world’s tallest brick minaret.
events.detail: After the capture of Delhi, Muhammad of Ghor’s slave general Qutb ud-Din Aibak built India’s first great mosque, the Quwwat-ul-Islam, in southern Delhi, using columns taken from more than twenty demolished Hindu and Jain temples. Around 1199 he began a minaret beside it as a monument to victory, but completed only the first storey. His successor Iltutmish added three more, and in the fourteenth century Firuz Shah Tughlaq repaired it after a lightning strike and added a fifth. The Qutb Minar is about 72.5 metres high, built of red sandstone and white marble, with alternating angular and rounded flutes and bands of Quranic inscriptions. Together with the iron pillar and other monuments, the Qutb complex became a World Heritage Site in 1993.

events.title: The Fall of Nalanda
events.short: Bakhtiyar Khalji led Turkic troops into Bihar and Bengal and destroyed Nalanda and Vikramashila, after which Buddhism faded in the land of its birth.
events.detail: Bakhtiyar Khalji was a Turkic commander in the service of the Ghurids. Around 1200 he led his cavalry east into Bihar, stormed monasteries that his men took for fortresses and killed many monks. The great monasteries of Nalanda, Vikramashila and Odantapuri were destroyed one after another and countless texts were burned. Around 1204 he made a surprise attack on Nadia, capital of the Sena kings of Bengal. Buddhism’s decline in India had begun long before: Hinduism had absorbed many Buddhist ideas, and Buddhism depended on royally endowed great monasteries rather than a broad popular base. After the monasteries fell, many monks fled to Tibet, Nepal and Southeast Asia, and Buddhism almost vanished from India until its revival in the twentieth century.

events.title: The Delhi Sultanate Is Founded
events.short: After Muhammad of Ghor was assassinated, his slave general Qutb ud-Din Aibak made himself sultan at Delhi, founding the Delhi Sultanate, which ruled northern India for over three centuries.
events.detail: Qutb ud-Din Aibak was born into a Turkic family in Central Asia and sold into slavery as a child. Bought by Muhammad of Ghor, he rose through his talents to become his most trusted general, in charge of the conquered lands in India. When Muhammad was assassinated in 1206, Aibak took power at Lahore and broke with the Ghurids, founding the first dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate. Because he and several of his successors had been slaves, it is also called the Slave or Mamluk dynasty. Aibak was famed for his generosity and called the giver of lakhs. In 1210 he died after falling from his horse during a game of polo at Lahore. The Delhi Sultanate passed through five dynasties until the Mughals replaced it in 1526.

events.title: Iltutmish Consolidates the Sultanate
events.short: Iltutmish fixed the capital at Delhi, won recognition from the Abbasid caliph and issued the silver tanka, laying the institutional foundations of the Sultanate.
events.detail: Iltutmish, also a former slave, became Aibak’s son-in-law and seized the throne in 1211, reigning until 1236. He defeated rival Ghurid commanders who claimed Indian territory, subdued Bengal and Sindh and made Delhi the capital of the Sultanate. Scholars and craftsmen fleeing the Mongols in Central Asia and Persia flocked to Delhi, making it a cultural centre of the eastern Islamic world. In 1229 the Abbasid caliph in Baghdad formally recognised him as sultan. He created the ruling group of forty Turkish nobles known as the Forty, developed the iqta system that assigned land revenues to officers, and issued a standard silver coin, the tanka, and a copper jital. He also completed the Qutb Minar.

events.title: Genghis Khan on the Indus
events.short: Genghis Khan defeated the Khwarazmian prince Jalal ad-Din on the banks of the Indus, bringing Mongol armies to India’s frontier for the first time, though they went no further.
events.detail: In 1219 Genghis Khan invaded the Khwarazmian Empire. Its prince Jalal ad-Din fought a retreating war until he reached the Indus, where Genghis caught up with him in November 1221. Defeated, Jalal ad-Din rode his horse into the river and swam across to escape, and Genghis is said to have admired his courage. In the Punjab Jalal ad-Din asked the Delhi sultan Iltutmish for help, but Iltutmish, wary of provoking the Mongols, politely refused. Genghis sent troops after him into the Punjab, but they withdrew without going deeper into India, partly because of the heat. Over the next century the Mongols repeatedly raided the Punjab and the country around Delhi, and defence against them became the Sultanate’s first concern.

events.title: Razia, the Woman Sultan
events.short: Iltutmish’s daughter Razia took the throne of Delhi, one of the very few Muslim women ever to rule in South Asia.
events.detail: Iltutmish thought his sons unfit to rule and named his daughter Razia as his heir. After his death the nobles first enthroned his son Ruknuddin, but the new sultan proved dissolute, and in 1236 the people of Delhi and some nobles raised Razia to the throne. Skilled in government and war, she put aside the veil, held court and led armies dressed as a man and riding an elephant, heard cases herself and called herself sultan rather than sultana. Her promotion of Jamal-ud-Din Yaqut, an Abyssinian rather than a Turk, to master of the stables angered the Turkish nobles of the Forty. In 1240 they rebelled, and she was defeated and killed after less than four years on the throne. Her story has inspired many novels, plays and films.

events.title: The Konark Sun Temple
events.short: The Eastern Ganga king Narasimhadeva I built the Konark Sun Temple on the Odisha coast, designed as the giant stone chariot of the sun god.
events.detail: The Konark Sun Temple stands on the coast about 35 kilometres north of Puri in Odisha. It was built around 1250 by the Eastern Ganga king Narasimhadeva I, reportedly to celebrate a victory over the Muslim armies of Bengal. The whole temple is designed as the chariot of the sun god Surya, with twenty-four great stone wheels about three metres across carved on its base and seven stone horses drawing it. The spokes and carvings of the wheels can be read like sundials to tell the time. Its walls teem with superb carvings of gods, musicians and dancers, animals and daily life. The main tower, about 70 metres high, had collapsed before the nineteenth century, and what survives is the assembly hall in front. Konark became a World Heritage Site in 1984, and one of its wheels appears on the back of India’s ten-rupee note.
