events.title: Balban’s Iron Rule
events.short: Sultan Balban broke the power of the Turkish nobles, proclaimed the divine right of kings and strengthened the army against the Mongols, restoring order to the Sultanate.
events.detail: Balban, once a slave of Iltutmish and one of the Forty, served for years as deputy to Sultan Nasiruddin and took the throne himself in 1266, reigning until 1287. He held that the sultan was the shadow of God on earth, introduced Persian court ceremonies of prostration and kissing the monarch’s feet, and kept up a stern royal dignity, never laughing in front of his courtiers. He destroyed the nobles of the Forty, who had once been his equals, set up a large network of spies to watch officials in the provinces, and ruthlessly crushed the bandits around Delhi and a rebellion in Bengal. He also built forts and stationed picked troops on the north-western frontier, successfully keeping the Mongols out.

events.title: The Reforms of Alauddin Khalji
events.short: Alauddin of the Khalji dynasty seized the throne, fixed market prices and reformed land tax to maintain a huge standing army that repeatedly repelled the Mongols.
events.detail: In 1290 the Khalji family replaced the Slave dynasty. In 1296 Alauddin Khalji murdered his uncle and father-in-law Jalaluddin and seized the throne, reigning until 1316. To pay for a standing army large enough to withstand the Mongols he imposed strict economic controls: markets in Delhi where officials fixed and enforced the prices of grain, cloth, horses and slaves on pain of harsh punishment, and a land tax raised to half the harvest, collected in kind. He also introduced the branding of horses and the registration of soldiers to stop fraud in military pay. During his reign the Sultanate’s armies defeated several large Mongol invasions. He built the new city of Siri and the Alai Darwaza gateway in the Qutb complex.

events.title: Amir Khusrau, Poet and Musician
events.short: The Delhi poet Amir Khusrau wrote in Persian and Hindavi, was hailed as the Parrot of India and is credited by tradition with founding qawwali music.
events.detail: Amir Khusrau was born in 1253 at Patiali in Uttar Pradesh to a Turkic father and an Indian mother. He served as poet at the courts of seven sultans of Delhi, writing a vast body of lyric and narrative poetry and history in Persian, while also composing riddles and songs in Hindavi, the popular speech that was the ancestor of Hindi and Urdu. He was the favourite disciple of the Sufi master Nizamuddin Auliya, and tradition says that he blended Persian, Arab and Indian music to create the Sufi devotional music of qawwali and invented the sitar and the tabla, though there is little firm evidence for these claims. He was buried beside his master’s tomb.

events.title: The Siege of Chittor
events.short: Alauddin Khalji captured the fortress of Chittor in Mewar, the event behind the later poetic legend of Queen Padmini, who chose death over surrender.
events.detail: Chittor fort stands on an isolated hill about 180 metres high in southern Rajasthan; it was the capital of the kingdom of Mewar and is one of the largest forts in India. In 1303 Alauddin Khalji besieged it for about eight months and finally took it, defeating King Ratan Singh of Mewar; Alauddin is said to have ordered the massacre of tens of thousands. More than two centuries later the Sufi poet Malik Muhammad Jayasi wrote the Padmavat, a narrative poem telling how Alauddin attacked Chittor because he coveted Ratan Singh’s beautiful queen Padmini, and how, when the fort fell, the queen led the women in jauhar, self-immolation, rather than surrender. The story became deeply rooted in Rajput tradition, but historians think Padmini is probably a literary invention.

events.title: Malik Kafur’s Southern Campaigns
events.short: Alauddin’s general Malik Kafur led expeditions into the Deccan and the far south, forcing the Yadava, Kakatiya and Hoysala kings to submit and reaching Madurai.
events.detail: Malik Kafur was a slave from Gujarat who was captured by Alauddin’s army and presented to the sultan, and his ability made him commander of the army. Between 1308 and 1311 he led campaigns south that forced the Yadavas of Devagiri, the Kakatiyas of Warangal and the Hoysalas of Dvarasamudra to surrender and pay tribute, and then pushed into the Tamil country and attacked the Pandya city of Madurai, the first time a northern power had reached the far south of the peninsula. He brought back hundreds of elephants, thousands of horses and vast treasures of gold, silver and jewels. After Alauddin’s death Malik Kafur tried to control the succession and was soon killed.

events.title: The Sufi Saint Nizamuddin Auliya
events.short: Nizamuddin Auliya, a Sufi saint of the Chishti order, preached love and tolerance in Delhi, and his shrine still draws pilgrims of every faith.
events.detail: Sufism is the mystical tradition of Islam, and the Chishti order was brought to India late in the twelfth century by Muinuddin Chishti, centred on Ajmer. Nizamuddin Auliya, born around 1238, was one of its most famous masters and received people of every class and faith at his lodge outside Delhi. He urged distance from the court and from power and taught love of God and of humanity and care for the poor, using the music and poetry of sama as a way to approach God. He had tense relations with several sultans and is said to have remarked that Delhi was still far away. After his death in 1325 his tomb in Delhi became a major place of pilgrimage, where qawwali singers perform every Thursday evening.

events.title: Muhammad bin Tughluq Moves the Capital
events.short: Sultan Muhammad bin Tughluq forced the people of Delhi to move to Daulatabad in the Deccan and back again a few years later; many of his bold schemes ended in failure.
events.detail: Muhammad bin Tughluq came to the throne in 1325. Learned in philosophy, mathematics and medicine, he was also erratic. To control his new southern conquests better, in 1327 he moved the capital from Delhi to Devagiri in the Deccan, renamed Daulatabad, and forced much of Delhi’s population to march more than a thousand kilometres there; many died on the way. A few years later, finding he could not hold the north from there, he let them return to Delhi. He also introduced a token currency of copper coins in place of silver, which failed amid mass forgery, and his planned expeditions to Khorasan and into the Himalayas ended in heavy losses. Rebellions broke out late in his reign, and Vijayanagara and the Bahmani kingdom in the south became independent.

events.title: Ibn Battuta in Delhi
events.short: The Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta served as a judge in Delhi for eight years before being sent as the sultan’s envoy to China; his account vividly describes fourteenth-century India.
events.detail: Ibn Battuta of Tangier in Morocco began his travels through the Islamic world in 1325. In 1334 he reached Delhi by way of Central Asia and Afghanistan, and Sultan Muhammad bin Tughluq appointed him a judge of Delhi on a generous salary. He lived there for about eight years, witnessing the sultan’s generosity and cruelty, the splendour of the court and famine among the people, and describing the Indian postal relays, betel, coconuts and the burning of widows. In 1342 the sultan sent him at the head of an embassy to the Yuan court of China; shipwrecked on the way, he wandered through the Maldives, Sri Lanka and Bengal before reaching Quanzhou in China. His dictated Travels is an important source for medieval India.

events.title: The Vijayanagara Empire Is Founded
events.short: The brothers Harihara and Bukka founded the Vijayanagara Empire on the Tungabhadra, which became the last great Hindu empire of southern India.
events.detail: Early in the fourteenth century the Delhi Sultanate’s southern campaigns had destroyed the old kingdoms of the south. In 1336 the brothers Harihara and Bukka of the Sangama family, formerly in the service of the Kakatiyas or Hoysalas, founded a new state on the Tungabhadra river with its capital at Vijayanagara, the City of Victory, at today’s Hampi in Karnataka. Legend says they were supported by the sage Vidyaranya of the Sringeri monastery. Vijayanagara gradually united all of southern India below the Krishna river and fought the Bahmani Sultanate to the north for generations over the fertile Raichur doab. Its capital was for a time one of the largest and richest cities in the world.

events.title: The Bahmani Sultanate of the Deccan
events.short: Deccan nobles rebelled against Tughluq and Alauddin Bahman Shah founded the Bahmani Sultanate, which later broke up into the five Deccan sultanates.
events.detail: In 1347 the Muslim nobles of the Deccan rebelled against Sultan Muhammad bin Tughluq and chose Hasan Gangu as their leader; taking the name Alauddin Bahman Shah, he founded the Bahmani Sultanate, with its capital first at Gulbarga and later at Bidar. It was the first independent Muslim kingdom of the Deccan and fought the Vijayanagara Empire to the south for generations. The Bahmanis attracted many immigrants from Persia, Arabia and Central Asia, and rivalry between these newcomers and the local Deccani Muslims ran deep at court. At the end of the fifteenth century the dynasty declined as its provincial governors broke away, forming the five sultanates of Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda, Bidar and Berar.

events.title: Firuz Shah Tughlaq
events.short: Sultan Firuz Shah built canals, towns and hospitals and moved two Ashokan pillars to Delhi, preserving them for later generations.
events.detail: Firuz Shah Tughlaq, cousin of Muhammad bin Tughluq, came to the throne in 1351 and reigned for thirty-seven years. Reversing his predecessor’s adventurous policies, he gave up trying to recover the south and concentrated on building at home. He dug several irrigation canals from the Yamuna and Sutlej, founded towns such as Firozabad, Hisar and Jaunpur, and built hospitals, colleges, rest houses and gardens. Fascinated by antiquities, he had two Ashokan pillars brought from Topra and Meerut to Delhi on specially built carts and boats and set up in his palace and hunting lodge, where they still stand. But he enforced Islamic law strictly and levied the jizya on non-Muslims, and the dynasty weakened in his later years.

events.title: The Bengal Sultanate
events.short: Ilyas Shah united Bengal and founded the independent Bengal Sultanate, famous for its rice and textiles, which exchanged frequent missions with Ming China.
events.detail: In 1352 Shamsuddin Ilyas Shah united the three regions of Bengal and founded an independent sultanate with its capital at Pandua, and for more than two centuries Bengal remained largely independent. The fertile delta produced rice, cotton cloth and silk in abundance and was one of the richest regions of Asia. The sultans built magnificent mosques such as the Adina Mosque at Pandua, once the largest in the subcontinent, and patronised Bengali literature, including translations of the Sanskrit epics into Bengali. Early in the fifteenth century the sultans sent several missions to Ming China, and Ma Huan, who sailed with Zheng He’s fleets, described the prosperity of the kingdom of Bangela in his book on the overseas lands.

events.title: Timur Sacks Delhi
events.short: The Central Asian conqueror Timur defeated the Tughluq sultan’s army, stormed Delhi and massacred and plundered its people, a blow from which the Sultanate never recovered.
events.detail: After Firuz Shah’s death the Tughluq dynasty sank into succession struggles. In 1398 Timur, the Turco-Mongol conqueror based at Samarkand, crossed the Indus, claiming that the sultan of Delhi was too tolerant of Hindus. In December he defeated the army of Sultan Nasiruddin Mahmud and his minister Mallu Iqbal outside Delhi; the sultan’s war elephants are said to have been routed by camels carrying burning hay. After Timur entered the city, clashes between his soldiers and the inhabitants led to three days of massacre and plunder; huge numbers were killed and many craftsmen were carried off to build mosques in Samarkand. A chronicler wrote that for two months afterwards not even a bird moved in Delhi. The Tughluq dynasty soon collapsed.

events.title: Infinite Series in the Kerala School
events.short: The Kerala mathematician Madhava discovered infinite series for sine, cosine and pi more than two centuries before Europe.
events.detail: Madhava lived from about 1340 to 1425 at Sangamagrama near Irinjalakuda in Kerala and founded the Kerala school of astronomy and mathematics. He found a way of computing pi by an infinite series, the formula now named after Leibniz, added correction terms to speed its convergence and calculated pi to eleven decimal places; he also gave infinite series for the sine, cosine and arctangent, results that Europe rediscovered only in the seventeenth century through Newton, Gregory and Leibniz. Most of his own writings are lost, but his work survives through those of his successors such as Nilakantha and Jyeshthadeva. Some scholars have speculated that this knowledge reached Europe through Portuguese missionaries, but there is no direct evidence.

events.title: Zheng He’s Fleet at Calicut
events.short: On each of its seven voyages, the Ming treasure fleet under Zheng He reached Calicut on India’s south-west coast, where he set up a memorial stone.
events.detail: Between 1405 and 1433 the Ming eunuch admiral Zheng He, on the orders of the Yongle Emperor, led huge fleets on seven voyages to the Western Ocean, reaching as far as East Africa. Each voyage called at Calicut, today’s Kozhikode in Kerala, then ruled by the Zamorin and a centre of the Indian Ocean spice trade. On the first voyage Zheng He set up a stone there declaring that though the land was more than a hundred thousand li from China, its people and customs shared in the same harmony. Ma Huan, who sailed with him, described Calicut’s king, merchants and goods and its custom of reckoning bargains on the fingers. Zheng He himself is said to have died near Calicut on the return from the seventh voyage. The fleets also visited Cochin and Bengal.

events.title: Ahmad Shah Founds Ahmedabad
events.short: Ahmad Shah of the Gujarat Sultanate founded his new capital Ahmedabad on the Sabarmati, later one of India’s great cities of textiles and trade.
events.detail: When the Tughluq dynasty collapsed, the governor of Gujarat declared his independence and founded the Gujarat Sultanate. In 1411 Sultan Ahmad Shah I founded a new capital near Ashaval on the east bank of the Sabarmati and named it Ahmedabad after himself. He built walls, palaces and the grand Jama Mosque, whose 260 pillars blend Islamic forms with the Jain and Hindu architecture of Gujarat. The sultanate controlled ports such as Cambay and was a major force in Indian Ocean trade. Ahmedabad later became famous for textiles and was called the Manchester of the East, and Gandhi’s Sabarmati Ashram is there. In 2017 its old city became India’s first World Heritage City.

events.title: The Poet Kabir
events.short: Kabir, a weaver-poet of Varanasi, used plain Hindi verse to mock the formalism of both Hinduism and Islam and taught inner devotion to the one God.
events.detail: Kabir lived in fifteenth-century Varanasi; his dates are uncertain. Born into a family of Muslim weavers, he is traditionally said to have been a disciple of Ramananda, a teacher of devotion to Rama. He could not read or write but composed many couplets and songs in plain language, using images from daily life to convey deep truths. He mocked the caste prejudice and idolatry of Brahmins and the empty rituals of Muslim clerics alike, teaching that God dwells not in temple or mosque but in every heart, and that Rama and Allah are one. His verses were later included in the Sikh scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib, and his followers formed the Kabir Panth. Legend says that when he died Hindus and Muslims quarrelled over how to bury him, but when they lifted the shroud they found only a heap of flowers.

events.title: The Tower of Victory at Chittor
events.short: Rana Kumbha of Mewar built the nine-storey Tower of Victory in Chittor fort to celebrate his defeat of the sultan of Malwa, its walls covered with Hindu deities.
events.detail: Rana Kumbha, who reigned from 1433 to 1468, was the most outstanding fifteenth-century king of Mewar. He repeatedly defeated the sultans of Malwa and Gujarat and built more than thirty forts in his kingdom, among them Kumbhalgarh, whose walls run for about 36 kilometres and are called the Great Wall of India. To celebrate his victory over Sultan Mahmud Khalji of Malwa around 1440, he built the Vijaya Stambha, or Tower of Victory, in Chittor fort, completed in 1448. About 37 metres high in nine storeys of red sandstone and white marble, it has a spiral stair to the top and is carved inside and out with images of Vishnu and other Hindu gods. Kumbha was also a musician and scholar who wrote on the theory of music.

events.title: The Afghan Lodi Dynasty
events.short: The Afghan Bahlul Lodi took Delhi and founded the last dynasty of the Sultanate; his son Sikandar moved the capital to Agra.
events.detail: After Timur’s invasion Delhi was ruled by the Sayyid dynasty, whose power barely reached beyond the city. In 1451 Bahlul Lodi, an Afghan noble of the Punjab, replaced the Sayyids and founded the Lodi dynasty, the first Afghan dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate. He annexed the Jaunpur Sultanate to the east and restored some of the Sultanate’s power. His son Sikandar Lodi, who came to the throne in 1489, founded the city of Agra in 1504 and made it his capital; he encouraged agriculture and learning but was harsh towards Hindus. Lodi rule rested on Afghan tribal nobles and was riven by quarrels. The dynasty’s tombs still stand in Delhi’s Lodi Gardens. In 1526 the last sultan, Ibrahim Lodi, was defeated and killed at Panipat.

events.title: Afanasy Nikitin’s Journey to India
events.short: Afanasy Nikitin, a merchant from Tver in Russia, travelled through Persia to the Bahmani Sultanate and left one of the earliest European accounts of India.
events.detail: Afanasy Nikitin, a merchant of Tver in Russia, set out down the Volga in 1466 to trade. Robbed of his goods on the way, he travelled on through Persia, sailed from Hormuz and landed around 1469 at Chaul on India’s west coast, some thirty years before Vasco da Gama. He spent about three years in the Bahmani Sultanate, including its capital Bidar, and his Journey Beyond Three Seas describes the Deccan’s courts, armies, religions, goods and customs, contrasting the luxury of the nobles with the poverty of the peasants and recording his loneliness as a Christian far from home. He started home in 1472 but died before reaching Tver. A memorial to him now stands near Chaul, where he landed.

events.title: The Madrasa of Mahmud Gawan at Bidar
events.short: Mahmud Gawan, chief minister of the Bahmani Sultanate, built a grand Islamic college at Bidar with thousands of books that drew scholars from many lands.
events.detail: Mahmud Gawan, born in Persia, began as a merchant and served for more than twenty years as chief minister of the Bahmani Sultanate, reforming its administration and finances and leading campaigns that enlarged the kingdom. In 1472 he built a great college of higher Islamic learning at the capital Bidar. Three storeys high, its facade faced with coloured glazed tiles and flanked by tall minarets, it resembles the buildings of Samarkand in Central Asia. It had a library said to hold three thousand volumes, lecture halls and lodgings for scholars, and taught theology, philosophy, mathematics and medicine. In 1481 Mahmud Gawan fell victim to factional intrigue, was falsely accused of treason and executed, after which the dynasty declined rapidly. Half the building was destroyed by a gunpowder explosion in the seventeenth century.

events.title: Vasco da Gama Reaches Calicut
events.short: The Portuguese navigator Vasco da Gama rounded the Cape of Good Hope and reached Calicut, opening a direct sea route from Europe to India and bringing Europeans into the Indian Ocean.
events.detail: To bypass the Ottoman and Venetian grip on the spice trade, the Portuguese had spent decades searching for a route to India around Africa. In July 1497 Vasco da Gama sailed from Lisbon with four ships, rounded the Cape of Good Hope, hired a pilot who knew the Indian Ocean at Malindi in East Africa and in May 1498 reached Kappad beach near Calicut. The Zamorin of Calicut received him but was unimpressed by his meagre gifts, and the Arab merchants there were hostile to the Portuguese. Da Gama returned to Lisbon with pepper and spices worth many times the cost of the voyage. His route changed the pattern of world trade, and the Portuguese were followed to India by the Dutch, the English and the French.

events.title: Guru Nanak Founds Sikhism
events.short: Nanak of the Punjab declared that there is no Hindu and no Muslim, taught worship of the one God and the equality of all, and founded Sikhism.
events.detail: Nanak was born in 1469 at Talwandi, now Nankana Sahib, near Lahore in present-day Pakistan, the son of a Hindu accountant. Tradition says that around 1500, while bathing in the Bein river at Sultanpur, he disappeared for three days and returned declaring that there is no Hindu and no Muslim. For more than twenty years he travelled with the Muslim musician Mardana across India and to Sri Lanka, Tibet and Mecca, spreading his teaching in song: God is one and formless and is approached by meditating on the divine name, honest work and sharing with others; caste and idol worship are rejected. In later life he founded a community at Kartarpur with the langar, a common kitchen where all castes eat together. He was the first guru of the Sikhs.

events.title: Krishnadevaraya and the Height of Vijayanagara
events.short: Krishnadevaraya defeated the Deccan sultans and patronised Telugu literature, bringing the Vijayanagara Empire to its height.
events.detail: Krishnadevaraya of the Tuluva dynasty reigned from 1509 to 1529 and was Vijayanagara’s greatest king. He defeated the sultan of Bijapur and took Raichur, and conquered the Gajapati kingdom of Odisha on the east coast. A poet himself, he wrote the long Telugu poem Amuktamalyada, and his court was graced by eight Telugu poets known as the eight elephants. He built and enlarged magnificent temples in the capital such as the Vittala and Hazara Rama temples. The Portuguese traveller Domingo Paes, who visited at this time, called the city as large as Rome, its markets heaped with jewels, silk and grain, and the best provided city in the world.

events.title: The Portuguese Seize Goa
events.short: The Portuguese governor Afonso de Albuquerque took Goa from the sultan of Bijapur and made it the capital of Portuguese Asia, which it remained for 450 years.
events.detail: In 1510 Afonso de Albuquerque, governor of Portuguese India, backed by a local Hindu chief, twice attacked Goa, a port of the Bijapur Sultanate, finally taking it in November. From Goa he went on to seize Malacca and Hormuz, building a maritime empire that controlled the sea lanes of the Indian Ocean and required passing ships to buy Portuguese passes. Goa became the capital of Portuguese India, called the Rome of the East, and was filled with baroque churches; the Basilica of Bom Jesus holds the body of the Jesuit missionary Francis Xavier. The Portuguese promoted Catholicism and set up an Inquisition in 1560. India did not recover Goa until 1961.

events.title: Chaitanya and the Krishna Devotion
events.short: The Bengali saint Chaitanya praised Krishna through communal singing and dancing, founding the Gaudiya Vaishnava tradition from which the modern Hare Krishna movement descends.
events.detail: Chaitanya was born in 1486 at Nabadwip in Bengal and was a learned Sanskrit scholar until, around 1510, he renounced the world to devote himself to Krishna and Radha. He promoted sankirtan, the communal chanting of Krishna’s names with drums and dancing in the streets, as the simplest and surest spiritual practice for the present age, open to people of every caste and creed. In his later years he lived at Puri in Odisha, often falling into religious ecstasy before the Jagannath temple. His disciples restored holy places linked with Krishna’s legends at Vrindavan and wrote many theological works, forming the Gaudiya Vaishnava tradition. In 1966 one of its teachers, A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, founded the International Society for Krishna Consciousness in New York, carrying the tradition around the world.

events.title: The First Battle of Panipat
events.short: Babur, a descendant of Timur, used cannon and cavalry to defeat the Lodi sultan at Panipat and founded the Mughal Empire.
events.detail: Babur was descended from Timur on his father’s side and from Genghis Khan on his mother’s. A minor prince of Fergana in Central Asia, he failed in his struggle for Samarkand and took Kabul instead. Invited by opponents of the Lodi regime, he entered India with about twelve thousand men. On 21 April 1526 at Panipat, north of Delhi, he faced Sultan Ibrahim Lodi’s army of perhaps a hundred thousand with a thousand elephants. Babur lashed carts together with ropes into a barricade, placed cannon and matchlockmen in the gaps and sent his cavalry round both flanks. The roar of the guns stampeded the elephants, the Lodi army was routed and Ibrahim was killed. Babur then occupied Delhi and Agra and founded the Mughal Empire. It was the first time gunpowder weapons decided a battle in India.

events.title: The Battle of Khanwa
events.short: Babur defeated the Rajput confederacy led by Rana Sanga of Mewar at Khanwa, securing Mughal rule in northern India.
events.detail: After Panipat the most powerful opponent in northern India was Rana Sanga of Mewar, a veteran of many battles said to bear eighty scars and to have lost an eye and an arm. He gathered the Rajput kings and Afghan nobles into a great army to drive Babur out of India. In March 1527 the two sides met at Khanwa, west of Agra. Before the battle, with his men’s morale low, Babur publicly smashed his wine vessels, swore to give up drink and proclaimed a holy war to rally them. Using once again his barricade of carts, cannon and flanking cavalry, he routed the Rajputs; Rana Sanga escaped wounded and died soon after. The victory gave the Mughals a firm foothold in India.

events.title: The Baburnama
events.short: Babur wrote a frank and vivid memoir in Chagatai Turkic, recording his life and his observations of India’s landscape, animals and plants.
events.detail: Babur was a poet and writer as well as a general. In his native Chagatai Turkic he wrote a memoir covering his life from his accession to the throne of Fergana at the age of twelve until 1529, including his victories, defeats, friendships, drinking and feelings for his family, with rare candour. His descriptions of India are especially lively: he complained that it had no good horses, meat, grapes or melons, no cold water and no gardens, but he also recorded its animals, plants, monsoons and peoples in detail and marvelled at its wealth and its multitude of craftsmen. He laid out Persian-style gardens at Agra, where he died in 1530. His grandson Akbar had the memoir translated into Persian and richly illustrated with miniature paintings.

events.title: Sher Shah Defeats Humayun
events.short: The Afghan general Sher Shah defeated the Mughal emperor Humayun at Kannauj and founded the Sur dynasty; his silver rupee and Grand Trunk Road had a lasting legacy.
events.detail: After Babur’s son Humayun came to the throne, Sher Khan, an Afghan noble of Bihar, steadily rose to power. He defeated Humayun at Chausa in 1539 and again at Kannauj in 1540, forcing him into fifteen years of exile in Persia. Taking the name Sher Shah, he founded the Sur dynasty and reigned for only five years, yet left a lasting legacy. He had the land surveyed again and fixed taxes by yield; he issued a standard silver coin of about 11.5 grams called the rupiya, from which the rupee became India’s currency; and he restored and extended the great road from Bengal to the Punjab, planting trees, digging wells and building rest houses along it, the road later called the Grand Trunk Road. In 1545 he was killed by a gunpowder explosion while besieging the fort of Kalinjar.

events.title: The Second Battle of Panipat and Akbar’s Accession
events.short: Soon after the thirteen-year-old Akbar came to the throne, the Mughal army defeated Hemu, who had crowned himself king, at Panipat, saving the empire.
events.detail: In 1555 Humayun, with Persian help, recovered Delhi, but early the next year he fell to his death down the stairs of his library, and his thirteen-year-old son Akbar was enthroned in the Punjab under the regency of the general Bairam Khan. Meanwhile Hemu, a Hindu general of the Sur dynasty, had taken Agra and Delhi and crowned himself king as Vikramaditya. On 5 November 1556 the two armies met at Panipat. Hemu’s army and elephants were gaining the upper hand when an arrow struck him in the eye and he lost consciousness; his leaderless army broke and fled, and Hemu was captured and executed. The victory saved the Mughal dynasty, and Akbar went on to reign for nearly fifty years.

events.title: The Hamzanama and Mughal Painting
events.short: The Hamzanama commissioned by Akbar had 1,400 large paintings blending Persian and Indian styles, founding the art of Mughal miniature painting.
events.detail: During his exile in Persia Humayun met the Persian painters Mir Sayyid Ali and Abd al-Samad and brought them to India. Akbar set up a royal atelier under these two masters and gathered more than a hundred Indian painters. Its first great project was to illustrate the Hamzanama, the Persian popular romance of the hero Amir Hamza. It took about fifteen years and produced some 1,400 large paintings on cotton cloth, each about seventy centimetres high. They combine the refined composition of Persian painting with the bright colours and lively figures of Indian art, creating the distinctive Mughal style. Only about two hundred survive, scattered among museums in Vienna, London and elsewhere.

events.title: Humayun’s Tomb
events.short: Humayun’s widow built a magnificent tomb for him in Delhi, India’s first garden tomb and a forerunner of the Taj Mahal.
events.detail: Humayun’s tomb stands in south-eastern Delhi near the shrine of the Sufi saint Nizamuddin. It was commissioned by his widow Bega Begum, begun in 1565 and finished in 1572, and designed by the Persian architect Mirak Mirza Ghiyas. It stands on a high platform at the centre of a Persian charbagh garden divided into four by water channels, built of red sandstone inlaid with white marble and crowned by a double dome of marble. It was the first garden tomb in the subcontinent and the first building to combine red sandstone and white marble on such a scale, and its layout and proportions strongly influenced the Taj Mahal. Many members of the Mughal family are buried there, and it became a World Heritage Site in 1993.

events.title: The Battle of Talikota
events.short: The Deccan sultans combined to defeat Vijayanagara at Talikota, and the splendid capital was sacked and burned, never to recover.
events.detail: In the mid-sixteenth century Rama Raya, the real power in the Vijayanagara Empire, played the five Deccan sultanates against one another, backing one and then attacking another, until they bore him a grudge. In 1564 Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda and Bidar formed an alliance, and in January 1565 they fought the decisive battle with Vijayanagara at Talikota near the Krishna river. During the battle two Muslim commanders in the Vijayanagara army changed sides, the aged Rama Raya was captured and beheaded and his army fled. The allies then entered the capital and spent some six months plundering and burning it, reducing one of the great cities of the world to ruins. The site at Hampi became a World Heritage Site in 1986.

events.title: The Fort at Agra
events.short: Akbar rebuilt Agra Fort on the Yamuna with red sandstone walls about 2.5 kilometres long; Shah Jahan later remade its palaces in marble.
events.detail: Agra Fort was originally a brick fortress of the Lodis. In 1565 Akbar ordered it rebuilt in red sandstone, and the work, said to have employed four thousand labourers, was finished eight years later. The crescent-shaped fort follows the Yamuna, with walls about 21 metres high and some 2.5 kilometres around, a moat and massive gates. Akbar built palaces inside blending Indian and Islamic styles, of which the Jahangiri Mahal survives. In the seventeenth century Shah Jahan pulled down some of them and built white marble halls of public and private audience and the Pearl Mosque. In his old age Shah Jahan was imprisoned here by his son Aurangzeb, and he is said to have gazed at the distant Taj Mahal from the octagonal tower every day until his death in 1666. The fort became a World Heritage Site in 1983.

events.title: Fatehpur Sikri, the City of Victory
events.short: In gratitude to a Sufi saint who foretold the birth of his son, Akbar built a new capital at Sikri, Fatehpur Sikri, which was abandoned little more than a decade later.
events.detail: For years Akbar had no son. He walked to the village of Sikri west of Agra to visit Salim Chishti, a Sufi saint of the Chishti order, who foretold that he would have three sons. In 1569 his eldest, Salim, the future Jahangir, was born. In gratitude Akbar began building a new capital at Sikri in 1571, and after conquering Gujarat in 1573 he named it Fatehpur Sikri, the City of Victory. It had palaces, a great mosque, a treasury and a hall where Akbar held religious debates, in a style blending Hindu, Jain and Islamic architecture, and its towering Buland Darwaza, Gate of Magnificence, is about 54 metres high. Partly for lack of water, the capital was abandoned around 1585, which is why it survives so intact; it became a World Heritage Site in 1986.

events.title: Tulsidas and the Ramcharitmanas
events.short: The poet Tulsidas retold the story of Rama in the popular Awadhi language, creating the best-loved religious work of northern India.
events.detail: Tulsidas, born around 1532, was a poet and saint devoted to Rama who lived mostly in Varanasi and Ayodhya. In 1574 he began the Ramcharitmanas, the lake of the deeds of Rama, a long poem in Awadhi, a popular language of northern India. In seven books, it follows Valmiki’s Ramayana but places greater stress on loving devotion to Rama, portraying him as a compassionate god and as the ideal king, son and husband. Written in the language of ordinary people, it soon spread across the north, and every autumn the Ramlila plays based on it are staged throughout the region; at Ramnagar near Varanasi the performance lasts a month. His Hanuman Chalisa is a prayer that many Hindus recite every day.

events.title: The Battle of Haldighati
events.short: Maharana Pratap of Mewar refused to submit to Akbar and fought the Mughal army in the Haldighati pass; defeated, he kept up guerrilla resistance.
events.detail: Akbar won over most of the Rajput kingdoms through marriage alliances and high office, but Pratap Singh of Mewar refused to submit. On 18 June 1576 Pratap, with about three thousand horsemen, faced a large Mughal army under Man Singh of Amber in the Haldighati pass in the Aravalli hills. The Rajput cavalry charged fiercely but was finally defeated by the Mughals’ firearms and numbers. Legend says that Pratap’s horse Chetak, though badly wounded, carried his master across a stream to safety before collapsing and dying. Pratap withdrew into the hills and forests and waged a guerrilla war for twenty years, recovering most of Mewar. He became a symbol of the unbending Rajput spirit.

events.title: Todar Mal’s Revenue Reform
events.short: Akbar’s finance minister Todar Mal surveyed the land and fixed taxes on ten-year average yields, creating a revenue system that lasted for centuries.
events.detail: Todar Mal, a Hindu who had earlier served Sher Shah, became Akbar’s finance minister and is counted among the nine gems of his court. Around 1580 he introduced the zabt system of land revenue: land was measured with bamboo rods of standard length and classified by fertility, and the tax on each crop was calculated in cash from the average yields and prices of the previous ten years, amounting to about a third of the harvest. It was more stable and fairer than earlier methods and limited officials’ arbitrary exactions. It went together with the mansabdari system, which gave officials graded military ranks and salaries. Together they formed the financial foundation of the Mughal Empire, and the British East India Company later kept much of the system.

events.title: Akbar’s Tolerance and the Din-i Ilahi
events.short: Akbar gathered scholars of every religion to debate in his House of Worship, abolished the tax on non-Muslims and proposed the syncretic Din-i Ilahi.
events.detail: In Akbar’s empire Muslims were a minority, and he understood that he had to win Hindu support. In 1563 and 1564 he abolished the pilgrim tax on Hindus and the jizya on non-Muslims, married Rajput princesses and appointed Hindus to high office. In 1575 he built the Ibadat Khana, the House of Worship, at Fatehpur Sikri, at first for debates among Muslim scholars and later open to Hindus, Jains, Zoroastrians and Jesuits from Goa. Having compared the religions, he promoted the principle of sulh-i kul, universal peace, and around 1582 founded a circle of disciples devoted to one God and moral discipline, later called the Din-i Ilahi, Divine Faith. It attracted very few followers and vanished after his death.

events.title: The Harmandir Sahib at Amritsar
events.short: Guru Arjan, the fifth Sikh guru, built the Harmandir Sahib in the middle of the sacred pool at Amritsar; later covered in gold leaf, it is known as the Golden Temple.
events.detail: The city of Amritsar was founded by the fourth guru, Ram Das, who dug a sacred pool from which the city takes its name, the pool of nectar. The fifth guru, Arjan, built the Harmandir Sahib, the holiest gurdwara of the Sikhs, in the middle of the pool; by tradition he invited the Sufi saint Mian Mir of Lahore to lay its foundation stone in 1589. Unlike a Hindu temple, it has a door on each of its four sides, symbolising openness to people of every caste and religion, and it stands lower than the surrounding ground as a sign of humility. In 1604 Arjan installed the newly compiled scripture, the Adi Granth, there. In the early nineteenth century the Sikh ruler Ranjit Singh covered its upper storeys in gold leaf, and it has been called the Golden Temple ever since.

events.title: The Charminar of Hyderabad
events.short: The Qutb Shahi dynasty of Golconda founded the new city of Hyderabad and built the four-towered Charminar at its heart, the symbol of the city.
events.detail: Golconda was one of the five Deccan sultanates that emerged from the Bahmani kingdom and was famous for its diamonds; the Koh-i-Noor is said to have come from its mines. Because Golconda fort was crowded and short of water, Sultan Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah founded the new city of Hyderabad to the east on the Musi river. In 1591 he built the Charminar, four minarets, at its centre, reportedly to mark the end of a plague. The square building is about twenty metres on each side, with a minaret about 56 metres high at each corner and a small mosque on its top floor. Bustling bazaars grew up around it, and it remains the landmark of Hyderabad.

events.title: The English East India Company Is Founded
events.short: Elizabeth I granted a charter to London merchants for the East India Company, with a monopoly of trade east of the Cape of Good Hope; it later became the colonial ruler of India.
events.detail: In the late sixteenth century the Dutch broke the Portuguese monopoly of the spice trade, and English merchants were eager for a share. On 31 December 1600 Queen Elizabeth I granted a charter to the Governor and Company of Merchants of London Trading into the East Indies, more than two hundred London merchants, giving them a monopoly of English trade east of the Cape of Good Hope: this was the East India Company. The Dutch formed their own company two years later. The English company first traded in Southeast Asian spices, but squeezed out by the Dutch it turned to India; its ships first reached Surat in 1608, and in 1613 it won permission to open a factory there. Over the next two hundred and fifty years this trading company acquired armies and finally became the government of India.

events.title: Guru Arjan Compiles the Scripture and Is Martyred
events.short: Guru Arjan compiled the hymns of the gurus and saints into the Sikh scripture and in 1606 was executed on Jahangir’s orders, becoming the first Sikh martyr.
events.detail: Guru Arjan, the fifth Sikh guru, succeeded in 1581. He gathered the hymns of the first four gurus, added his own and those of saints such as Kabir and Namdev, Hindu and Muslim alike, and in 1604 compiled the Adi Granth, which later became the Guru Granth Sahib, the eternal guru of the Sikhs. He completed the Golden Temple at Amritsar and organised the faithful to give a tenth of their income, strengthening the community. After Akbar’s death in 1605, Arjan was accused of supporting Jahangir’s rebellious son Khusrau, arrested on Jahangir’s orders and in 1606 died under torture at Lahore. His martyrdom led the Sikh community to begin taking up arms.

events.title: Empress Nur Jahan
events.short: Jahangir married Nur Jahan, a noblewoman of Persian descent, who effectively ran the government and had her name struck on coins, the most powerful woman in Mughal history.
events.detail: Nur Jahan, born Mehr-un-Nissa into a Persian noble family that had settled in India, entered the court after the death of her first husband and in 1611 married the emperor Jahangir, who gave her the title Light of the World. As Jahangir grew dependent on drink, he left more and more state business to her. With her father and brother she formed a powerful family faction; she issued decrees and received foreign envoys, and coins were struck in her name as well as the emperor’s, unique in Mughal history. She was a skilled hunter, said to have killed a tiger with a single shot, and loved poetry, fashion and perfume; she built the exquisite tomb of her father, Itimad-ud-Daulah, known as the Baby Taj. Her niece Mumtaz Mahal became the wife of Shah Jahan.

events.title: Sir Thomas Roe at Jahangir’s Court
events.short: James I sent Sir Thomas Roe as ambassador to the Mughal court, where he won the East India Company the right to trade and keep factories at Surat and elsewhere.
events.detail: In 1612 East India Company ships defeated a Portuguese fleet in the battle of Swally near Surat, winning the Mughals’ respect. In 1615 King James I sent the diplomat Sir Thomas Roe to India as his official ambassador, and he followed Jahangir’s court around Ajmer, Mandu and elsewhere for nearly four years. Roe’s journal describes the splendour of the Mughal court, the emperor’s tastes and its ceremonies, and he found that the English gifts were nothing beside the court’s wealth. He eventually obtained an imperial order allowing the English to trade and live at Surat and other ports. He advised the company not to fight wars on land as the Portuguese had, but to concentrate on trade by sea.

events.title: The Shalimar Garden of Srinagar
events.short: Jahangir laid out the Shalimar garden by Dal Lake in Kashmir, whose terraces, channels and fountains show Mughal garden art at its finest.
events.detail: The Mughal emperors inherited the garden traditions of Persia and Central Asia and loved the charbagh, a garden divided into four by water channels. Jahangir was especially devoted to Kashmir; on his deathbed, it is said, his only wish was for Kashmir. In 1619 he laid out the Shalimar garden on the north-eastern shore of Dal Lake at Srinagar for Nur Jahan. It descends the hillside in three terraces; a stream brought down from the mountains runs along a stone channel on the central axis, falling from level to level in cascades and fountains, flanked by plane trees and flowers. The top terrace, reserved for the emperor and the ladies of the harem, has a pavilion of black marble. Shah Jahan later built a garden of the same name at Lahore, now a World Heritage Site.

events.title: The Taj Mahal
events.short: In memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal, Shah Jahan built the white marble Taj Mahal on the Yamuna at Agra, hailed as the jewel of India.
events.detail: In 1631 Shah Jahan’s beloved wife Mumtaz Mahal died giving birth to their fourteenth child. The grieving emperor began building her tomb on the Yamuna at Agra the following year; the mausoleum itself was finished around 1643 and the whole complex in 1653, employing, it is said, twenty thousand craftsmen and a thousand elephants, and its chief architect was probably Ustad Ahmad Lahauri. Built of white marble inlaid with flowers of precious stones and Quranic verses, it is crowned by a central dome about 73 metres high, with a minaret at each corner, and is fronted by a garden with a long reflecting pool. Shah Jahan was later buried beside his wife. The Taj Mahal became a World Heritage Site in 1983 and was named one of the New Seven Wonders of the World in 2007.

events.title: The Peacock Throne
events.short: Shah Jahan spent seven years making the Peacock Throne of gold and jewels, said to have cost twice as much as the Taj Mahal; it was later carried off by Nader Shah of Persia.
events.detail: Soon after his accession Shah Jahan ordered a new throne made from the gold and jewels of the imperial treasury. It took seven years and was first used at a celebration in 1635. Contemporary accounts describe it as made of solid gold, shaped like a canopied bed resting on twelve emerald-studded columns, with two peacocks on its canopy decorated with sapphires and other stones, and encrusted with diamonds, rubies, emeralds and pearls; the Koh-i-Noor is said to have been set in it. The French jeweller Jean-Baptiste Tavernier, who saw it, valued it at about a hundred million livres. In 1739 Nader Shah of Persia carried it off to Iran after sacking Delhi, and it was later broken up amid the turmoil there.

events.title: The Company Founds Madras
events.short: The East India Company acquired land on the Coromandel coast and built Fort St George, around which grew the city now called Chennai.
events.detail: To buy the fine cotton cloth of the Coromandel coast, the East India Company’s Francis Day and Andrew Cogan obtained a strip of beach from a local Nayaka chief in 1639, and by 1644 they had built Fort St George there, the first English fortress in India. Around it grew a White Town for Europeans and a Black Town for Indian weavers and merchants, and the settlement became the city of Madras, renamed Chennai in 1996. St Mary’s Church inside the fort, built in 1680, is the oldest Anglican church east of Suez. Madras later became the capital of one of the three presidencies of British India, and Fort St George still houses the legislature and government of Tamil Nadu.

events.title: The Red Fort and Shahjahanabad
events.short: Shah Jahan built his new capital Shahjahanabad and the Red Fort in Delhi; the fort later became a symbol of Indian independence, where the prime minister raises the flag each year.
events.detail: In 1639 Shah Jahan decided to move his capital from Agra back to Delhi and built a new city, Shahjahanabad, today’s Old Delhi, on the west bank of the Yamuna. At its heart stood a fortress of red sandstone, finished in 1648 and called the Red Fort after the colour of its walls. Inside were halls of public and private audience, royal baths, gardens and the harem; the hall of private audience bears the Persian verse: if there is a paradise on earth, it is this, it is this, it is this. Outside the fort ran the bustling Chandni Chowk and stood the Jama Masjid. After the failure of the 1857 uprising the British occupied the fort and demolished many of its buildings. On 15 August 1947 Nehru raised the Indian flag here, and every Independence Day since, the prime minister has spoken from the Red Fort.

events.title: Dara Shikoh and the Mingling of Two Oceans
events.short: Shah Jahan’s eldest son Dara Shikoh argued that Islam and Hinduism share the same essence and had fifty Upanishads translated into Persian.
events.detail: Dara Shikoh, Shah Jahan’s eldest son and chosen heir, was deeply influenced by Sufi mysticism. In 1655 he wrote Majma-ul-Bahrain, the Mingling of the Two Oceans, comparing concepts of Islamic Sufism with Hindu Vedanta and arguing that both seek the same single truth. In 1657, with the help of scholars from Varanasi, he translated fifty Upanishads into Persian under the title Sirr-i-Akbar, the Great Secret. This Persian version was later rendered into Latin by the French scholar Anquetil-Duperron, giving Europeans their first reading of the Upanishads; Schopenhauer called it the consolation of his life and of his death. But his ideas made him enemies among the orthodox, and in 1658 he lost the war of succession to his brother Aurangzeb and was executed for apostasy the following year.

events.title: The Gol Gumbaz of Bijapur
events.short: The Gol Gumbaz, tomb of Sultan Muhammad Adil Shah of Bijapur, has one of the largest domes in the world and a whispering gallery that carries a murmur across the hall.
events.detail: Bijapur in northern Karnataka was the capital of the Adil Shahi dynasty. Sultan Muhammad Adil Shah began building his own tomb during his lifetime, and it was completed on his death in 1656. It is a cube about 47 metres on each side, with a seven-storey octagonal tower at each corner, crowned by a vast hemispherical dome about 44 metres across with no internal supports, one of the largest domes in the world. Around its base runs a whispering gallery: a whisper or a handclap on one side can be heard clearly on the other and echoes seven or eight times. The sultan and his family are buried inside. Aurangzeb conquered Bijapur in 1686.

events.title: Aurangzeb Seizes the Throne
events.short: Aurangzeb defeated his brothers in a war of succession, imprisoned his father Shah Jahan and took the throne; the empire reached its greatest size under him but also sowed the seeds of decline.
events.detail: In 1657 Shah Jahan fell gravely ill, and his four sons, Dara Shikoh, Shuja, Aurangzeb and Murad, fought for the throne. Aurangzeb joined forces with Murad, defeated Dara at Samugarh in 1658, occupied Agra and confined his father in Agra Fort; he then got rid of Murad and eliminated Dara and Shuja in turn. He reigned for forty-nine years, lived austerely and was a devout Muslim; in 1679 he reimposed the jizya on non-Muslims, banned music at court and destroyed some Hindu temples. In his later years he devoted himself to conquering the Deccan, annexing Bijapur and Golconda and bringing the empire to its greatest extent, but the endless wars drained its strength and provoked resistance from the Marathas, Sikhs and Rajputs.

events.title: Shivaji Defeats Afzal Khan at Pratapgarh
events.short: The Maratha leader Shivaji killed the Bijapur general Afzal Khan with steel tiger claws during a parley and then routed his army in the forested hills.
events.detail: Shivaji was born in 1630 into a Maratha noble family in Maharashtra and as a young man began seizing hill forts of the Bijapur Sultanate in the Western Ghats. In 1659 Bijapur sent its general Afzal Khan with a large army against him. Shivaji withdrew to the hill fort of Pratapgarh and proposed a private meeting. When they met on 10 November, according to Maratha accounts, the towering Afzal Khan tried to stab Shivaji with a dagger as he embraced him, but Shivaji, wearing armour beneath his clothes and steel tiger claws on his hand, killed him instead. Maratha soldiers hidden in the forests then fell on the leaderless Bijapur army and won a complete victory. The episode made Shivaji famous and became a celebrated tale of Maratha heroism.

events.title: Bombay Passes to the Company
events.short: A Portuguese princess brought the islands of Bombay to Charles II as dowry, and in 1668 the king leased them to the East India Company; Bombay grew into a great port.
events.detail: Bombay was originally seven small islands on the Arabian Sea, taken by the Portuguese from the sultan of Gujarat in the sixteenth century. In 1661 the Portuguese princess Catherine of Braganza married King Charles II of England, and Bombay passed to England as part of her dowry. Finding the islands hard to manage, Charles leased them in 1668 to the East India Company for a token rent of ten pounds a year. The company governor Gerald Aungier built fortifications and courts and attracted Parsis, Gujarati merchants and craftsmen to settle by promising religious freedom. In 1687 the company moved its west-coast headquarters from Surat to Bombay. From the eighteenth century the islands were joined by land reclamation, and Bombay grew into India’s largest port and commercial city.

events.title: The Battle of Saraighat
events.short: Lachit Borphukan, general of the Ahom kingdom of Assam, defeated a Mughal fleet on the Brahmaputra, preserving the independence of the north-east.
events.detail: The Ahom kingdom was founded in the thirteenth century by Tai chiefs from what is now northern Myanmar and ruled the Brahmaputra valley for nearly six hundred years. In the seventeenth century the Mughals repeatedly invaded Assam and for a time held Guwahati. In 1671 Aurangzeb sent Raja Ram Singh of Amber with a large army and fleet to attack again. The Ahom general Lachit Borphukan used the narrows of the Brahmaputra at Saraighat, building earthworks and fighting the Mughal fleet with nimble small boats. He is said to have been gravely ill at the decisive battle yet insisted on directing it from a boat, and the Mughals were driven back. Assam was never absorbed into the Mughal Empire. Today the Lachit Borphukan Gold Medal is awarded each year to the best cadet of India’s National Defence Academy.

events.title: Shivaji Is Crowned
events.short: Shivaji was crowned Chhatrapati at the hill fort of Raigad, formally founding the Maratha kingdom and laying the foundations of the later Maratha ascendancy.
events.detail: Shivaji built a base in the Western Ghats centred on hill forts, from which he outmanoeuvred Bijapur and the Mughal Empire. In 1664 he raided Surat, the Mughals’ richest port. In 1666 he was lured to Agra and placed under house arrest by Aurangzeb, but escaped, reportedly hidden in a basket of sweets. On 6 June 1674 he was crowned at Raigad fort with ancient Vedic rites, taking the title Chhatrapati, lord of the parasol, and proclaiming the independence of the Maratha kingdom. He set up a council of eight ministers, built a navy, introduced revenue assessments based on actual harvests, and used Marathi and Sanskrit at court. Shivaji died in 1680, but the resistance he kindled eventually mired the Mughal Empire in the Deccan.

events.title: The French Found Pondicherry
events.short: The French East India Company founded Pondicherry on the Coromandel coast, which became the capital of French India until its transfer to India in 1954.
events.detail: The French East India Company was founded in 1664, well after its English and Dutch rivals. In 1674 the company official François Martin obtained a small village on the Coromandel coast from a local governor of the Bijapur Sultanate and began building a trading post there: this was Pondicherry. The town was later occupied by the Dutch and returned to France in 1699, growing into the capital of French India, laid out on a grid that still preserves its French streets and buildings. In the mid-eighteenth century Governor Dupleix used Pondicherry as his base in the struggle with the British for southern India. In 1954 Pondicherry, Karaikal and the other French settlements were transferred to India, and they now form a union territory.

events.title: The Martyrdom of Guru Tegh Bahadur
events.short: The ninth Sikh guru, Tegh Bahadur, spoke up for the religious freedom of Kashmiri Brahmins and was beheaded in Delhi on Aurangzeb’s orders.
events.detail: Tegh Bahadur, son of the sixth guru Hargobind, became the ninth Sikh guru in 1664. According to Sikh tradition, Brahmins from Kashmir who were under pressure to convert came to ask for his help, and he resolved to go to Delhi himself to plead their cause, declaring that if the emperor could convert him, the others would follow. In 1675 he was arrested in Delhi; refusing either to convert to Islam or to perform a miracle, he was publicly beheaded, and several of his disciples were tortured to death. Sikhs honour him as Hind di Chadar, the shield of India, because he gave his life for the freedom of people of another faith. The place of his martyrdom is now the Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib in Delhi’s Chandni Chowk.

events.title: Sambhaji’s Death and the Twenty-Seven Years’ War
events.short: Shivaji’s son Sambhaji was captured and executed by the Mughals, but the Marathas fought on in scattered bands, and Aurangzeb struggled in the Deccan until his death without victory.
events.detail: In 1681 Aurangzeb himself marched south into the Deccan with his huge court and army and never returned to the north. He conquered Bijapur and Golconda and then turned his full strength on the Marathas. In 1689 Shivaji’s son, the Maratha king Sambhaji, was captured by Mughal troops in the Konkan; refusing to surrender or convert, he was tortured and put to death. But the Marathas did not give in. Sambhaji’s brother Rajaram escaped south to Gingee, and after his death his widow Tarabai led the resistance. The Marathas broke into many mobile cavalry bands that raided Mughal supply lines and towns, and the war dragged on for twenty-seven years, draining the Mughal Empire of money and men in the Deccan.

events.title: Job Charnock Founds Calcutta
events.short: The Company agent Job Charnock set up a trading post at the village of Sutanuti on the Hooghly, which grew into Calcutta, the capital of British India.
events.detail: In the late seventeenth century the East India Company’s trade in Bengal was dogged by conflict with Mughal officials, and in 1686–90 it even fought a war with the Mughal Empire, Child’s War, which the English lost and had to sue for peace. On 24 August 1690 the Company agent Job Charnock was allowed to return to Bengal and landed at the village of Sutanuti on the east bank of the Hooghly to set up a trading post. In 1698 the Company bought the zamindari rights to three villages, Sutanuti, Gobindapur and Kalikata, and built Fort William. Calcutta grew rapidly and in 1772 became the capital of British India, remaining so until the capital moved to Delhi in 1911. Today it is the capital of West Bengal, officially renamed Kolkata in 2001.

events.title: Guru Gobind Singh Creates the Khalsa
events.short: The tenth guru, Gobind Singh, created the Khalsa order at Anandpur and required Sikhs to wear the five Ks, giving the Sikhs their distinctive identity.
events.detail: Gobind Singh was the son of Guru Tegh Bahadur and became the tenth guru at the age of nine after his father’s martyrdom. At the Baisakhi festival of 1699 he gathered his followers at Anandpur, drew his sword and called for those ready to die for their faith. One after another five men came forward, of different castes and regions, and became known as the Panj Pyare, the five beloved. The guru initiated them with sweetened water stirred with a sword, founding the Khalsa, the order of the pure, and then asked them to initiate him in turn. Initiated men took the name Singh, lion, and women Kaur, princess, and all were to wear the five Ks: uncut hair, a wooden comb, a steel bracelet, short breeches and a short sword. Before his death in 1708 he declared that there would be no more human gurus; the scripture would be the guru.

events.title: Aurangzeb Dies and the Empire Declines
events.short: Aurangzeb died in the Deccan and was buried in a simple grave; endless succession struggles followed, and the Mughal Empire declined rapidly as provinces broke away.
events.detail: On 3 March 1707 Aurangzeb died at Ahmednagar in the Deccan at the age of eighty-eight. As he wished, he was buried in a plain open-air grave at Khuldabad, paid for, it is said, with money he had earned by sewing caps. His three sons fought for the throne; the eldest, Bahadur Shah I, won but died five years later, and over the next twelve years six emperors sat on the throne of Delhi while real power passed to ambitious ministers. Provincial governors such as the Nizam of Hyderabad and the nawabs of Bengal and Awadh became effectively independent while still nominally acknowledging the emperor. The Marathas, Sikhs, Jats and Rajputs rose up, and the Mughal Empire shrank to a small area around Delhi.

events.title: The Rising of Banda Singh Bahadur
events.short: Banda Singh Bahadur, a follower of Gobind Singh, led a Sikh peasant uprising, captured Sirhind and established the first Sikh state.
events.detail: Banda Singh Bahadur, originally an ascetic, met Guru Gobind Singh in the Deccan in 1708, became a Sikh and was sent back to the Punjab to lead the Sikhs against Mughal rule. He raised a large following of peasants and in 1710 captured Sirhind, killing its governor Wazir Khan, who had ordered the execution of Gobind Singh’s two young sons. He set up a Sikh government at Lohgarh, struck coins in the name of the gurus and abolished the zamindari system, giving land to those who tilled it. The Mughal court sent large armies against him, and in 1715 Banda was captured at Gurdas Nangal; the following year he was executed in Delhi together with hundreds of his followers. His rising laid the groundwork for the later rise of the Sikhs.

events.title: The Rise of the Nawabs of Bengal
events.short: Murshid Quli Khan became governor of Bengal and moved its capital to Murshidabad; under its nawabs Bengal became effectively independent and the richest province of India.
events.detail: Murshid Quli Khan was a revenue official appointed by Aurangzeb in Bengal and was famed for his financial skill; he reorganised the collection of land revenue and sent large sums to Delhi every year, winning the emperor’s confidence. He moved the capital of Bengal from Dhaka to a town on the Ganges that he named Murshidabad after himself. In 1717 the emperor Farrukhsiyar formally appointed him governor of Bengal, and he became the first Nawab of Bengal, a hereditary post; though nominally loyal to Delhi, he was in practice independent. Under his rule Bengal’s textile industry and silk trade flourished, the European East India companies all kept factories there, and Bengal became the richest region of India.

events.title: The Peshwa Baji Rao I
events.short: The Maratha prime minister Baji Rao I led his cavalry on campaigns across India without ever losing a battle, extending Maratha power from the Deccan into the north.
events.detail: When Shivaji’s grandson Shahu was released and returned to Maharashtra, he appointed the Brahmin Balaji Vishwanath as Peshwa, or chief minister; the office became hereditary and held real power in the Maratha state. In 1720 Balaji’s son Baji Rao I became Peshwa at the age of twenty. A brilliant cavalry commander, he fought more than forty battles in twenty years and is said never to have lost one. In 1728 he defeated the Nizam of Hyderabad at Palkhed, then marched north to take Malwa and Bundelkhand, and in 1737 he even raided to the gates of Delhi. Under his leadership the Marathas built a vast power centred on Pune, and the families of Maratha generals such as the Scindias, Holkars and Gaekwads rose to prominence.

events.title: The Nizams of Hyderabad
events.short: The Mughal minister Asaf Jah I made himself independent in the Deccan, founding the Nizam dynasty of Hyderabad, later the largest and richest princely state in India.
events.detail: Chin Qilich Khan, a noble who had served Aurangzeb, received the title Nizam-ul-Mulk, administrator of the realm, in 1713 and became governor of the Deccan. In 1722 he briefly served as wazir of the Mughal Empire but, disillusioned by the corruption of the court, returned to the Deccan in 1724 and defeated the governor sent by the emperor at the battle of Shakar Kheda. From then on he ruled the Deccan independently; known to posterity as Asaf Jah I, he founded the Nizam dynasty centred on Hyderabad. The dynasty lasted until 1948, and Hyderabad became the largest and richest princely state of British India; the last Nizam, Mir Osman Ali Khan, was once called the richest man in the world.

events.title: Jai Singh II’s Observatories
events.short: King Jai Singh II of Amber built giant masonry astronomical instruments in five cities including Delhi and Jaipur; the Jaipur sundial is 27 metres tall.
events.detail: Sawai Jai Singh II, the Rajput king of Amber, later Jaipur, was a keen astronomer. Finding small brass instruments too imprecise, from 1724 he built five large observatories of stone and plaster, known as Jantar Mantar, at Delhi, Jaipur, Ujjain, Varanasi and Mathura. The largest, at Jaipur, has nineteen instruments; its Samrat Yantra sundial is about 27 metres high, and its shadow moves about six centimetres a minute across the dial, telling the time to within two seconds. He also had Arabic and European astronomical tables collected and compiled new star tables. The Jaipur observatory became a World Heritage Site in 2010.

events.title: The Founding of Jaipur
events.short: Jai Singh II laid out his new capital Jaipur according to the principles of traditional Indian architecture, with a grid of streets later painted pink.
events.detail: As the population grew and water ran short, Jai Singh II decided to move his capital from Amber in the hills down to the plain. In 1727 he began building a new city, named Jaipur after himself. It was designed by the Bengali architect Vidyadhar Bhattacharya on the principles of the traditional Indian science of architecture, divided into nine blocks symbolising the nine planets, with broad main streets crossing at right angles, quarters assigned by trade and caste, and walls and gates all round. In 1876, to welcome the visiting Prince of Wales, the whole city was painted a terracotta pink, and it has been called the Pink City ever since. Its Hawa Mahal, Palace of Winds, has 953 small windows through which the women of the court could watch the street. The walled city became a World Heritage Site in 2019.

events.title: Nader Shah Sacks Delhi
events.short: Nader Shah of Persia defeated the Mughals at Karnal, sacked Delhi and carried off the Peacock Throne and the Koh-i-Noor diamond, shattering the empire’s prestige.
events.detail: Nader Shah, founder of Persia’s Afsharid dynasty, was a famous soldier. In February 1739 he crossed the Khyber Pass, defeated the army of the emperor Muhammad Shah at Karnal north of Delhi and entered the capital. When rumours spread that he had been killed, townspeople attacked Persian soldiers, and Nader Shah ordered a massacre in which some twenty to thirty thousand people died in a single day. He stayed in Delhi for two months and carried off treasure of incalculable value, including the Peacock Throne and the Koh-i-Noor diamond, to which he is said to have given its name, Mountain of Light. So great was the loot that on returning home he remitted Persia’s taxes for three years. The sack left the Mughal Empire an empty shell and revealed its weakness to the Europeans.

events.title: The Battle of Colachel
events.short: King Marthanda Varma of Travancore defeated the Dutch East India Company at Colachel, one of the first major defeats of a European force by an Asian state.
events.detail: Marthanda Varma became king of Travancore in southern Kerala in 1729. He united the surrounding petty kingdoms by force and sought control of the lucrative pepper trade, bringing him into conflict with the Dutch East India Company. In 1741 the Dutch landed troops from Ceylon at Colachel. Travancore’s army surrounded them and on 10 August launched a general assault, defeating the Dutch and capturing some two dozen of their officers. One of them, the Fleming Eustachius De Lannoy, entered Travancore’s service, trained its army on European lines and built its forts, rising to command its forces. After this defeat Dutch power in India declined. In 1750 Marthanda Varma dedicated his kingdom to its patron deity Padmanabha and ruled as the god’s servant.

events.title: The Carnatic Wars
events.short: The British and French East India companies fought three wars in the Carnatic of southern India, backing rival claimants to local thrones, until the British gained the upper hand.
events.detail: In the mid-eighteenth century the European wars of the Austrian Succession and the Seven Years’ War spread to India. In 1746 the French under Dupleix, governor of Pondicherry, captured British Madras. Dupleix realised that a small force of well-trained European soldiers and Indian sepoys could decide local succession struggles, and he intervened in the disputes over the thrones of the Nawab of the Carnatic and the Nizam of Hyderabad, installing pro-French rulers. The British soon did the same, backing the rival claimants, and the two sides fought three Carnatic Wars. In 1760 the British defeated the French at Wandiwash and in 1761 took Pondicherry, after which French power in India never recovered. From these wars the British learned how to meddle in Indian politics and build armies of Indian sepoys.

events.title: The Invasions of Ahmad Shah Durrani
events.short: Ahmad Shah Durrani, founder of the Afghan kingdom, invaded northern India eight times, seized the Punjab and sacked Delhi and Mathura.
events.detail: Ahmad Shah had been an Afghan cavalry commander under Nader Shah. After Nader Shah’s assassination in 1747 he was chosen king at Kandahar and founded the Durrani Empire, and he is regarded as the founder of modern Afghanistan. Between 1748 and 1767 he invaded India eight times, seizing the Punjab, Kashmir and Sindh. In 1757 he sacked Delhi and Mathura, massacring many pilgrims at Mathura and Vrindavan, and in 1761 he defeated the Marathas at the Third Battle of Panipat. He also fought the Sikhs of the Punjab repeatedly and in 1762 blew up the Golden Temple at Amritsar. But the Sikhs retook the Punjab again and again, and Durrani was never able to establish lasting rule in India.

events.title: Mir and the Rise of Urdu Poetry
events.short: Mir Taqi Mir of Delhi wrote hundreds of poignant ghazals in Urdu and is revered as a master of Urdu poetry.
events.detail: Urdu grew from the spoken language of the Delhi region, enriched with many Persian and Arabic words and written in the Perso-Arabic script. Early in the eighteenth century the Deccani poet Wali came to Delhi, and his Urdu verse caused a sensation; thereafter the poets of Delhi gradually turned from Persian to Urdu. Mir Taqi Mir, born around 1723, lived through the sacks of Delhi by Nader Shah and Durrani and moved to Lucknow in later life. His collections contain some two thousand ghazals in plain language, full of love, loss and the transience of the world, deeply expressing the melancholy of the Mughal twilight. The later great poet Ghalib held him in the highest esteem.

events.title: Bani Thani and the Kishangarh School
events.short: Painters of Kishangarh in Rajasthan portrayed Radha with elongated eyes and an elegant profile; their Bani Thani is called the Mona Lisa of India.
events.detail: As the Mughal Empire declined, many court painters moved to the small kingdoms of Rajasthan and the Himalayan foothills, giving rise to the rich Rajput and Pahari schools of painting. Kishangarh was a small Rajasthani kingdom whose king, Sawant Singh, was a poet who fell in love with Bani Thani, a singer at court. The court painter Nihal Chand used her as his model for Radha, Krishna’s beloved, with arched brows, long upturned lotus-shaped eyes and a pointed chin, creating the distinctive Kishangarh style. This profile portrait, painted around 1750, is called the Mona Lisa of India and appeared on an Indian postage stamp in 1973.

events.title: Clive’s Defence of Arcot
events.short: Robert Clive, a young Company clerk, seized Arcot with a few hundred men and held it for fifty days, turning the tide of the Second Carnatic War.
events.detail: Robert Clive began as a junior clerk of the East India Company at Madras and later took up soldiering. In 1751 the French-backed Chanda Sahib was besieging Tiruchirappalli, held by the British-backed Muhammad Ali. To relieve the pressure, the 26-year-old Clive, with about two hundred European and three hundred Indian soldiers, made a surprise attack on Chanda Sahib’s capital Arcot and held it for about fifty days against thousands of besiegers. Chanda Sahib had to divide his forces, and the British eventually turned the war around. The victory made Clive famous and convinced the British that small, well-drilled forces could win decisive victories in India. Clive went on to win the Battle of Plassey.

events.title: Siraj ud-Daulah Takes Calcutta
events.short: Angered by British fortifications, the Nawab of Bengal, Siraj ud-Daulah, captured Calcutta; many British prisoners died in the cell known as the Black Hole.
events.detail: In 1756 the young Siraj ud-Daulah became Nawab of Bengal. The East India Company had strengthened Fort William at Calcutta without permission, abused its tax-free trading privileges and sheltered his political enemies, and when his warnings went unheeded he marched on Calcutta and took it in June. According to the later account of the prisoner John Zephaniah Holwell, on the night of 20 June 146 British captives were shut in a small guardroom cell in the fort, and only twenty-three came out alive the next morning: the Black Hole of Calcutta. Modern historians think Holwell exaggerated the numbers and that perhaps only a few dozen were confined. But the episode caused outrage in Britain and became the justification for a punitive expedition.

events.title: The Battle of Plassey
events.short: Clive bribed the Nawab’s general Mir Jafar and defeated Siraj at Plassey; the East India Company gained control of Bengal, and British rule in India began.
events.detail: Early in 1757 Clive sailed north from Madras and recaptured Calcutta. He then made a secret agreement with Siraj’s general Mir Jafar and the great Bengali banker Jagat Seth to make Mir Jafar nawab. On 23 June, with about three thousand men, Clive faced Siraj’s army of some fifty thousand at Plassey on the Bhagirathi, a branch of the Ganges. A downpour soaked the nawab’s gunpowder while the British had covered theirs, and most of the troops under Mir Jafar stood by without fighting, so the nawab’s army soon broke. Siraj fled and was killed, and Mir Jafar became a puppet nawab who paid the Company enormous sums. This small battle marked the beginning of British rule in India.

events.title: The Battle of Wandiwash
events.short: The British defeated the French at Wandiwash and took Pondicherry the next year, ending France’s bid for supremacy in India.
events.detail: During the Seven Years’ War Britain and France fought again in India. France sent the Comte de Lally with an army to regain the upper hand; he took Fort St David but failed to capture Madras. On 22 January 1760 the British general Eyre Coote met Lally’s army at Wandiwash in Tamil Nadu and won a decisive victory, capturing the French commander Bussy. The British then besieged Pondicherry, which surrendered in January 1761, and razed its walls. The Treaty of Paris of 1763 returned Pondicherry and other trading posts to France but barred it from keeping troops or fortifications in India. France was left with only a few small settlements, and Britain became the only European power contending for India.

events.title: The Third Battle of Panipat
events.short: Ahmad Shah Durrani crushed the Maratha army at Panipat, where tens of thousands died, halting the Marathas’ bid to dominate northern India.
events.detail: By the mid-eighteenth century Maratha power had spread to the Punjab and Delhi, bringing it into conflict with Ahmad Shah Durrani of Afghanistan. In 1760 the Peshwa sent his cousin Sadashivrao Bhau north with a great army, while the Afghans won the support of the Rohillas and the Nawab of Awadh. The two armies faced each other at Panipat for more than two months until the Maratha camp ran out of food. On 14 January 1761 the Marathas were forced to attack; their artillery at first had the advantage, but they collapsed under the counter-attack of Afghan cavalry and camel-mounted swivel guns. Sadashivrao Bhau and the Peshwa’s eldest son Vishwasrao were killed, and by some estimates as many as a hundred thousand died in the battle and the slaughter that followed. The disaster weakened the Marathas and left room for British expansion.

events.title: Buxar and the Diwani of Bengal
events.short: The Company defeated the combined forces of the Mughal emperor and the nawabs of Bengal and Awadh at Buxar and won the right to collect revenue in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa.
events.detail: After Plassey the Company’s nawab Mir Qasim tried to free himself from its control and went to war with it. He allied with Shuja-ud-Daulah, Nawab of Awadh, and the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II. On 22 October 1764 a Company army under Hector Munro defeated the allies at Buxar in Bihar. In 1765 Clive, back in India, concluded the Treaty of Allahabad with Shah Alam II, under which the emperor granted the Company the diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, the right to collect their land revenue. A British trading company thus became the real ruler of India’s richest region, able to use local taxes to buy goods for export and to pay for its armies.

events.title: The Bengal Famine of 1770
events.short: Drought and the Company’s heavy taxes caused a great famine in Bengal that killed perhaps a third of the population, exposing the harshness of Company rule.
events.detail: In 1768 and 1769 the monsoon failed badly in Bengal and Bihar and the rice harvests were lost. Yet the East India Company and its revenue collectors, who now held the diwani, did not reduce the land tax and in some places even raised it, while some Company servants and merchants hoarded grain for profit. The famine peaked in 1770, with the dead lying in the fields; Company officials at the time estimated that some ten million people died in Bengal, about a third of the population. Much farmland went out of cultivation, and the Company’s revenues fell for years afterwards. News of the famine caused an outcry in Britain and helped push Parliament to pass the Regulating Act of 1773, the first step towards supervising the Company’s rule in India.
