events.title: Warren Hastings Becomes the First Governor-General
events.short: Parliament’s Regulating Act created a governor-general of Bengal over the presidencies; Warren Hastings became the first, and was later impeached in a trial lasting seven years.
events.detail: In 1773 Parliament passed the Regulating Act, which placed the presidencies of Madras and Bombay under the governor of Bengal and set up a supreme court in Calcutta, the start of British government supervision of the East India Company. Warren Hastings became the first governor-general, serving from 1774 to 1785. He made Calcutta the capital, reorganised revenue and justice and sponsored the study of India’s classical languages and texts, supporting William Jones in founding the Asiatic Society. But his wars against the Marathas and Mysore cost vast sums, and he extorted money from the Begums of Awadh and the Raja of Benares. On his return he was impeached by Parliament on charges of corruption and tyranny led by Edmund Burke; the trial lasted seven years, and he was acquitted only in 1795.

events.title: Hyder Ali and the Anglo-Mysore Wars
events.short: Hyder Ali, ruler of Mysore, built a modern army and in the Second Anglo-Mysore War came close to the gates of Madras, Britain’s most formidable opponent in the south.
events.detail: Hyder Ali came from a soldier’s family and rose as a commander under the Wodeyar kings of Mysore, taking real power in the kingdom in 1761. He had his troops trained by the French and introduced artillery and rockets, building a disciplined army with which he expanded on every side. In the First Anglo-Mysore War of 1767–69 he advanced to the outskirts of Madras and forced the British to accept a peace on his terms. In 1780, allied with the Marathas and the Nizam, he launched the Second Anglo-Mysore War, destroyed a British force at Pollilur and ravaged the Carnatic, putting Madras in danger. He died in 1782 in the midst of the war, and his son Tipu Sultan fought on.

events.title: William Jones Founds the Asiatic Society
events.short: The philologist William Jones founded the Asiatic Society in Calcutta and argued that Sanskrit shares a common origin with Greek and Latin, founding modern comparative linguistics.
events.detail: William Jones was an English jurist and philologist who knew more than a dozen languages and became a judge of the Supreme Court in Calcutta in 1783. On 15 January 1784 he founded the Asiatic Society in Calcutta to study the history, literature, science and arts of Asia. In his anniversary discourse of 1786 he declared that Sanskrit was of a wonderful structure, more perfect than Greek and more copious than Latin, and that its resemblance to both in verbal roots and grammatical forms was too strong to be accidental: all three must have sprung from some common source which perhaps no longer exists. This insight laid the foundation of the theory of the Indo-European language family. Jones also translated Shakuntala and the Laws of Manu. The Asiatic Society awakened European interest in ancient Indian civilisation and helped Indians rediscover their own history.

events.title: The Permanent Settlement of Bengal
events.short: Governor-General Cornwallis fixed the land revenue of Bengal permanently and recognised the zamindars as landowners, while the peasants suffered heavier exploitation.
events.detail: Cornwallis, who had surrendered the British army in the American War of Independence, became governor-general of India in 1786. To guarantee the Company a steady income and to create, on the British model, a class of landlords loyal to Britain, in 1793 he introduced the Permanent Settlement: the zamindars of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, until then revenue collectors, were recognised as owners of the land, and the revenue each paid the Company was fixed for ever. If they failed to pay on time, their estates were auctioned. Many old landed families were ruined by arrears, and merchants and moneylenders of Calcutta bought up large estates as absentee landlords, while the peasants who worked the land lost their customary rights and were left exposed to rack-renting and eviction.

events.title: The Death of Tipu Sultan, Tiger of Mysore
events.short: Tipu Sultan of Mysore resisted the British stubbornly and died fighting when his capital Seringapatam fell, leaving the British masters of southern India.
events.detail: Tipu Sultan, son of Hyder Ali, succeeded in 1782 and was known as the Tiger of Mysore. He reformed the calendar, coinage and weights and measures, promoted silk-making and used iron-cased rockets in battle on a large scale, rockets that later inspired Britain’s Congreve rockets. He allied with France and even sent envoys to France and the Ottoman Empire seeking help. After the Third Anglo-Mysore War he was forced to cede half his territory. In 1799 Governor-General Wellesley, accusing him of intriguing with Napoleon, launched the Fourth War; British troops besieged his capital Seringapatam and on 4 May breached its walls, and Tipu died fighting near a gate. The British restored the Wodeyars as vassals, and his famous mechanical toy, Tipu’s Tiger, is now in the Victoria and Albert Museum in London.

events.title: Ranjit Singh Founds the Sikh Empire
events.short: At nineteen Ranjit Singh captured Lahore and united the Sikh confederacies of the Punjab into a powerful Sikh Empire; he was called the Lion of the Punjab.
events.detail: In the late eighteenth century the Sikhs of the Punjab were divided into twelve armed confederacies called misls. Ranjit Singh was born into the ruling family of one of them and lost an eye to smallpox as a child. In 1799, at nineteen, he captured Lahore, and in 1801 he proclaimed himself Maharaja of the Punjab. He went on to unite the misls and took Multan, Kashmir and Peshawar from the Afghans, building a Sikh Empire from the Khyber Pass to the Sutlej. He hired French and Italian officers to train his army, creating one of the finest armies in Asia. He appointed officials regardless of religion, covered the Golden Temple in gold and acquired the Koh-i-Noor. In 1809 he signed a treaty with the British fixing the Sutlej as the boundary. After his death in 1839 the empire quickly fell into turmoil.

events.title: The Great Trigonometrical Survey
events.short: Starting from Madras, the British mapped the whole subcontinent by triangulation over seventy years and measured the height of Everest, the world’s highest peak.
events.detail: In 1802 the British surveyor William Lambton measured the first baseline near Madras, beginning the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India. Using theodolites weighing half a tonne, the survey teams built chains of triangles northwards along the meridian from Cape Comorin to the Himalayas over several decades, and many died of malaria and accidents. Lambton’s successor George Everest completed the measurement of the Great Arc of the meridian, determining the shape of the earth with new precision. In 1852 the Bengali mathematician Radhanath Sikdar calculated from the observations that Peak XV was the highest mountain in the world; its height was announced in 1856 as 29,002 feet, about 8,840 metres, and it was named after Everest. In Chinese it is called Qomolangma.

events.title: Assaye and the Second Anglo-Maratha War
events.short: Arthur Wellesley, the future Duke of Wellington, defeated the Marathas at Assaye, and the British occupied Delhi, taking the Mughal emperor under their protection.
events.detail: At the end of the eighteenth century the great families of the Maratha confederacy, such as the Scindias and Holkars, fought among themselves, and the Peshwa Baji Rao II fled to the British, accepting their protection by the Treaty of Bassein in 1802. Scindia and the Bhonsle of Berar refused to accept it, and the Second Anglo-Maratha War broke out. On 23 September 1803 Arthur Wellesley, the governor-general’s brother, with about 9,500 men, defeated a much larger army of Scindia at Assaye in the Deccan; he later called it the hardest fight he ever saw, harder even than Waterloo. The same year Lord Lake captured Delhi and Agra in the north, and the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II became a pensioner of the British.

events.title: The Vellore Mutiny
events.short: British orders forbidding sepoys to wear religious marks and imposing a new style of turban led Indian soldiers at Vellore fort to mutiny, a foretaste of 1857.
events.detail: In 1805 the commander-in-chief of the Madras army issued new dress regulations forbidding sepoys to wear religious marks on their foreheads or grow beards and requiring a new turban resembling a European hat with a leather cockade. Hindu and Muslim soldiers alike believed this was a step towards forcing them to become Christians, and the family of Tipu Sultan, confined in Vellore fort, were suspected of encouraging their anger. In the early hours of 10 July 1806 the sepoys at Vellore mutinied, killed more than a hundred British soldiers and officers and raised Tipu’s flag. Within hours British cavalry arrived from Arcot and crushed the revolt, killing hundreds of mutineers. The British then withdrew the new regulations and moved Tipu’s family to Calcutta.

events.title: The Hindu College of Calcutta
events.short: Indian gentlemen of Calcutta founded the Hindu College to teach Western science and English literature, educating the generation of the Bengal Renaissance.
events.detail: In 1817 Hindu gentlemen of Calcutta, together with the Scottish watchmaker David Hare and others, founded the Hindu College, one of the first institutions in Asia to offer Western higher education. Teaching mathematics, natural science, history and English literature in English, it drew the sons of Bengal’s leading families. The young Anglo-Indian teacher Henry Derozio encouraged his students to think for themselves and question tradition; known as Young Bengal, they openly attacked caste, idolatry and old customs, some even eating beef and drinking wine to defy orthodoxy. Conservatives were outraged, and Derozio was dismissed in 1831 and died soon after. The college became Presidency College in 1855 and Presidency University in 2010.

events.title: The Third Anglo-Maratha War
events.short: The British defeated the Peshwa and the Maratha chiefs, abolished the Peshwaship and annexed its lands, becoming the paramount power in India.
events.detail: In 1817 Governor-General the Marquess of Hastings assembled a large army, ostensibly to suppress the Pindari raiders of central India, and the Peshwa Baji Rao II, the Bhonsle of Nagpur and the Holkar rose against the British. On 1 January 1818 a small Company force made up largely of soldiers of the Mahar caste held off the Peshwa’s army at Koregaon near Pune; Mahars later came to see the battle as a symbol of resistance to high-caste oppression and commemorate it there every year. Later that year the Peshwa surrendered and was exiled on a pension to Bithur near Kanpur, and his lands were added to the Bombay Presidency. The Maratha states became subsidiary princely states, and the East India Company became the paramount power over all India.

events.title: The Revolt of Rani Chennamma of Kittur
events.short: Rani Chennamma of Kittur in Karnataka refused to let the British annex her kingdom and defeated a British force, one of the first Indian women to take up arms against British rule.
events.detail: Kittur was a small kingdom in what is now northern Karnataka. In 1824, after the death of its king and his only son, Queen Chennamma adopted a boy as heir. The East India Company refused to recognise the adopted son and prepared to take over the kingdom and seize its treasury. Chennamma refused to yield, and in October 1824 her forces defeated the British troops sent to take possession; the British collector Thackeray was killed and two British officers were taken prisoner. The British then brought up a larger army and besieged Kittur, and Chennamma was captured in the second battle; she died in prison in 1829. Her story is celebrated throughout Karnataka, and her stand came more than thirty years before that of the Rani of Jhansi.

events.title: Ram Mohan Roy and the Brahmo Samaj
events.short: Ram Mohan Roy, called the father of modern India, founded the Brahmo Sabha, taught worship of one God, opposed idolatry and widow burning and championed Western education.
events.detail: Ram Mohan Roy was born in 1772 into a Brahmin family in Bengal, mastered Sanskrit, Persian, Arabic and English and worked for the East India Company. Studying the Upanishads, the Quran and the Bible, he concluded that the core of every great religion was worship of the one God, and that idolatry and many customs of Hinduism were later corruptions. In 1828 he founded the Brahmo Sabha in Calcutta, later the Brahmo Samaj, to reform Hinduism through reason and monotheism. He campaigned to abolish sati, supported women’s property rights, promoted English and scientific education and founded newspapers in Bengali and Persian, fighting for press freedom. He died in Bristol in 1833 while visiting England as an envoy of the Mughal emperor.

events.title: The Abolition of Sati
events.short: Prompted by reformers such as Ram Mohan Roy, Governor-General William Bentinck issued a regulation making sati, the burning of widows, illegal and punishable as homicide.
events.detail: Sati was the custom of a widow burning herself on her husband’s funeral pyre, practised among certain castes in Bengal and elsewhere; in the Bengal Presidency alone more than eight thousand cases were recorded between 1815 and 1828. Many widows were burned under family pressure or even by force. Ram Mohan Roy’s sister-in-law died this way, and he devoted himself to ending the practice, citing ancient texts to show that it was no religious duty. The East India Company, fearing that interfering in religion would provoke unrest, hesitated for years. On 4 December 1829 Governor-General William Bentinck issued the Bengal Sati Regulation, declaring that anyone who assisted in a sati would be guilty of culpable homicide. Conservatives appealed to the Privy Council in London, which rejected their petition in 1832.

events.title: The Suppression of the Thugs
events.short: The British officer William Sleeman led a campaign against the Thugs, gangs said to pose as travellers and strangle their fellow wayfarers for their goods.
events.detail: According to British colonial accounts, the Thugs were hereditary gangs whose members posed as merchants or pilgrims, joined travellers on the road, won their trust and then strangled them with yellow scarves and robbed them, treating the killings as worship of the goddess Kali. In the 1830s the British officer William Sleeman set up a special department that hunted the Thugs using the confessions of captured members and informers; over a decade some 3,700 were arrested, hundreds were hanged and many were transported or imprisoned for life. The English word thug comes from their name. Modern historians argue that colonial descriptions of Thuggee were exaggerated and misunderstood, and served to portray Indian society as savage and in need of British rule.

events.title: Macaulay and English Education
events.short: Macaulay’s Minute on Education urged teaching Western knowledge in English to create a class Indian in blood but English in taste; English became the language of India’s elite.
events.detail: In the early nineteenth century Company officials were divided over education policy: the Orientalists wanted to fund traditional learning in Sanskrit, Persian and Arabic, while the Anglicists wanted to promote English and Western science. In 1835 Thomas Babington Macaulay, a member of the governor-general’s council, wrote his Minute on Education, claiming that a single shelf of a good European library was worth the whole native literature of India and Arabia, and calling for a class of persons Indian in blood and colour but English in taste, opinions, morals and intellect, to act as interpreters between the British and the Indian masses. Governor-General Bentinck adopted his view, and Company funds were redirected to English education. The policy had lasting effects, and English remains one of India’s official languages.

events.title: The First Dissection
events.short: Madhusudan Gupta of the Calcutta Medical College broke a taboo by performing India’s first modern dissection of a human body, opening Western medical education in India.
events.detail: The Calcutta Medical College was founded in 1835, one of the first schools in Asia to teach modern Western medicine. But many Hindus then believed that touching a corpse would pollute a person of high caste, and the students did not dare to dissect. On 10 January 1836 Madhusudan Gupta, an Ayurvedic scholar of Brahmin birth, and four students carried out the first modern human dissection in India at the college; Fort William is said to have fired a salute in honour of the event. The college went on to train many Indian doctors and students from across Asia, and Madhusudan Gupta also translated many English medical works into Bengali.

events.title: Indentured Labour and the Indian Diaspora
events.short: After Britain abolished slavery, more than a million Indian indentured labourers were shipped to plantations in Mauritius, the Caribbean, Fiji and elsewhere, creating Indian communities around the world.
events.detail: After Britain abolished slavery in 1833, the sugar plantations of its colonies lacked labour. From 1834 the British began recruiting Indian indentured labourers, who signed contracts of about five years to work on plantations in Mauritius, British Guiana, Trinidad, Fiji, Natal in South Africa and elsewhere, after which they could return home or stay. Many came from poor villages of Bihar and eastern Uttar Pradesh and were lured by recruiters’ false promises. On the long voyages and on the plantations they suffered disease, abuse and low wages, in conditions not far from slavery. By the time the system was abolished in 1917, about one and a half million Indians had been sent overseas. Today Mauritius, Fiji, Guyana and Trinidad all have large populations of Indian descent.

events.title: The Rise of Assam Tea
events.short: After finding wild tea in Assam the British planted tea gardens, breaking China’s monopoly; India later became one of the world’s largest tea producers.
events.detail: In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries the British were passionate tea drinkers, and all their tea came from China, draining Britain’s silver, one reason why Britain smuggled opium into China. In 1823 the Scotsman Robert Bruce saw wild tea plants used by the Singpho people of Assam. The East India Company at first tried to grow Chinese tea plants but found that the local broad-leaved Assam variety suited the climate better. In 1839 the Assam Company was founded and the first Assam tea was auctioned in London. Tea gardens then spread across Assam, Darjeeling and the Nilgiri hills of southern India, worked by labourers recruited from far away. By the end of the century India’s tea exports exceeded China’s. Today India is the world’s second-largest tea producer and its largest consumer.

events.title: Indian Opium and the Opium War
events.short: The East India Company monopolised opium growing in Bengal and sold the drug in China; when the Qing banned it, Britain went to war, with many Indian soldiers in its forces.
events.detail: To offset the huge deficit from buying Chinese tea, the East India Company from 1773 monopolised opium production in Bengal and Bihar, processing it in factories at Patna and Ghazipur and auctioning it in Calcutta to private traders, who smuggled it to Canton. Opium from Malwa in western India was also exported through Bombay. At one point opium revenue made up more than a sixth of the income of British India. In 1839 the Chinese commissioner Lin Zexu destroyed confiscated opium at Humen, and Britain launched the First Opium War; the expeditionary force sent to China included many Indian soldiers from Madras and Bengal. China was defeated and signed the Treaty of Nanjing in 1842. The opium trade continued until 1913 and brought great suffering to China.

events.title: Savitribai Phule Opens a School for Girls
events.short: Savitribai Phule and her husband Jyotirao opened the first school for girls run by Indians in Pune; she is seen as India’s first woman teacher.
events.detail: Savitribai Phule was born in 1831 into a farming family in Maharashtra and at nine was married to Jyotirao Phule of the low Mali caste, who taught her to read and write. In 1848 the couple opened a school for girls at Bhide Wada in Pune, and later several schools for children of low castes and untouchables. Many people then thought that educating girls defied tradition, and on her way to school Savitribai was pelted with mud and dung; she carried a spare sari to change into when she arrived. She also opened a shelter for abandoned widows and opposed child marriage and the shaving of widows’ heads, and she wrote poetry in Marathi. In 1897 she caught plague while nursing victims and died. Her birthday, 3 January, is celebrated in Maharashtra as a day for girls’ education.

events.title: Dalhousie’s Doctrine of Lapse
events.short: Governor-General Dalhousie decreed that princely states without a natural heir would pass to Britain, annexing Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur and others and enraging the princes.
events.detail: The Marquess of Dalhousie became governor-general in 1848 at the age of thirty-five, determined to bring as much land as possible under direct British rule. He applied the doctrine of lapse: when the ruler of a dependent princely state died without a natural male heir, his adopted heir would not be recognised and the state would lapse to the British. Under it he annexed Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur, Sambalpur and other states, and he stopped the pension of Nana Sahib, the adopted son of the last Peshwa. In 1856 he annexed Awadh on the ground of misgovernment. These policies left many princes, nobles and their followers bitter, and the Rani of Jhansi and Nana Sahib both became leaders of the great uprising of 1857.

events.title: The Anglo-Sikh Wars and the Annexation of the Punjab
events.short: After Ranjit Singh’s death the Sikh Empire fell into chaos; the British defeated the Sikh army in two wars, annexed the Punjab in 1849 and took the Koh-i-Noor for the British Crown.
events.detail: After Ranjit Singh died in 1839 the Sikh court sank into bloody power struggles, with several rulers in six years, and the powerful Khalsa army slipped out of control. In 1845 the Sikh army crossed the Sutlej and the First Anglo-Sikh War broke out; after hard battles at Mudki, Ferozeshah and Sobraon the Sikhs were defeated and forced to cede territory and pay an indemnity. In 1848 a revolt at Multan sparked the Second Anglo-Sikh War; the British suffered heavy losses at Chillianwala but defeated the Sikhs at the battle of Gujrat in February 1849. Dalhousie then annexed the Punjab, the ten-year-old last Maharaja, Duleep Singh, was sent to England, and the Koh-i-Noor was presented to Queen Victoria.

events.title: The Poet Ghalib
events.short: The Delhi poet Ghalib, writing in Urdu and Persian, was renowned for his philosophical depth and wit, the last great poet of the Mughal age.
events.detail: Mirza Asadullah Khan Ghalib was born in 1797 into a Turkic noble family in Agra, moved to Delhi and became a poet at the court of the last Mughal emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar. He wrote a great many ghazals in Urdu and Persian on love, the pain of life, questions about God and mockery of the worldly, in language both terse and rich with meaning, and many of his lines are still quoted in everyday life in India and Pakistan. He was poor all his life, fond of wine and gambling, and was once jailed for gambling. During the uprising of 1857 he witnessed the destruction of Delhi and recorded its sufferings in his letters and diary; his Urdu letters are regarded as the beginning of modern Urdu prose.

events.title: India’s First Passenger Train
events.short: India’s first passenger train ran 34 kilometres from Bombay to Thane; railways then spread rapidly and transformed India’s economy and society.
events.detail: At 3.35 on the afternoon of 16 April 1853 a train hauled by three steam locomotives and carrying about four hundred passengers left Bori Bunder in Bombay to a salute of twenty-one guns and reached Thane, 34 kilometres away, about an hour later. It was India’s first passenger railway, built by the Great Indian Peninsula Railway. Governor-General Dalhousie pushed railway building hard, seeing it as a way to move troops quickly, carry raw materials such as cotton and sell British manufactures. By 1900 India had more than 40,000 kilometres of track, one of the largest networks in the world. The railways bound the country together, though they also made it easier to export grain in times of famine. Indian Railways today is one of the world’s largest employers.

events.title: The Ganges Canal Opens
events.short: The Ganges Canal, built under the engineer Proby Cautley, opened; drawing water from the Ganges at Haridwar to irrigate the Doab, it was then the largest irrigation work in the world.
events.detail: In 1837–38 a terrible famine in the Ganges–Yamuna Doab killed some 800,000 people. The British engineer Proby Cautley proposed a great irrigation canal that would take water from the Ganges at Haridwar and carry it south along the high ground of the Doab. Work began in 1842 and overcame the problem of crossing many torrent beds, including a great aqueduct carrying the canal over the Solani river near Roorkee. The canal opened in April 1854; its main channel ran some 560 kilometres and, with its branches, thousands of kilometres in all, irrigating about 300,000 hectares. To train engineers the British founded Asia’s first engineering college at Roorkee, now the Indian Institute of Technology Roorkee.

events.title: A National Post and the Telegraph
events.short: India set up a unified postal service with stamps valid nationwide, and telegraph lines linked Calcutta, Bombay and Madras, bringing India into the age of rapid communication.
events.detail: In 1852 Bartle Frere, commissioner of Sindh, issued the Scinde Dawk, the first postage stamps in Asia. On 1 October 1854 British India created a unified Post Office that charged by weight rather than distance and issued stamps valid throughout the country, so that ordinary people could send letters cheaply for the first time. At the same time William O’Shaughnessy, professor of chemistry at the Calcutta Medical College, directed the building of India’s telegraph network, and between 1854 and 1856 lines linked Calcutta, Agra, Bombay, Peshawar and Madras. In the uprising of 1857 the telegraph helped the British pass on news and move troops quickly; one rebel on his way to execution is said to have called it the accursed string that strangled us.

events.title: The Santal Rebellion
events.short: The Santal tribes of the hills of Bihar and Bengal rose under the brothers Sidhu and Kanhu against moneylenders, landlords and colonial officials.
events.detail: The Santals are a tribal people of eastern India who in the early nineteenth century were encouraged by the British to settle and clear the forests of the Rajmahal hills in what is now Jharkhand. As the land was developed, moneylenders, traders and landlords from outside used usury and fraud to take their land, while police and officials sided with the exploiters. On 30 June 1855 the brothers Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu gathered some ten thousand Santals at the village of Bhognadih and declared that they would drive out the outsiders and rule themselves. Armed with bows and axes, the rebels attacked moneylenders, police posts and railway works. The British sent troops and war elephants, and by early 1856 some fifteen thousand Santals had been killed. Afterwards the British created a separate Santal Parganas district to protect tribal land.

events.title: The Widow Remarriage Act
events.short: Urged by the scholar Vidyasagar, British India passed a law allowing Hindu widows to remarry, challenging a taboo centuries old.
events.detail: Among high-caste Hindus in the nineteenth century, girls were often married as small children, and many became widows in their teens or even earlier. Widows could not remarry; they had their heads shaved, wore white, ate a restricted diet and lived out their lives scorned. The Bengali Sanskrit scholar Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar searched the ancient lawbooks for evidence that widow remarriage was permitted by scripture, and in 1855 he submitted a petition with about a thousand signatures to the government, while opponents gathered many times that number. Even so, the Hindu Widows’ Remarriage Act was passed on 26 July 1856. That December Vidyasagar arranged the first legal widow remarriage in Calcutta, and he later had his own son marry a widow.

events.title: The Annexation of Awadh
events.short: The British deposed Wajid Ali Shah, Nawab of Awadh, on grounds of misrule and annexed his rich kingdom, angering the many sepoys who came from Awadh.
events.detail: Awadh, on the middle Ganges with its capital at Lucknow, broke away from the Mughal Empire in the eighteenth century. Its nawabs built magnificent monuments such as the Bara Imambara and patronised poetry, music and dance, making Lucknow a cultural capital of the north. The last nawab, Wajid Ali Shah, was himself a poet, musician and patron of Kathak dance. In February 1856 Governor-General Dalhousie unilaterally deposed him on grounds of misgovernment and annexed Awadh to British India, and the nawab was exiled to Calcutta. Because many soldiers of the Bengal army came from the villages of Awadh, the annexation cost them their home kingdom, and the landholdings of its gentry were reassessed; it was one of the main causes of the great uprising a year later.

events.title: The Universities of Calcutta, Bombay and Madras
events.short: British India founded universities at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras on the model of the University of London; they educated the generation of intellectuals who led the national movement.
events.detail: Following the Education Dispatch of 1854 by Charles Wood, president of the Company’s Board of Control, British India founded three universities between January and September 1857, at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras. Modelled on the University of London, they at first mainly set examinations and conferred degrees, while teaching was done by affiliated colleges. English was the medium of instruction, and the courses covered English literature, history, philosophy, mathematics and natural science. Their graduates became lawyers, teachers, journalists and government clerks, forming a new middle class, and many leaders of the national movement, such as Gokhale, Tilak and later Nehru, received this kind of education. They turned the Western ideas of liberty, equality and national self-determination they had learned against British rule.

events.title: The Indian Rebellion of 1857
events.short: Sepoys at Meerut rose in revolt and proclaimed the last Mughal emperor; the uprising swept northern India before being crushed, ending Company rule.
events.detail: On 10 May 1857 sepoys at Meerut, angered by rumours that the cartridges of the new rifle were greased with beef and pork fat and by long resentment over annexations, interference with religious custom and unequal treatment, killed their British officers, marched on Delhi and proclaimed the 82-year-old Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah II their leader. The revolt spread to Kanpur, Lucknow, Jhansi and Bihar, joined by dispossessed princes, landlords and peasants. Both sides committed terrible massacres. British forces retook Delhi in September and had subdued most areas by mid-1858; the last emperor was exiled to Rangoon, ending the Mughal dynasty. Britain then abolished the East India Company and ruled India directly.

events.title: The siege of Lucknow
events.short: Rebels besieged the British Residency at Lucknow for nearly five months, while Begum Hazrat Mahal of Awadh led resistance in the region.
events.detail: Awadh had been annexed by Britain only in 1856 on grounds of 'misgovernment', and the 1857 rising found wide support there. At the end of June some 1,700 Britons and loyal Indian soldiers withdrew into the Lucknow Residency and were besieged. They held out for nearly five months through bombardment, disease and hunger until a relief force under Colin Campbell evacuated them in November. Begum Hazrat Mahal, wife of the deposed king, placed her young son on the throne and organised continued resistance; after Lucknow fell in 1858 she refused a British pardon and went into exile in Nepal. The shell-scarred Residency is preserved as a ruin.

events.title: Death of the Rani of Jhansi
events.short: Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi led her troops against the British and fell in battle near Gwalior, becoming the most celebrated heroine of Indian nationalism.
events.detail: Jhansi was a small Maratha kingdom in northern India. When its raja died in 1853, Governor-General Dalhousie refused to recognise his adopted son under the Doctrine of Lapse and annexed the state. After the 1857 rising the young queen Lakshmibai took control. When British forces stormed Jhansi in March 1858 she escaped with her son, joined other rebel leaders such as Tantia Tope and seized Gwalior. On 18 June, riding into battle dressed as a man, she was killed near Gwalior at about 29. Even the British commander Hugh Rose called her the bravest of the rebels. Later nationalists made her a symbol of resistance, and the women's regiment of the Indian National Army bore her name.

events.title: The British Crown takes over India
events.short: Parliament passed the Government of India Act, abolishing the East India Company; the Crown took direct rule and Queen Victoria's proclamation promised religious tolerance.
events.detail: The rebellion shook Britain. In August 1858 Parliament passed the Government of India Act, transferring the Company's territories, armies and powers to the Crown. A Secretary of State for India and a Council of India were set up in London, and the Governor-General also became Viceroy representing the queen, the first being Lord Canning. On 1 November Queen Victoria's proclamation was read at Allahabad, renouncing further annexation, promising to respect the rights of the princes, not to interfere with her subjects' religion, and to open public office to all races. The period of direct British rule that followed, until 1947, is known as the British Raj.

images.caption: Queen Victoria's proclamation to the princes and people of India, 1 November 1858

events.title: The Indigo Revolt in Bengal
events.short: Bengali peasants refused to grow indigo for European planters, protesting forced cultivation and debt; the play Nil Darpan exposed their suffering.
events.detail: Nineteenth-century Bengal was the world's largest producer of indigo dye. European planters used advances and contracts to force peasants to grow indigo on their best land at very low prices, often beating or imprisoning those who refused. In 1859 peasants in Nadia and other districts refused en masse to sow it and attacked plantations for more than a year, supported by many Bengali intellectuals and missionaries. Dinabandhu Mitra's 1860 play Nil Darpan portrayed their misery; the missionary James Long, who published an English translation, was convicted of libel, causing a sensation. A government commission acknowledged abuses, and forced cultivation declined.

events.title: The Indian Penal Code
events.short: The Indian Penal Code, based on Macaulay's draft, was enacted, unifying criminal law across British India and remaining in force long after independence.
events.detail: In the 1830s a law commission headed by the historian Thomas Macaulay drafted a single criminal code to replace the patchwork of Islamic law, Hindu custom and Company regulations. Shelved for years, it was enacted only after the rebellion, in 1860, and took effect in 1862. Its 511 sections in 23 chapters, clearly worded and illustrated with examples, made it one of the most successful pieces of colonial legislation, later adopted in Singapore, Malaysia and Burma. A Code of Criminal Procedure followed in 1861. Independent India kept the code until it was replaced by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita in 2024.

events.title: Birth of Rabindranath Tagore
events.short: Rabindranath Tagore was born at the family mansion of Jorasanko in Calcutta, home of the most creative family of the Bengal Renaissance.
events.detail: On 7 May 1861 Rabindranath Tagore was born at the Tagore family mansion in Jorasanko, Calcutta, the fourteenth child of the Brahmo Samaj leader Debendranath Tagore. The wealthy and enlightened family filled the house with music, theatre and literature; his siblings included the first Indian to enter the civil service, a composer, a philosopher and a woman novelist. Tagore rarely attended school, learning at home and on travels, and began writing poetry at eight. The mansion is now the Tagore museum and part of Rabindra Bharati University.

events.title: The Archaeological Survey of India
events.short: Alexander Cunningham became the first head of the Archaeological Survey of India, systematically surveying Buddhist sites and founding Indian archaeology.
events.detail: The British army engineer Alexander Cunningham, long fascinated by Indian antiquities, used the travel accounts of Xuanzang and Faxian to locate Buddhist holy places. In 1861 Viceroy Canning created an archaeological survey and put him in charge. Cunningham identified Sanchi, Sarnath, Bodh Gaya and the ancient city of Taxila, and was the first to record a seal from Harappa, though he did not grasp its age. In 1902 Curzon appointed John Marshall director-general and strengthened conservation; Marshall excavated Taxila and Mohenjo-daro. The Survey still manages India's major monuments.

images.caption: Alexander Cunningham, founder of the Archaeological Survey of India

events.title: The first High Courts
events.short: High Courts were set up at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras, replacing the old Supreme and Company courts and forming the judicial system of British India.
events.detail: Under the Indian High Courts Act of 1861, High Courts were established in the three presidency capitals, merging the Crown's Supreme Courts, which served Europeans, with the Company's courts for Indians. The Calcutta High Court is the oldest in India; its Gothic Revival building was modelled on the Cloth Hall at Ypres. An Indian judge sat on the Bombay bench as early as 1864. The courts produced a large class of Indian lawyers, and nationalist leaders such as Gandhi, Nehru, Jinnah and Patel were all trained in law.

events.title: Ramakrishna at Dakshineswar
events.short: Ramakrishna practised at the Kali temple of Dakshineswar near Calcutta, teaching that all religions lead to the same God and drawing many educated young men.
events.detail: Ramakrishna was born to a Brahmin family in rural Bengal and had little formal schooling. From 1855 he served as priest of the new Kali temple at Dakshineswar on the Ganges north of Calcutta, worshipping the goddess with ecstatic devotion and entering mystical trances. He also practised according to Vedanta, Tantra, Islam and Christianity, concluding that all religions are paths to the same truth. His teaching through simple parables attracted many Western-educated young men, the most famous being Narendranath Datta, later known as Swami Vivekananda.

events.title: The Suez Canal opens
events.short: The Suez Canal opened, cutting thousands of kilometres off the voyage from Europe; Bombay became the main port for Britain and India was drawn deeper into world markets.
events.detail: Before the canal, ships from Britain to India had to round the Cape of Good Hope, a voyage of months. After it opened in 1869 a steamer could reach Bombay from London in about three weeks, tightening Britain's control and trade. Bombay, the nearest port, boomed into India's busiest harbour and commercial centre. India exported cotton, jute, wheat, tea and opium and imported British machine-made cloth. In 1870 a telegraph cable also linked London directly to India. The canal accelerated the commercialisation of the Indian economy and made it easier for educated Indians to study in Britain.

events.title: Birth of Mohandas Gandhi
events.short: Mohandas Gandhi was born in the Gujarati port of Porbandar, son of the princely state's chief minister and a deeply devout Vaishnava mother.
events.detail: On 2 October 1869 Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi was born in Porbandar, a small princely state on the Kathiawar peninsula, into a merchant-caste family whose men had served as the state's chief ministers. His mother Putlibai fasted often, worshipped Vishnu and was touched by the Jain ideal of non-violence, which shaped him deeply. He was married at 13 to Kasturba, as was the custom, and in 1888 went to London to study law. His birthplace is now the Kirti Mandir memorial; his birthday, 2 October, is a national holiday and the UN's International Day of Non-Violence.

events.title: The first census of British India
events.short: British India held its first census, counting people by religion and caste; repeated every ten years, it deeply shaped Indian identity politics.
events.detail: In 1872 the colonial government carried out its first census across most of India; from 1881 it was held simultaneously across the country every ten years, a tradition continued after independence. The census recorded population, age, occupation and literacy, and classified people by religion, caste and language, even trying to rank thousands of castes. These official categories hardened identities that had been fluid and local, prompting caste and religious groups to organise for higher status and representation. The census also left historians a wealth of social data.

events.title: Phule founds the Satyashodhak Samaj
events.short: The reformer Jyotirao Phule founded the Satyashodhak Samaj in Pune, opposing Brahmin privilege and caste discrimination and championing education for lower castes and women.
events.detail: Jyotirao Phule, from the Mali gardener caste of Maharashtra, turned against the caste system after being insulted at a Brahmin friend's wedding. In 1848 he and his wife Savitribai opened in Pune the first girls' school run by Indians; Savitribai became one of India's first women teachers, often pelted with mud and dung on her way to class. They also founded schools for untouchable children and shelters for widows and abandoned infants. In 1873 Phule founded the Satyashodhak Samaj, preaching equality and rejecting the Brahmin monopoly of ritual. His book Gulamgiri likened caste oppression to American slavery. Ambedkar revered him as one of his three gurus.

events.title: Founding of the Arya Samaj
events.short: Dayananda Saraswati founded the Arya Samaj in Bombay, calling for a 'return to the Vedas' and rejecting idol worship and hereditary caste; it was strongest in Punjab.
events.detail: Dayananda Saraswati, born to a Gujarati Brahmin family, left home young as an ascetic and came to believe that later Hinduism had strayed from the Vedas. In 1875 he founded the Arya Samaj in Bombay, holding the Vedas as the sole authority and opposing idol worship, child marriage, the ban on widow remarriage and caste by birth, while promoting women's education. His book Satyarth Prakash criticised other religions as well as orthodox Hinduism. The Samaj spread rapidly in Punjab and the north, founding many Dayanand Anglo-Vedic schools and promoting shuddhi, the 'reconversion' of converts to Hinduism, which influenced later Hindu nationalism.

events.title: The Aligarh college
events.short: Syed Ahmad Khan founded the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College at Aligarh, urging Muslims to learn modern science and English and training a Muslim elite.
events.detail: After the rebellion many Britons blamed Muslims as its instigators, and the Muslim elite of northern India fell behind Hindus in education and employment. Syed Ahmad Khan, from a Mughal noble family that had sided with the British in 1857, argued that Muslims must embrace modern education and that Islam was compatible with reason and science. After visiting England he founded a college at Aligarh on the Cambridge model; it became Aligarh Muslim University in 1920. It trained generations of Muslim politicians and intellectuals, and the Aligarh movement supplied ideas and leaders for the later Muslim League and the Pakistan movement.

events.title: The Great Famine of 1876–1878
events.short: Failed monsoons brought drought to southern and western India; with grain still exported and relief cut back, the famine killed some five to six million people.
events.detail: In 1876 El Niño disrupted the monsoon, and Madras, Mysore, Hyderabad and the Bombay Presidency suffered two years of drought. Committed to laissez-faire, the colonial government believed intervention in grain markets was harmful, and grain continued to be exported to Britain. To save money Viceroy Lytton restricted relief, requiring the starving to do heavy labour in camps for rations below those given in jails. Estimates of the dead range from about 5.5 to 9.6 million. A Famine Commission afterwards drew up the Famine Codes, but great famines recurred in the late nineteenth century and became central to nationalist critiques of the colonial economy.

events.title: Victoria proclaimed Empress of India
events.short: Viceroy Lytton held a grand durbar at Delhi proclaiming Queen Victoria Empress of India, even as famine ravaged the south.
events.detail: In 1876 Prime Minister Disraeli steered through Parliament a bill giving Queen Victoria the title Empress of India. On 1 January 1877 Viceroy Lytton held an Imperial Assemblage outside Delhi, attended by hundreds of princes and officials, borrowing Mughal court ritual to present the British Crown as heir to India's imperial tradition. At the same time famine was killing millions in the south, and the extravagance drew nationalist criticism. Further durbars followed in 1903 and 1911; at the latter George V attended in person and announced the transfer of the capital from Calcutta to Delhi.

events.title: The Darjeeling Himalayan Railway
events.short: A narrow-gauge mountain railway opened to the tea gardens and hill station of Darjeeling, climbing two thousand metres with loops and zigzags; it is now a World Heritage Site.
events.detail: Darjeeling was developed by the British in the mid-nineteenth century as a hill station and planted with tea, and Darjeeling tea soon became famous. In 1881 a narrow-gauge line from Siliguri on the plains to Darjeeling opened. With a gauge of only 610 mm and a length of about 88 km, it climbs to over 2,200 metres with loops and zigzag reverses; its little steam engines are known as the 'toy train'. British officials moved each summer to hill stations such as Simla and Darjeeling to escape the heat. The railway became a World Heritage Site in 1999, later joined by the Nilgiri and Kalka–Shimla lines.

events.title: Vande Mataram
events.short: Bankim Chandra Chatterjee published the song Vande Mataram in his novel Anandamath, hailing the motherland as a goddess; it became a nationalist rallying cry.
events.detail: Bankim Chandra Chatterjee, among Bengal's first university graduates, served as a deputy magistrate under the colonial government and pioneered the modern Bengali novel. His 1882 novel Anandamath, set during an eighteenth-century ascetics' rebellion, contains the song Vande Mataram, written in Sanskrit and Bengali, which hails Bengal and India as a bountiful mother goddess. Tagore sang it at the 1896 Congress session, and during the 1905 protests against the partition of Bengal it became the rallying cry. Because its later verses equate the nation with Hindu goddesses, some Muslims had reservations. In 1950 it was adopted as India's National Song, alongside the national anthem.

events.title: The Ilbert Bill controversy
events.short: A bill allowing Indian judges to try Europeans met fierce opposition from British residents and was watered down, showing educated Indians the need to organise.
events.detail: Viceroy Ripon, a liberal, promoted local self-government and repealed restrictions on the vernacular press. In 1883 the law member Courtenay Ilbert introduced a bill allowing Indian district judges to try Europeans in criminal cases. British planters, merchants and officials in India protested furiously that it was a racial humiliation for 'natives' to judge whites; they held rallies in Calcutta, raised funds and even plotted to kidnap the viceroy. The government compromised, letting European defendants demand a jury half of Europeans. The episode exposed the racism of colonial rule and showed the Indian elite the power of organised agitation; the Congress was founded two years later.

events.title: Founding of the Indian National Congress
events.short: Seventy-two delegates met in Bombay to found the Indian National Congress, which first politely sought a share in government and later led India to independence.
events.detail: On 28 December 1885 seventy-two lawyers, journalists, teachers and merchants from all the presidencies met at the Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College in Bombay and founded the Indian National Congress; the retired British civil servant A. O. Hume was a key organiser and W. C. Bonnerjee its first president. Early Congress met once a year; its members, mostly British-educated elites, professed loyalty to Britain and petitioned for more Indians in the legislative councils and civil service and for lower taxes and military spending. Moderates such as Naoroji and Gokhale dominated its first two decades. Under Gandhi the Congress later organised mass movements, and it governed India for long periods after independence.

events.title: India's first women doctors
events.short: Anandibai Joshi graduated from the Woman's Medical College of Pennsylvania; she and Kadambini Ganguly became the first Indian women with degrees in Western medicine.
events.detail: Anandibai Joshi was married at nine to a widower nearly twenty years older; when the child she bore at fourteen died for want of care, she resolved to study medicine. With her husband's support she travelled alone to the United States in 1883 despite public criticism, and in March 1886 graduated from the Woman's Medical College of Pennsylvania with a thesis on obstetrics among Hindu women. The same year Kadambini Ganguly of Bengal graduated from Calcutta Medical College; she practised for decades and was among the first women delegates to Congress. Anandibai was appointed physician of a women's ward in Kolhapur but died of tuberculosis soon after, aged only 21.

events.title: Victoria Terminus, Bombay
events.short: Bombay's Victoria Terminus was completed, blending Victorian Gothic with Indian traditions; one of the grandest buildings of the Raj, it is now a World Heritage Site.
events.detail: Victoria Terminus, headquarters and terminus of the Great Indian Peninsula Railway, was designed by the British architect F. W. Stevens and took ten years to build; it was named for Queen Victoria on her Golden Jubilee in 1887 and completed in 1888. Its Gothic Revival design, with pointed arches, stained glass and a great central dome, incorporates traditional Indian carving and animal and plant motifs, much of it by students of the Bombay School of Art. It symbolised Bombay's prosperity as the 'Gateway of the East'. Renamed Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus in 1996 and inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 2004, it remains one of Mumbai's busiest stations.

events.title: Naoroji elected to Parliament
events.short: The Parsi scholar Dadabhai Naoroji was elected to the British House of Commons; his 'drain theory' showed how British rule drained India's wealth.
events.detail: Dadabhai Naoroji, born to a Parsi family in Bombay, was India's first professor of mathematics and natural philosophy and later spent decades in business and politics in London; he was called the 'Grand Old Man of India'. Estimating India's national income, he argued that India lost vast wealth to Britain every year through officials' salaries, pensions, military charges and interest, and that this 'drain' was the root of Indian poverty, a theory that founded economic nationalism. In 1892 he won Finsbury Central in London as a Liberal by five votes, becoming the first Asian member of the House of Commons. Three times president of Congress, in 1906 he first set swaraj, self-rule, as its goal.

images.caption: Dadabhai Naoroji, c. 1889

events.title: Vivekananda in Chicago
events.short: Swami Vivekananda addressed the World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago, introducing Vedanta to the West; back home he founded the Ramakrishna Mission and inspired national pride.
events.detail: Vivekananda, born Narendranath Datta, was a Calcutta student who became a disciple of Ramakrishna; after his master's death he wandered India as a monk and was moved by the poverty of its people. On 11 September 1893 he opened his address to the World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago with 'Sisters and brothers of America', winning a long ovation. He preached Vedanta and religious tolerance and lectured in America and Britain for several years. Returning in 1897 he founded the Ramakrishna Mission, combining spiritual practice with famine relief, medicine and education, and urged the young to 'arise, awake'. He died in 1902 at only 39; his birthday, 12 January, is India's National Youth Day.

images.caption: Vivekananda in Chicago, September 1893
Vivekananda's ancestral house in Kolkata
images.author: Biswarup Ganguly

events.title: Gandhi thrown off the train
events.short: Working as a lawyer in South Africa, Gandhi was thrown off a first-class carriage because of his colour; the humiliation set him on a struggle in which he developed non-violent resistance.
events.detail: In 1893 Gandhi went to South Africa to handle a lawsuit for an Indian firm. On 7 June, travelling to Pretoria on a first-class ticket, he was forced off the train at Pietermaritzburg when a white passenger objected, and spent a cold night in the waiting room. He decided to stay and fight for the rights of Indians there, founding the Natal Indian Congress in 1894, a newspaper and communal farms. When the Transvaal required Indians to register and carry passes in 1906, he organised mass civil disobedience that he called satyagraha, 'holding firmly to truth', or non-violent resistance. He spent 21 years in South Africa, returning to India in 1914 after an agreement with the government.

sources.title: Wikipedia - Mahatma Gandhi#Civil rights activist in South Africa (1893–1914)

events.title: Tilak and the public festivals
events.short: The radical leader Tilak turned the Ganesh festival and Shivaji's anniversary into public celebrations, mobilising people through religion and history and declaring 'Swaraj is my birthright'.
events.detail: Bal Gangadhar Tilak, a Pune mathematics teacher and scholar, founded the Marathi newspaper Kesari and attacked the Moderates for merely petitioning Britain. From 1893 he turned the household festival of Ganesh into a public street celebration, and in 1895 launched a festival honouring the Maratha founder Shivaji, drawing ordinary people into politics. During the Pune plague of 1897, when British officials' heavy-handed house searches caused outrage, he was convicted of sedition for his articles. His slogan 'Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it' earned him the title Lokmanya, 'beloved of the people', though his Hindu-centred mobilisation also worried Muslims.

Tilak's birthplace in Ratnagiri

events.title: J. C. Bose's radio experiments
events.short: The physicist Jagadish Chandra Bose demonstrated millimetre-wave radio transmission in Calcutta, pioneering radio and microwave research.
events.detail: After studying at Cambridge, Jagadish Chandra Bose returned to teach at Presidency College, Calcutta, researching in poor conditions despite being paid less than British colleagues. In 1895 he publicly demonstrated in Calcutta electromagnetic waves of about 5 mm wavelength passing through walls to ring a bell and ignite gunpowder, and invented a galena crystal detector for radio waves, one of the earliest semiconductor devices. He did not patent these inventions. He later turned to plant physiology, inventing instruments to record tiny plant movements and showing that plants respond to stimuli. He founded the Bose Institute in 1917, and a lunar crater bears his name.

events.title: Plague in Bombay
events.short: Plague reached Bombay from Hong Kong and spread across India, killing over ten million in two decades; Waldemar Haffkine developed a plague vaccine in Bombay.
events.detail: The third plague pandemic began in Yunnan, reached Hong Kong in 1894 and arrived in Bombay on merchant ships in 1896, spreading to Pune, Calcutta and Punjab. By the 1920s it had killed some ten to twelve million people in India. The colonial government imposed forcible segregation, house searches and burning of belongings, provoking intense anger; Walter Rand, the plague commissioner in Pune, was assassinated in 1897. The Russian-Jewish bacteriologist Waldemar Haffkine, working in Bombay, developed a plague vaccine and tested it on himself; his laboratory became the Haffkine Institute. The epidemic also spurred the rebuilding of Bombay.

events.title: Curzon becomes Viceroy
events.short: Lord Curzon became Viceroy, pursuing administrative reform and the preservation of monuments and building the Victoria Memorial, but his autocratic style antagonised nationalists.
events.detail: George Curzon became Viceroy at 39, one of the most ambitious governors of the British Empire. He reformed the police, education and railway administration, created the North-West Frontier Province and strengthened the protection of monuments, overseeing the restoration of the Taj Mahal and proposing a white marble memorial to Queen Victoria, completed in Calcutta in 1921. He held a lavish Delhi durbar in 1903 and sent an expedition into Tibet. Believing Indians unfit for self-government, he disdained the Congress; his most controversial act was the 1905 partition of Bengal, which provoked mass protest. That same year he resigned after a dispute with the army commander, Kitchener.

images.caption: Lord Curzon as Viceroy, 1899–1905

events.title: Partition of Bengal and the Swadeshi movement
events.short: Curzon partitioned Bengal on administrative grounds, sparking mass protest; people boycotted British goods and promoted swadeshi, turning nationalism into a mass movement.
events.detail: The Bengal Presidency had nearly 80 million people, and in 1905 Britain, citing administrative difficulty, split it into a western Bengal and a Muslim-majority province of Eastern Bengal and Assam. Nationalists saw it as 'divide and rule', aimed at weakening the politically active Bengalis. On 16 October, the day it took effect, Calcutta observed a general strike; people bathed in the Ganges and tied rakhi bands on one another as a sign of unity, and Tagore wrote songs for the occasion. The Swadeshi movement of boycotting British cloth, burning foreign goods and founding Indian factories and national schools spread rapidly, and some young men turned to secret revolutionary activity. The partition was annulled in 1911.

images.caption: A 1930s bazaar poster promoting the spinning wheel and swadeshi goods

events.title: Founding of the All-India Muslim League
events.short: Muslim notables founded the All-India Muslim League in Dhaka to protect Muslim political interests; under Jinnah it later demanded Pakistan.
events.detail: The Hindu-led protests against the partition of Bengal alarmed some Muslim leaders, who feared that under electoral politics Muslims as a minority would lose their voice. In October 1906 the Aga Khan III led a deputation to Viceroy Minto asking for separate electorates for Muslims. On 30 December, at the All-India Muhammadan Educational Conference in Dhaka, delegates founded the All-India Muslim League to promote Muslim loyalty to Britain and protect Muslim political rights. Initially of limited influence, it cooperated with Congress in 1916, grew strong under Jinnah from the 1930s and in 1940 demanded a separate Muslim homeland.

images.caption: Delegates at the 1906 conference in Dhaka

events.title: The Surat Split
events.short: At its Surat session the Congress split between the Moderates led by Gokhale and the Extremists led by Tilak, amid a brawl in the hall.
events.detail: After the partition of Bengal, divisions within Congress over methods sharpened. The Moderates, led by Gokhale and Pherozeshah Mehta, sought reform within the constitutional framework; the Extremists, Tilak, Lala Lajpat Rai and Bipin Chandra Pal ('Lal, Bal, Pal'), demanded a full boycott of British goods and complete self-rule. At the Surat session in December 1907 the two sides deadlocked over the presidency; a shoe was thrown at the platform, the hall descended into chaos and the session was abandoned, with the Extremists leaving Congress. Britain seized the chance to repress them, and Tilak was sentenced in 1908 to six years' exile in Burma. The factions reunited only in 1916.

images.caption: Gopal Krishna Gokhale, leader of the moderates

events.title: Founding of Tata Steel
events.short: The Tata family founded Tata Iron and Steel, financed entirely by Indians, building one of Asia's first large steelworks and the industrial city of Jamshedpur in Bihar.
events.detail: The Parsi merchant Jamsetji Tata, called the 'father of Indian industry', founded textile mills in Bombay, built the Taj Mahal Hotel and dreamed of giving India its own steel industry, hydroelectric power and a science institute. After his death in 1904 his son Dorabji carried on, founding Tata Iron and Steel in 1907 amid swadeshi enthusiasm and raising capital from the public; thousands of Indians bought shares. The works at Sakchi in Bihar (now Jharkhand) produced steel in 1912, and around them grew a planned industrial city later named Jamshedpur after the founder. The Tata Group is today one of India's largest conglomerates.

events.title: Bengali revolutionaries and the Alipore bomb case
events.short: Eighteen-year-old Khudiram Bose was hanged for an attempt on a British judge, and Aurobindo Ghose and others were tried in the Alipore bomb case as Bengal's secret revolutionaries were suppressed.
events.detail: During the Swadeshi movement secret revolutionary societies such as the Anushilan Samiti arose in Bengal, training in martial arts and making bombs to drive out the British by assassination. In April 1908 Khudiram Bose and a companion threw a bomb at the carriage of Kingsford, a notoriously harsh magistrate, at Muzaffarpur, but killed two Englishwomen instead. Captured, Khudiram was hanged in August at just 18 and became a hero of Bengali folk songs. Police then raided a bomb workshop near Calcutta and arrested many revolutionaries; the radical leader Aurobindo Ghose was tried in the Alipore bomb case and acquitted. He later withdrew to Pondicherry and became a renowned philosopher and yogi.

events.title: The Morley–Minto reforms
events.short: The Indian Councils Act enlarged the Indian membership of the legislative councils and created separate electorates for Muslims, deepening religious divisions in politics.
events.detail: To win over the Moderates and isolate the Extremists, Secretary of State John Morley and Viceroy Minto introduced reforms through the Indian Councils Act of 1909. The central and provincial legislative councils were enlarged, partly through indirect election, and an Indian joined the Viceroy's Executive Council for the first time. Meeting the Muslim League's demand, the act created separate electorates in which only Muslims could vote and stand. The councils remained advisory, without real power. Nationalists condemned separate electorates as 'divide and rule', and many historians see them as a step toward the eventual partition.

events.title: The Indian Institute of Science
events.short: Fulfilling Jamsetji Tata's wish, the Indian Institute of Science opened in Bangalore on land given by the Maharaja of Mysore, later becoming India's leading research institution.
events.detail: In 1893 Jamsetji Tata met Swami Vivekananda on a ship to Chicago, and they discussed India's need to train its own scientists. Tata endowed extensive property for a research university, but the plan met coolness from Curzon and other officials and was delayed for years. With land and funds from the Maharaja of Mysore, the Indian Institute of Science was founded in Bangalore in 1909 and admitted its first students in 1911. The Nobel physicist C. V. Raman later served as its director, and many leading Indian scientists worked there. The institute laid the foundation for Bangalore's later rise as India's technology hub.

events.title: The capital moves to Delhi
events.short: At the Delhi Durbar George V annulled the partition of Bengal and moved the capital from Calcutta to Delhi; Lutyens's New Delhi was inaugurated in 1931.
events.detail: On 12 December 1911 King George V and Queen Mary attended the Delhi Durbar in person, the only time a British monarch did so. The durbar announced the annulment of the partition of Bengal and the transfer of the capital of British India from Calcutta to Delhi. Delhi was the ancient seat of empires; the move both put distance between the government and Bengali nationalism and presented Britain as heir to the Mughals. The architects Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker laid out New Delhi south of the old city; its grand Viceroy's House (now Rashtrapati Bhavan) and Secretariat blended classical and Indian elements, and it was inaugurated in 1931.

images.caption: The Delhi Durbar of 1911, where George V announced the move of the capital

events.title: India's first feature film
events.short: Dadasaheb Phalke's silent film Raja Harishchandra, based on a myth, premiered in Bombay, marking the birth of the Indian film industry.
events.detail: Dadasaheb Phalke, a printer and photographer, decided to tell India's own myths on film after seeing a film about the life of Christ in Bombay in 1910. He sold his possessions to learn film-making and buy equipment in London, then wrote, directed and processed the film himself, helped by his wife. Because women from respectable families would not act, the queen was played by a man. On 3 May 1913 Raja Harishchandra, the story of an honest king who keeps his word through every trial, opened at the Coronation Cinema in Bombay to great success. India's highest film award, the Dadasaheb Phalke Award, bears his name.

events.title: Tagore wins the Nobel Prize
events.short: Tagore won the Nobel Prize in Literature for the English Gitanjali, the first Asian Nobel laureate; his songs later became the national anthems of India and Bangladesh.
events.detail: Tagore wrote over two thousand songs and a vast body of poetry, fiction, drama and essays that transformed Bengali literature. In 1912 he rendered his Bengali poems into English prose poems as Gitanjali, 'Song Offerings', published in London with a preface by W. B. Yeats to great acclaim. In November 1913 he won the Nobel Prize in Literature, the first non-European laureate. In 1901 he had founded an open-air school at Santiniketan, which grew into Visva-Bharati University. After the Amritsar massacre of 1919 he renounced his British knighthood in protest. He visited China in 1924. His Jana Gana Mana is India's national anthem and Amar Shonar Bangla that of Bangladesh.

events.title: The Ghadar Party
events.short: Punjabi emigrants in North America founded the Ghadar Party in San Francisco and its newspaper Ghadar ('Revolt'), and tried to launch an armed rising in India during the First World War.
events.detail: In the early twentieth century thousands of Punjabi Sikh farmers and ex-soldiers emigrated to the American West Coast and Canada, working on farms, in lumber mills and on railways and facing harsh racism. In 1913, with exiled intellectuals such as Lala Har Dayal, they founded the Ghadar Party in San Francisco, 'ghadar' meaning revolt, and published a newspaper of that name in Urdu, Punjabi and other languages calling for the overthrow of British rule. When the First World War began, thousands returned to India, planning a mutiny with Indian soldiers in February 1915, but British intelligence uncovered the plot and many were executed or imprisoned. The movement inspired later revolutionaries such as Bhagat Singh.

events.title: Ramanujan goes to Cambridge
events.short: The self-taught mathematician Srinivasa Ramanujan went to Cambridge at G. H. Hardy's invitation and made astonishing discoveries in number theory and infinite series before dying at 32.
events.detail: Srinivasa Ramanujan, born to a poor Brahmin family in Tamil Nadu, taught himself mathematics almost entirely from an old book of formulae; he failed twice at college because he studied nothing else, and worked as a clerk at the Madras Port Trust. In 1913 he wrote to the Cambridge mathematician G. H. Hardy, enclosing pages of unproved formulae; Hardy recognised his genius and invited him to Cambridge. From 1914 to 1919 the two published landmark papers on partitions, modular forms and infinite series, and in 1918 he was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society. Unable to adapt to the English climate and diet, he fell seriously ill and died after returning home in 1920, aged only 32; mathematicians still study his notebooks.

events.title: The Komagata Maru incident
events.short: The Japanese ship Komagata Maru, carrying 376 Indian migrants, was refused entry by Canada and forced back; at Calcutta British troops fired on the passengers, killing and wounding dozens.
events.detail: To restrict Asian immigration, Canada required migrants to arrive by 'continuous journey' from their country of birth, though no direct route existed from India. In 1914 the Sikh businessman Gurdit Singh chartered the Japanese freighter Komagata Maru and sailed from Hong Kong to Vancouver with 376 passengers, mostly Punjabi Sikhs, to challenge the rule. The ship lay off Vancouver for two months; only a few were allowed ashore and the rest were forced to return. When it reached Budge Budge near Calcutta in September, the authorities suspected the passengers of being revolutionaries, and in the clash soldiers opened fire, killing about twenty. In 2016 Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau formally apologised in Parliament.

events.title: India in the First World War
events.short: Over a million Indian soldiers fought for Britain in France, Mesopotamia, East Africa and Gallipoli, more than seventy thousand died, and Indians expected self-government in return.
events.detail: When the First World War broke out, British India was declared at war without consultation. In autumn 1914 the Indian Corps was rushed to France and fought in the cold trenches of Ypres and Neuve Chapelle; most Indian forces were later sent to Mesopotamia, where a British-Indian army surrendered to the Ottomans at Kut in 1916. Some 1.3 million Indians served and more than 70,000 died, and India bore heavy war costs and supplied vast materials. Gandhi and other nationalists supported recruitment in hope of self-government after the war, but Britain's response proved disappointing. India Gate in New Delhi commemorates the Indian soldiers who died in the war.

events.title: Gandhi returns to India
events.short: Gandhi returned to Bombay after 21 years of struggle in South Africa and, on Gokhale's advice, spent a year travelling across India to learn how its peasants lived.
events.detail: On 9 January 1915 the 45-year-old Gandhi and his wife Kasturba landed in Bombay to a warm welcome; the date is now celebrated as Pravasi Bharatiya Divas, the day of overseas Indians. His non-violent campaigns in South Africa were already famous. His political mentor Gokhale advised him to stay silent on politics for a year and travel India in third-class carriages to observe ordinary life. Gandhi gave up Western clothes for the coarse dress of Indian peasants and founded an ashram near Ahmedabad, where he and his followers lived simply, spinning and farming. Over the next three decades he turned Congress from an elite body into a mass movement and was revered as the Mahatma, 'great soul'.

events.title: The Lucknow Pact and Home Rule
events.short: Congress and the Muslim League signed the Lucknow Pact, jointly demanding self-government, while Tilak and Annie Besant launched the Home Rule Leagues.
events.detail: During the war the national movement revived. In 1916 Tilak, back from prison, and the British Theosophist Annie Besant each founded a Home Rule League on the Irish model, demanding self-government within the Empire and enrolling tens of thousands of young townspeople. That December Congress and the Muslim League held their sessions together in Lucknow; Moderates and Extremists reunited, and the two parties signed a pact presenting a joint scheme of constitutional reform, Congress accepting separate electorates for Muslims. The young lawyer Muhammad Ali Jinnah was instrumental in the pact and was hailed as the 'ambassador of Hindu–Muslim unity'.

events.title: The Champaran Satyagraha
events.short: Gandhi went to Champaran in Bihar to help peasants forced to grow indigo; he defied an order to leave, and his inquiry led to the abolition of forced cultivation.
events.detail: In Champaran in northern Bihar, European planters forced tenants to grow indigo on three-twentieths of their land and demanded compensation even when indigo prices fell. In 1917, after repeated appeals from the peasant Rajkumar Shukla, Gandhi went to investigate. Ordered by the magistrate to leave, he declared himself willing to accept punishment but refused to obey; crowds of peasants gathered outside the court, and the order was withdrawn. With lawyers such as Rajendra Prasad, Gandhi collected testimony from thousands of peasants, and the official inquiry that followed accepted their case and abolished the system. It was Gandhi's first satyagraha in India.

events.title: The Montagu Declaration
events.short: Secretary of State Montagu announced Britain's aim of gradually establishing responsible government in India; the 1919 reforms introduced 'dyarchy' in the provinces.
events.detail: To answer wartime Indian hopes for self-rule, Secretary of State Edwin Montagu told Parliament on 20 August 1917 that British policy was the increasing association of Indians in every branch of administration and the gradual development of self-governing institutions, leading to responsible government within the Empire. He and Viceroy Chelmsford drew up reforms enacted as the Government of India Act 1919. In the provinces 'dyarchy' handed education, health and agriculture to Indian ministers responsible to the legislature, while finance, police and justice stayed with the governor; the electorate grew to about five million. Nationalists found the reforms far too limited, and the Rowlatt Act passed almost simultaneously provoked widespread anger.

images.caption: Lord Chelmsford, Viceroy of India

events.title: The Rowlatt Act and the national hartal
events.short: The Rowlatt Act allowed detention of political suspects without trial; Gandhi called a nationwide hartal and satyagraha, his first all-India mass movement.
events.detail: After the war Britain wished to keep its wartime emergency powers, and in March 1919 the Imperial Legislative Council, over the opposition of every Indian member, passed laws based on Justice Rowlatt's report allowing detention of suspected 'terrorists' without trial and trials without jury or appeal. Indians called it the 'black act' of 'no vakil, no appeal, no daleel'. Gandhi formed a Satyagraha Sabha and called for a nationwide hartal of strikes, fasting and prayer on 6 April; cities across India responded, though violence broke out in some places. Tension was greatest in Punjab, culminating in the Amritsar massacre.

images.caption: Sidney Rowlatt, who chaired the committee behind the act

events.title: The Jallianwala Bagh massacre
events.short: Brigadier Dyer ordered troops to fire on a peaceful crowd in Jallianwala Bagh at Amritsar, killing hundreds; the massacre turned many Indians decisively against British rule.
events.detail: On 13 April 1919, the Sikh harvest festival of Baisakhi, some ten thousand people gathered in the Jallianwala Bagh at Amritsar, some to protest the arrest of two nationalist leaders and many simply villagers in town for the festival, unaware that meetings had been banned. Brigadier Reginald Dyer led his troops into the walled garden, which had only narrow exits, and without warning ordered them to fire into the crowd for about ten minutes, expending 1,650 rounds. Official figures gave 379 dead; Indian estimates exceeded a thousand, and many jumped into a well to escape. The House of Commons censured Dyer, but the Lords and many Britons in India hailed him a hero. Tagore renounced his knighthood, and Gandhi resolved to end all cooperation with Britain.

events.title: The Non-cooperation Movement
events.short: Allied with the Khilafat movement, Gandhi launched non-cooperation: Indians boycotted British schools, courts, elections and cloth, until Gandhi halted it after violence at Chauri Chaura.
events.detail: After the Ottoman defeat in the First World War, Indian Muslims launched the Khilafat movement to preserve the caliphate. Seeing a chance to unite Hindus and Muslims, Gandhi allied with the Ali brothers, and in 1920 Congress adopted his programme of non-cooperation: giving up British titles, boycotting government schools, courts, council elections and British cloth, and spinning and weaving at home. Tens of thousands of students left college, lawyers stopped practising, foreign cloth was burned across the country and many were jailed; Congress for the first time took root in the villages. In February 1922, after a crowd at Chauri Chaura in the United Provinces burned 22 policemen to death, Gandhi declared that the people were not ready for non-violence and called the movement off; he was then sentenced to six years.

events.title: The spinning wheel and khadi
events.short: Gandhi urged everyone to spin on the charkha and wear hand-woven khadi, boycotting British mill cloth and reviving the villages; the spinning wheel became the emblem of the movement.
events.detail: Gandhi held that British machine-made cloth had destroyed the village hand-spinning industry and the livelihoods of millions, and that self-rule required economic self-reliance. From 1921 he urged every Indian to spin daily and wear hand-spun, hand-woven khadi; Congress members had to wear it and could pay their dues in yarn. Gandhi himself spun every day and often wore only a loincloth. Khadi was both a boycott of British goods and a symbol of equality between urban elites and peasants. The Congress flag adopted in 1931 bore a spinning wheel at its centre; independent India's flag replaced it with Ashoka's wheel.
