events.title: The Malabar Rebellion
events.short: Muslim tenant farmers of Malabar in Kerala rose during the Khilafat movement against the British and landlords; the revolt turned to violence against Hindus and was crushed.
events.detail: The Mappilas of Malabar were Malayalam-speaking Muslims, mostly tenants of Hindu landlords, long aggrieved by heavy rents and arbitrary evictions. In August 1921 a police raid on Khilafat leaders sparked a rising; rebels attacked police stations, government offices and landlords and briefly set up their own rule in some areas. As the conflict escalated many Hindus were killed or forcibly converted, straining Hindu–Muslim relations. British troops took months to suppress the revolt, which cost about ten thousand lives. In November nearly a hundred captured rebels were shut in a closed goods wagon for transport and 67 suffocated, the 'Wagon Tragedy'.

events.title: The Vaikom Satyagraha
events.short: People in Travancore campaigned non-violently for lower castes' right to use the roads around the Vaikom temple, a landmark struggle against untouchability.
events.detail: In the kingdom of Travancore in Kerala, Ezhavas and untouchables were barred not only from temples but even from the roads around them, lest they 'pollute' higher castes. Inspired by the reformer Sree Narayana Guru's teaching of 'one caste, one religion, one God for man', local Congressmen in March 1924 organised volunteers of different castes to walk together toward the roads by the Vaikom temple; stopped by police, they sat before the barricades through the monsoon rains for more than 600 days. Gandhi came to mediate, and the Tamil reformer Periyar also took part. The roads were partly opened in 1925, and in 1936 the Maharaja of Travancore proclaimed temple entry for all Hindus.

events.title: The Indus Civilisation revealed
events.short: Archaeological Survey chief John Marshall announced that Harappa and Mohenjo-daro belonged to a previously unknown ancient civilisation, pushing Indian history back two thousand years.
events.detail: In the early 1920s Daya Ram Sahni at Harappa in Punjab and R. D. Banerji at Mohenjo-daro in Sindh excavated similar seals, pottery and brick buildings. On 20 September 1924 John Marshall, director-general of the Archaeological Survey, announced in the Illustrated London News that both sites belonged to a Bronze Age civilisation contemporary with Mesopotamia, causing a worldwide sensation. Until then Indian civilisation had generally been thought to begin with the Vedic age. Later excavations revealed the vast extent and orderly town planning of what became known as the Indus or Harappan Civilisation, whose script remains undeciphered.

events.title: Periyar and the Self-Respect Movement
events.short: The Tamil reformer Periyar launched the Self-Respect Movement against Brahmin privilege, caste and religious superstition, profoundly shaping Tamil Nadu politics.
events.detail: E. V. Ramasamy, known as Periyar, 'the elder', was a Congress leader in the Madras Presidency who left the party in protest at caste discrimination within it. In 1925 he launched the Self-Respect Movement, urging non-Brahmins to reclaim their dignity and attacking Brahmin privilege in religion, education and government, as well as caste, child marriage and the treatment of widows; he promoted 'self-respect marriages' without Brahmin priests and equal rights for women. A firm atheist, he also opposed the imposition of Hindi. His ideas gave rise to the Dravidian movement, and parties such as the DMK have long dominated Tamil Nadu politics.

events.title: Protests against the Simon Commission
events.short: Britain sent the all-British Simon Commission to review India's constitution; protesters met it with 'Simon go back', and Lala Lajpat Rai died after being beaten by police.
events.detail: In 1927 the British government appointed a seven-member commission under Sir John Simon to review the 1919 reforms; not one member was Indian. When it landed in Bombay in February 1928 it was met by a nationwide hartal and black flags, with crowds shouting 'Simon go back'. At Lahore in October police beat demonstrators with lathis, and the 63-year-old Punjab leader Lala Lajpat Rai was badly injured, dying weeks later. To answer British claims that Indians could not agree on a constitution, Congress published a draft written by Motilal Nehru, the Nehru Report, but failed to reach agreement with the Muslim League.

events.title: The Bardoli Satyagraha
events.short: Farmers of Bardoli in Gujarat, led by Vallabhbhai Patel, refused to pay a steep rise in land revenue and forced the government to yield; Patel was hailed as 'Sardar'.
events.detail: In 1928 the Bombay government raised land revenue in the Bardoli district of Gujarat by about 22 per cent despite a recent poor harvest. The lawyer Vallabhbhai Patel organised the farmers to refuse payment collectively, dividing villages into disciplined camps committed to non-violence. When the government confiscated land and cattle, farmers hid their animals and no one dared buy auctioned land; women took an active part. After a few months the government agreed to a new assessment and returned confiscated property, and the increase was cut to about 6 per cent. The women of Bardoli called Patel 'Sardar', 'leader'; he later became independent India's deputy prime minister and integrated hundreds of princely states.

events.title: The Raman effect
events.short: The physicist C. V. Raman discovered the inelastic scattering of light, the Raman effect, in Calcutta, winning the 1930 Nobel Prize in Physics, the first Asian science laureate.
events.detail: Chandrasekhara Venkata Raman, born in Tamil Nadu, worked in the finance service while researching in his spare time at the Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science in Calcutta, later becoming professor of physics at Calcutta University. On a voyage to England in 1921 he became curious about the deep blue of the Mediterranean and began studying the scattering of light. On 28 February 1928 he and his student K. S. Krishnan found, with simple apparatus, that monochromatic light passing through a liquid produces a little scattered light of changed frequency, the shift revealing the vibrations of the molecules. The Raman effect is still widely used in chemical analysis. He won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1930, and 28 February is India's National Science Day.

events.title: Bhagat Singh
events.short: The young revolutionary Bhagat Singh threw harmless bombs into the Central Legislative Assembly shouting 'Long live revolution', and was hanged in 1931 at just 23.
events.detail: Bhagat Singh, born to a Sikh family in Punjab and inspired by the Ghadar movement and socialism, joined the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association. In 1928, to avenge Lala Lajpat Rai, he and comrades shot a British police officer in Lahore. On 8 April 1929 he and Batukeshwar Dutt threw two deliberately harmless bombs into the Central Legislative Assembly in Delhi, scattered leaflets, shouted 'Inquilab Zindabad', long live revolution, and waited to be arrested so as to use the court as a platform. In prison he fasted in protest at the treatment of political prisoners and read and wrote prolifically. He was hanged on 23 March 1931 with Sukhdev and Rajguru and remains one of India's most revered martyrs.

events.title: The demand for complete independence
events.short: At the Lahore session under Jawaharlal Nehru, Congress declared complete independence its goal and named 26 January 1930 Independence Day.
events.detail: With Britain still withholding dominion status, Congress met at Lahore in December 1929 and elected the 40-year-old Jawaharlal Nehru president. It resolved that complete independence, Purna Swaraj, was its goal and authorised Gandhi to launch civil disobedience. At midnight on 31 December Nehru raised the tricolour on the banks of the Ravi. On 26 January 1930 people across the country gathered to read a declaration of independence stating that British rule had ruined India politically, economically, culturally and spiritually, and that submitting to it was a crime against man and God. The day was marked every year thereafter, and India's constitution came into force on 26 January 1950, now Republic Day.

events.title: The Salt March
events.short: Gandhi and his followers walked nearly 400 km to the sea at Dandi and made salt in defiance of the British monopoly, sparking nationwide civil disobedience and over sixty thousand arrests.
events.detail: Britain held a monopoly on salt in India, banning private manufacture and taxing it, a burden that fell hardest on the poorest. Gandhi chose salt to launch civil disobedience because it touched everyone. On 12 March 1930 the 61-year-old Gandhi and 78 followers set out from his ashram at Ahmedabad and walked some 390 km in 24 days, joined by villagers along the way and followed by the world's press. At dawn on 6 April he picked up a handful of salty mud on the beach at Dandi, breaking the salt law. Illegal salt-making, boycotts and tax refusal spread across India, with women taking part in great numbers. Gandhi and more than sixty thousand others were arrested, and reports of non-violent protesters being clubbed by police at the Dharasana salt works shocked the world.

events.title: Gandhi at the Round Table Conference
events.short: Gandhi signed a pact with Viceroy Irwin suspending civil disobedience and attended the second Round Table Conference in London as Congress's sole delegate, but no agreement was reached.
events.detail: Britain convened the first Round Table Conference in London in 1930 to discuss India's constitutional future, but Congress boycotted it. In March 1931 Gandhi negotiated with Viceroy Irwin; under the Gandhi–Irwin Pact political prisoners were freed and coastal people allowed to make salt, while Congress suspended civil disobedience and agreed to attend. In September Gandhi, in his loincloth, went to London, stayed in a poor East End settlement and visited Lancashire mill workers left jobless by the Indian boycott, who welcomed him warmly. But the conference deadlocked over minority representation, with religious and caste groups each pressing their claims; Gandhi returned empty-handed and was soon arrested again.

events.title: The Poona Pact
events.short: When Britain granted untouchables separate electorates, Gandhi fasted in prison; Ambedkar finally agreed to reserved seats within the general electorate instead.
events.detail: In August 1932 the British Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald announced the Communal Award, granting separate electorates not only to Muslims, Sikhs and others but also to the untouchables. B. R. Ambedkar, a jurist born an untouchable, saw this as a safeguard for the oppressed; Gandhi believed it would permanently divide Hindu society and began a fast unto death in Yerwada jail at Pune. Immense national pressure fell on Ambedkar. After negotiations the Poona Pact of 24 September abolished the separate electorates in exchange for a larger number of seats reserved for the 'Depressed Classes' within the general electorate. Gandhi then called the untouchables Harijans, 'children of God', and campaigned against untouchability; Ambedkar remained bitter about the pact.

events.title: The Reserve Bank of India
events.short: The Reserve Bank of India was founded in Calcutta to issue currency and regulate banks; nationalised after independence, it is India's central bank.
events.detail: During the Depression, currency and financial management in British India were divided between the government and the privately owned Imperial Bank, with no single central bank. Under the Reserve Bank of India Act of 1934 the bank opened in Calcutta on 1 April 1935, initially a shareholder-owned institution; its headquarters moved to Bombay in 1937. It issued rupee notes, managed foreign exchange and government debt, supervised commercial banks and at first also served as Burma's central bank. It was nationalised in 1949. After independence its notes bore the lion capital of Ashoka's pillar, and later a portrait of Gandhi.

events.title: The Government of India Act 1935
events.short: Parliament passed its longest act, granting provincial autonomy and planning a federation; in the 1937 provincial elections Congress won and formed ministries in most provinces.
events.detail: After years of Round Table Conferences and white papers, Parliament passed the Government of India Act in August 1935; with 321 sections it was then the longest act ever passed at Westminster. It ended dyarchy and granted provincial autonomy, with Indian ministers responsible to the legislatures running provincial governments, and enlarged the electorate to about thirty million. It also planned a federation of British provinces and princely states, never realised because the princes would not join, and separated Burma from India. In the 1937 elections Congress formed ministries in eight of eleven provinces, while the Muslim League fared poorly. Much of the act was later absorbed into independent India's constitution.

events.title: Premchand and the Progressive Writers
events.short: The Hindi writer Premchand published Godaan, a novel of peasant suffering, and presided over the founding of the Progressive Writers' Association, launching a realist literary current.
events.detail: Premchand, born Dhanpat Rai, was a schoolteacher in the United Provinces who first wrote in Urdu and later in Hindi, producing some three hundred short stories and a dozen novels; he is called the 'emperor of novelists'. His early story collection was burned by the colonial authorities for its patriotism. His work portrayed rural poverty, caste oppression, debt and the lives of women with stark realism. Godaan, published in 1936, tells of the poor peasant Hori's lifelong, unfulfilled wish to own a cow and is considered the summit of modern Hindi literature. In April that year he presided over the founding conference of the All-India Progressive Writers' Association in Lucknow; he died in October.

events.title: India in the Second World War
events.short: The Viceroy declared India at war without consultation, and Congress ministries resigned in protest; 2.5 million Indian soldiers fought in North Africa, Italy and Burma, repelling Japan at Imphal and Kohima.
events.detail: In September 1939 Viceroy Linlithgow declared India at war with Germany without consulting Indian leaders; the Congress provincial ministries resigned en masse, while the Muslim League celebrated a 'Day of Deliverance' and expanded its influence. During the war the Indian Army grew to about 2.5 million men, the largest volunteer army in history, fighting in North and East Africa, Italy and Southeast Asia; some 87,000 died. In 1944 Japanese and Indian National Army forces attacked Imphal and Kohima in northeastern India, and British-Indian troops threw them back after months of fierce fighting, turning the tide in Burma. India was also the base for the Allied 'Hump' airlift of supplies to China.

events.title: The Lahore Resolution
events.short: The Muslim League resolved at Lahore that the Muslim-majority regions of the north-west and east should form independent states, becoming the charter of the Pakistan movement.
events.detail: Muhammad Ali Jinnah, once a Congressman and champion of Hindu–Muslim unity, grew disillusioned with Congress and led the Muslim League from the 1930s. He advanced the 'two-nation theory', holding that Hindus and Muslims were distinct nations in religion, culture and history, and that Muslims could not be secure in a single Hindu-majority state. On 23 March 1940 the League resolved at Lahore that the Muslim-majority areas should be grouped into 'independent states'. Though the word 'Pakistan' did not appear, it became known as the Pakistan Resolution. The Minar-e-Pakistan in Lahore stands where the session was held.

events.title: The Quit India Movement
events.short: Gandhi demanded that Britain 'Quit India' with the call 'Do or die'; the Congress leadership was arrested and mass uprisings across India were harshly suppressed.
events.detail: In spring 1942, with Japan approaching India, Britain sent Stafford Cripps to offer dominion status after the war, but the offer was rejected. On 8 August Congress passed the Quit India resolution at Gowalia Tank in Bombay, and Gandhi called on the people to 'do or die'. Early next morning Gandhi, Nehru, Patel and the rest of the leadership were arrested. Leaderless crowds rose spontaneously, attacking police stations, post offices and railways and cutting telegraph lines; parts of Bihar and eastern United Provinces briefly slipped out of British control, and parallel governments were set up in some places. The authorities used troops and even aircraft to suppress the revolt; about a hundred thousand were arrested and over a thousand killed. Though crushed, the movement convinced Britain it could not rule India after the war.

events.title: The Bengal famine of 1943
events.short: War, the loss of Burmese rice, natural disaster and colonial mismanagement brought famine to Bengal, killing some two to three million people.
events.detail: Japan's occupation of Burma in 1942 cut off Bengal's rice imports, and a cyclone that year destroyed coastal crops. Fearing a Japanese invasion, the British confiscated boats and grain along the coast, while wartime inflation and hoarding drove rice prices up several times. The colonial government at first denied there was a famine and prioritised supplies to Calcutta and the army, and London refused most requests for emergency grain shipments. In 1943 tens of thousands of starving people poured into the streets of Calcutta, many dying on the pavements. The famine and the disease that followed killed an estimated 2.1 to 3 million people. The artist Zainul Abedin's sketches recorded the tragedy, and the economist Amartya Sen later studied its causes.

events.title: Subhas Chandra Bose and the Indian National Army
events.short: Subhas Chandra Bose, a former Congress president, proclaimed the Provisional Government of Free India in Singapore and led the Indian National Army alongside Japan against India.
events.detail: Subhas Chandra Bose, a radical Bengali nationalist, was twice elected Congress president, in 1938 and 1939, but resigned after differences with Gandhi over methods. In 1941 he escaped house arrest, travelled through Afghanistan to Germany and later reached Japanese-occupied Southeast Asia by submarine, taking command of the Indian National Army of captured Indian soldiers. On 21 October 1943 in Singapore he proclaimed the Provisional Government of Free India, declaring 'Give me blood and I will give you freedom'. The INA's advance on Imphal with the Japanese in 1944 failed. He died after a plane crash in Taipei in August 1945. Britain's postwar trials of INA officers aroused wide sympathy in India and hastened British withdrawal.

events.title: The Royal Indian Navy mutiny
events.short: Ratings of the Royal Indian Navy mutinied in Bombay, with over seventy ships involved; though it ended within days, it showed Britain it could no longer rely on Indian forces.
events.detail: After the war Britain's public trial of Indian National Army officers at Delhi's Red Fort provoked nationwide protest, and even the armed forces sympathised with the accused. On 18 February 1946 ratings on the signals training ship HMIS Talwar in Bombay struck over poor food, racial discrimination and unfair treatment; the strike spread to Karachi, Madras, Calcutta and other ports, involving some twenty thousand sailors and more than seventy ships and shore establishments, which hoisted the flags of Congress, the League and the Communists. Bombay workers struck in support, and clashes with troops and police left over two hundred dead. Persuaded by Congress and League leaders, the sailors surrendered within days. The British Cabinet then sent a mission to negotiate the transfer of power.

events.title: Direct Action Day and the Calcutta killings
events.short: After the Cabinet Mission plan collapsed, the Muslim League called a 'Direct Action Day'; massive communal riots in Calcutta killed thousands, and violence spread to Noakhali and Bihar.
events.detail: In 1946 the British Cabinet Mission proposed keeping India united as a loose federation with provinces grouped by religion; Congress and the League at first accepted, but mutual distrust over details wrecked the plan. Jinnah declared 16 August 'Direct Action Day' to press for Pakistan. That day Calcutta erupted into Hindu–Muslim killing that lasted for days, leaving about four thousand dead and a hundred thousand homeless, the 'Great Calcutta Killings'. In October Hindus were attacked in Noakhali in eastern Bengal, and Gandhi walked barefoot from village to village pleading for peace; massacres of Muslims followed in Bihar. Partition had become all but inevitable.

events.title: The Constituent Assembly convenes
events.short: India's Constituent Assembly first met in New Delhi and spent nearly three years drafting the constitution, with B. R. Ambedkar chairing the drafting committee.
events.detail: Under the Cabinet Mission plan the provincial legislatures indirectly elected a Constituent Assembly, which first met on 9 December 1946 in the Central Hall of Parliament House in New Delhi; the Muslim League boycotted it. Rajendra Prasad was elected president, and Nehru moved the Objectives Resolution declaring that India would be an independent sovereign republic. After partition the assembly also served as the provisional parliament. In August 1947 Ambedkar was appointed chairman of the drafting committee. Meeting for 165 days and debating the draft clause by clause, the assembly adopted on 26 November 1949 one of the longest written constitutions in the world, guaranteeing universal suffrage, fundamental rights and protections for the untouchables.

events.title: The Mountbatten Plan
events.short: The last Viceroy, Mountbatten, announced the partition plan: India and Pakistan would become independent, Punjab and Bengal would be divided, and the handover was brought forward to 15 August.
events.detail: In February 1947 Prime Minister Attlee announced that Britain would leave India by June 1948 and sent Lord Mountbatten as Viceroy. After talks with the leaders, Mountbatten concluded partition was unavoidable and on 3 June announced his plan: British India would become two dominions, India and Pakistan; Punjab and Bengal would be divided by religious majority; and the princely states would choose which to join. Congress and the League both accepted, to Gandhi's deep sorrow. Mountbatten brought the handover forward to 15 August 1947. Cyril Radcliffe, a British lawyer who had never been to India, drew the boundary on maps in just five weeks; it was published only two days after independence.

events.title: Indian independence
events.short: At the stroke of midnight India became independent; Nehru gave his 'Tryst with Destiny' speech, raised the tricolour at the Red Fort and became the first prime minister.
events.detail: Under the Indian Independence Act passed by Parliament, at midnight on 14 August 1947 British India was divided and India and Pakistan became independent dominions. In the Constituent Assembly in New Delhi Nehru declared: 'Long years ago we made a tryst with destiny… At the stroke of the midnight hour, when the world sleeps, India will awake to life and freedom.' On 15 August he raised the saffron, white and green tricolour with Ashoka's wheel at the Red Fort and became India's first prime minister, with Mountbatten invited to stay as first Governor-General. Gandhi did not attend; he was in Calcutta, fasting and praying to quell communal violence. 15 August is India's Independence Day.

events.title: The great migration of Partition
events.short: Partition set off one of the largest migrations in history: some fifteen million people crossed the new borders, and communal killing left hundreds of thousands to two million dead.
events.detail: When the boundary was published, millions in Punjab and Bengal found themselves on the 'wrong' side. Hindus and Sikhs fled West Punjab and East Bengal for India while Muslims moved to Pakistan, on foot or crammed into trains, so that within months some ten to twenty million people were uprooted. The communal killing in Punjab was especially savage: 'ghost trains' full of corpses crossed the border and tens of thousands of women were abducted. Estimates of the dead range from two hundred thousand to two million. Delhi, Calcutta and other cities were flooded with refugees, and the trauma marked families for generations. The memory of Partition still shapes India–Pakistan relations.

events.title: The first Kashmir war
events.short: Tribal forces from Pakistan entered Kashmir; Maharaja Hari Singh signed the accession to India, war followed, and a UN-brokered ceasefire came in 1949.
events.detail: The princely state of Jammu and Kashmir had a mostly Muslim population but a Hindu ruler, Maharaja Hari Singh, who delayed choosing between the two dominions. In October 1947 Pashtun tribal forces from Pakistan's North-West Frontier invaded Kashmir and approached the capital, Srinagar. Hari Singh appealed to India for help and on 26 October signed the Instrument of Accession; Indian troops were airlifted to Srinagar and fought the tribesmen and, later, the Pakistani army. India referred the dispute to the United Nations, and a ceasefire took effect on 1 January 1949, leaving a line dividing Kashmir into Indian- and Pakistani-administered parts. Kashmir remains the core dispute between the two countries.

events.title: The assassination of Gandhi
events.short: Gandhi was shot dead by the Hindu extremist Nathuram Godse on his way to evening prayers at Birla House, Delhi, aged 78; Nehru said 'the light has gone out of our lives'.
events.detail: After independence Gandhi kept working to stop communal conflict; in January 1948 he fasted in Delhi, demanding an end to violence against Muslims and that India pay Pakistan its share of assets. Some Hindu extremists blamed him for favouring Muslims and for partition. On the evening of 30 January, as Gandhi walked to his prayer meeting in the garden of Birla House, Nathuram Godse stepped forward and fired three shots into his chest, killing him. Nehru said on the radio: 'The light has gone out of our lives and there is darkness everywhere.' Millions attended the funeral the next day, and he was cremated at Raj Ghat by the Yamuna. Godse was hanged in 1949.

events.title: Independent India's first Olympic gold
events.short: India's hockey team beat Britain 4–0 in the final of the London Olympics, winning independent India's first Olympic gold and extending its golden age of hockey.
events.detail: Since the 1928 Amsterdam Olympics India had won three consecutive hockey golds, led by the legendary Dhyan Chand, the 'wizard'. London 1948 was independent India's first Olympics, and the team had been rebuilt after several players went to Pakistan at partition. On 12 August, in the final at Wembley, India beat the hosts Britain 4–0 and raised the tricolour in the land of the former colonial power, a moment of great national pride. India won gold again in 1952 and 1956 and has eight Olympic hockey golds in all. The story was later told in the film Gold.

events.title: Integrating the princely states
events.short: Patel and V. P. Menon persuaded over five hundred princely states to join India; the Nizam of Hyderabad, who refused, was brought in after an Indian 'police action'.
events.detail: At independence there were over 560 princely states outside British India, covering about two-fifths of the subcontinent. Home Minister Vallabhbhai Patel and his secretary V. P. Menon used negotiation, privy purses and the retention of titles to persuade nearly all the princes to sign accession before independence. The Muslim Nizam of Hyderabad, ruler of the largest and richest state in the south, sought independence while Razakar militias terrorised his subjects. On 13 September 1948 the Indian army launched a 'police action', Operation Polo, and the Nizam surrendered four days later. Junagadh, Travancore and others were also resolved. Patel became known as the 'Iron Man of India'.

events.title: India becomes a republic
events.short: The Constitution came into force and India became a sovereign democratic republic, with Rajendra Prasad as first president; it guaranteed universal suffrage and fundamental rights and abolished untouchability.
events.detail: On 26 January 1950, anniversary of the 1930 declaration of complete independence, the Constitution came into force and India changed from a Commonwealth dominion into a republic; the British monarch ceased to be head of state. Rajendra Prasad was sworn in as first president. With 395 articles, the constitution was among the longest in the world, establishing a federal parliamentary democracy, universal adult suffrage and fundamental rights such as freedom of speech and religion; it abolished untouchability and reserved seats and posts for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. The lion capital of Ashoka became the national emblem and Tagore's Jana Gana Mana the anthem. A grand parade is held in New Delhi every year on this day.

events.title: Mother Teresa founds the Missionaries of Charity
events.short: The Albanian-born nun Teresa founded the Missionaries of Charity in Calcutta to care for the dying, lepers and orphans, winning the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979.
events.detail: Teresa was born to an Albanian family in Skopje, now in North Macedonia, joined the Irish Loreto Sisters at 18 and came to India in 1929, teaching at a girls' school in Calcutta for nearly twenty years. In 1946, on a train, she felt a 'call within a call' to leave the convent and serve the poorest of the poor. Adopting a white sari with a blue border and Indian citizenship, she received Vatican approval to found the Missionaries of Charity on 7 October 1950. In 1952 she opened a home for the dying beside the Kali temple, so that people dying on the streets could die with dignity, and later leprosy homes and orphanages. She won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979 and was canonised in 2016.

events.title: The First Five-Year Plan
events.short: Nehru's Planning Commission launched the First Five-Year Plan, focused on agriculture and irrigation, setting India on a state-led mixed economy.
events.detail: Influenced by Fabian socialism and Soviet planning, Nehru believed the state must lead industrialisation and the fight against poverty. A Planning Commission chaired by the prime minister was set up in 1950, and the First Five-Year Plan began in 1951, emphasising agriculture, irrigation and power and building great projects such as Bhakra–Nangal and the Damodar Valley; Nehru called dams 'the temples of modern India'. The Second Plan from 1956 shifted to heavy industry, building state steel plants at Bhilai, Rourkela and Durgapur. This mixed economy of public and private sectors under tight state control lasted until the reforms of 1991.

events.title: The first general election
events.short: India held its first general election under universal suffrage; most of its 173 million voters were illiterate and voted using party symbols, and Congress won a landslide.
events.detail: It was the largest democratic election the world had yet seen. Chief Election Commissioner Sukumar Sen organised the immense task: about 173 million voters, some 85 per cent of them illiterate, voting at nearly two hundred thousand polling stations over more than four months. So that illiterate people could vote, every party had a pictorial symbol, such as Congress's pair of bullocks, and each candidate a ballot box bearing a symbol, into which voters dropped their paper. Indelible ink on the finger prevented repeat voting. Congress won 364 of the 489 seats in the Lok Sabha and Nehru remained prime minister. The election showed that democracy could work in a vast, poor and diverse country.

events.title: Vinoba Bhave's land-gift movement
events.short: Gandhi's disciple Vinoba Bhave walked across India persuading landlords to give land voluntarily to the landless, collecting pledges of over four million acres.
events.detail: In 1951 Telangana was the scene of a Communist-led peasant armed struggle over land. Gandhi's disciple Vinoba Bhave went there, and on 18 April in the village of Pochampally landless untouchables told him of their plight, whereupon a landlord offered a hundred acres on the spot. Thus began the Bhoodan, land-gift, movement: for more than a decade Bhave walked all over India asking landowners to give a sixth of their land to the landless, later extending it to gifts of whole villages. Pledges exceeded four million acres, though much was poor land and only part was actually distributed. Bhave was the first recipient of the Magsaysay Award and was posthumously awarded the Bharat Ratna.

events.title: Le Corbusier's Chandigarh
events.short: Having lost Lahore at Partition, Punjab needed a new capital; Nehru invited Le Corbusier to design Chandigarh, a landmark of modernist planning.
events.detail: Partition gave the old capital, Lahore, to Pakistan, and Indian Punjab needed a new one. Nehru wanted a city 'unfettered by the traditions of the past, a symbol of the nation's faith in the future'. In 1951 the Swiss-French architect Le Corbusier was engaged to plan it; he divided the city into self-contained grid sectors on the analogy of the human body, with the government at the 'head'. His raw-concrete Assembly, High Court and Secretariat are monumental, fronted by the Open Hand monument symbolising giving and receiving. In 2016 Chandigarh's Capitol Complex was inscribed as a World Heritage Site among Le Corbusier's works.

events.title: The first Indian Institute of Technology
events.short: The first Indian Institute of Technology opened in the former Hijli detention camp for political prisoners; the IITs went on to train world-class engineers.
events.detail: Independent India urgently needed engineers to build the nation. On the Sarkar Committee's recommendation, the government founded higher technical institutes modelled on MIT; the first opened in 1951 at Kharagpur in West Bengal, housed in the colonial Hijli detention camp for political prisoners. Nehru said: 'Here in the place of that Hijli detention camp stands this fine monument of India, representing India's urges, India's future.' IITs followed at Bombay, Madras, Kanpur and Delhi, with aid from the US, the USSR, West Germany and Britain. Admission is fiercely competitive, and many graduates have become leaders of global technology firms.

events.title: The first Asian Games in New Delhi
events.short: The first Asian Games were held in New Delhi, with nearly five hundred athletes from eleven nations, expressing the solidarity of newly independent Asian countries.
events.detail: At the Asian Relations Conference in New Delhi in 1947, the Indian sports official G. D. Sondhi proposed games for Asians. From 4 to 11 March 1951 the first Asian Games were held at the National Stadium in New Delhi; Nehru supplied the motto 'Ever onward', still the Games' motto today. About five hundred athletes from eleven countries, including Afghanistan, Burma, Ceylon, Indonesia, Iran and Japan, competed in six sports such as athletics, swimming and football; Japan topped the medal table and India came second. New Delhi hosted the Games again in 1982, which spurred the spread of colour television in India.

events.title: The Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence
events.short: China and India set out the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence in their agreement on trade with Tibet; Zhou Enlai and Nehru exchanged visits amid the slogan 'Indians and Chinese are brothers'.
events.detail: In April 1954 China and India signed an agreement on trade and intercourse between the Tibet region of China and India, whose preamble set out five principles: mutual respect for territorial integrity and sovereignty, non-aggression, non-interference in internal affairs, equality and mutual benefit, and peaceful coexistence; India called them Panchsheel. In June Zhou Enlai visited India and reaffirmed them with Nehru in a joint statement, and Nehru visited China in October, amid the popular slogan 'Hindi-Chini bhai-bhai'. The principles were adopted by the Bandung Conference of 1955 and became an important norm of international relations, though differences over the boundary soon emerged and relations grew tense by the end of the decade.

events.title: Satyajit Ray's Pather Panchali
events.short: Satyajit Ray's debut Pather Panchali, a realist portrait of childhood in rural Bengal, won a prize at Cannes and brought Indian art cinema to the world.
events.detail: Satyajit Ray was a graphic designer at a Calcutta advertising agency who resolved to make films after seeing Bicycle Thieves in London. Working in his spare time with non-professional actors and very little money, he took nearly three years to shoot Pather Panchali; when funds ran out the West Bengal government stepped in. Adapted from a Bengali novel, it follows the boy Apu and his sister Durga growing up in a poor Brahmin family in a village, with music by the sitar master Ravi Shankar. At Cannes in 1956 it won the prize for Best Human Document. With its sequels it forms the Apu Trilogy. Ray received an honorary Academy Award in 1992.

events.title: The Hindu Code Bills
events.short: Parliament passed the Hindu Marriage Act, Succession Act and related laws, establishing monogamy, permitting divorce and giving daughters the right to inherit.
events.detail: Before independence Hindu marriage, inheritance and family matters were governed by ancient local custom and scripture, and women had almost no right to divorce or inherit. Law Minister Ambedkar drafted a unified Hindu Code, but it met fierce opposition from conservative members and President Prasad; when the bill stalled in 1951 Ambedkar resigned in protest. After the 1952 election Nehru split the code into separate laws, passing in 1955–56 the Hindu Marriage Act, Hindu Succession Act, Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act and Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act. They established monogamy, allowed divorce and inter-caste marriage, and gave daughters a share of their father's property alongside sons.

events.title: States reorganised by language
events.short: After Potti Sreeramulu fasted to death for a Telugu-speaking Andhra state, India redrew its states along linguistic lines, laying the basis of today's federal map.
events.detail: At first independent India kept the colonial provinces and princely boundaries, and many states contained speakers of several languages. Nehru, fearing that linguistic states would encourage separatism, long resisted change. In 1952 Gandhi's follower Potti Sreeramulu fasted for a Telugu-speaking Andhra state to be carved from Madras; his death after 58 days sparked mass riots, and the government agreed to create Andhra. In 1956 Parliament, following the States Reorganisation Commission, passed a law that from 1 November divided the country along linguistic lines into 14 states and 6 union territories, creating Kerala, Mysore (Karnataka) and others. In 1960 Bombay State was split into Maharashtra and Gujarat.

events.title: Ambedkar embraces Buddhism
events.short: Constitution-maker Ambedkar led about half a million followers to embrace Buddhism at Nagpur to escape caste oppression, launching the Dalit Buddhist movement.
events.detail: Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar was born into an untouchable family in Maharashtra; as a schoolboy he was not allowed to drink water with his classmates. He went on to earn doctorates from Columbia University and the London School of Economics, became a jurist, economist and leader of the untouchables, and chaired the drafting of India's constitution. Long convinced that caste discrimination could not be ended within Hinduism, he declared in 1935: 'I was born a Hindu, but I will not die a Hindu.' On 14 October 1956 at Nagpur he and his wife took Buddhist vows, and he then led some half a million followers in mass conversion. He died seven weeks later in Delhi. The site, Deekshabhoomi, draws hundreds of thousands every year.

events.title: Asia's first nuclear reactor
events.short: The Apsara research reactor, built under Homi Bhabha, went critical at Trombay near Bombay, Asia's first nuclear reactor and the start of India's nuclear programme.
events.detail: Homi Jehangir Bhabha, from a prominent Bombay Parsi family, researched cosmic rays at Cambridge and stayed in India during the Second World War, working at the Indian Institute of Science. He persuaded the Tatas and Nehru to back nuclear physics, founded the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research in 1945 and in 1948 became chairman of the Atomic Energy Commission, devising a three-stage nuclear programme to exploit India's large thorium reserves. On 4 August 1956 the Apsara swimming-pool research reactor, built with British help, went critical at Trombay, the first nuclear reactor in Asia. Bhabha died in an air crash near Mont Blanc in 1966; the Trombay research centre bears his name.

events.title: The film Mother India
events.short: Mehboob Khan's Mother India, the story of a poor peasant woman keeping her dignity through hardship, became a Bollywood classic and India's first Oscar nominee for foreign-language film.
events.detail: The 1950s were a golden age of Hindi cinema in Bombay; stars such as Raj Kapoor and Dilip Kumar were household names, and film songs became part of everyday life. In 1957 Mehboob Khan's Mother India was released. Nargis plays Radha, a peasant woman who raises her children alone through her husband's desertion, floods and the moneylender's oppression, and finally shoots her own son, who has become a bandit, to uphold the village's honour. Making a mother the symbol of the new nation and celebrating labour and sacrifice, the film was a huge success and was nominated for the 1958 Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film, losing by a single vote. It is still counted among India's greatest films.

events.title: A Communist government in Kerala
events.short: The Communist Party of India won the Kerala state election and E. M. S. Namboodiripad became chief minister, one of the world's first elected Communist governments.
events.detail: In Kerala's second state election in 1957 the Communist Party of India won a majority, and on 5 April E. M. S. Namboodiripad, from a Brahmin landlord family, formed the state government, one of the first Communist governments anywhere to come to power through elections. It pursued land reform, restricting the eviction of tenants, and education reform, increasing control over private schools. The education bill provoked fierce opposition from the Catholic Church and caste organisations, and in 1959 a mass 'Liberation Struggle' led the central government to dismiss the ministry for breakdown of order. Since then Kerala has alternated between left and Congress-led coalitions and leads India in literacy, health and life expectancy.

events.title: India takes Goa
events.short: When Portugal refused to give up Goa, its colony for 450 years, the Indian army launched Operation Vijay and took Goa, Daman and Diu in two days.
events.detail: After independence France returned Pondicherry and its other enclaves in 1954, but Salazar's Portugal insisted Goa was an overseas province and refused to negotiate. Goan independence activists were repressed, and in 1955 Portuguese forces fired on Indian non-violent marchers entering Goa. Nehru long advocated a peaceful settlement but finally lost patience in 1961. On 18 December Indian land, sea and air forces launched Operation Vijay; the heavily outnumbered Portuguese garrison barely resisted, and the governor signed the surrender on the 19th, ending Portuguese rule in Goa dating from 1510. Western countries criticised India's use of force, and Portugal recognised Indian sovereignty only after its 1974 revolution.

events.title: The Non-Aligned Movement
events.short: Nehru, with Tito, Nasser, Sukarno and Nkrumah, launched the Non-Aligned Movement in Belgrade, urging new nations to join neither the US nor the Soviet bloc.
events.detail: As the Cold War began, Nehru insisted that India join neither the American- nor the Soviet-led military alliances, judging each international issue independently while cooperating with and accepting aid from both blocs. He worked to mediate in the Korean War and played a leading role at the Asian–African Conference at Bandung in Indonesia in 1955. In September 1961 Nehru, Tito of Yugoslavia, Nasser of Egypt, Sukarno of Indonesia and Nkrumah of Ghana convened the first summit of non-aligned countries in Belgrade, attended by 25 states, formally launching the Non-Aligned Movement. Non-alignment long remained a basic principle of Indian foreign policy.

events.title: The Sino-Indian War
events.short: A month-long war broke out between China and India over their disputed boundary in the eastern and western sectors; India was defeated, China declared a ceasefire and withdrew, and India's defence policy changed profoundly.
events.detail: China and India disagreed over the alignment of their boundary, chiefly over Aksai Chin in the west and the area south of the McMahon Line in the east. In the late 1950s relations deteriorated over the boundary and Tibet, and India's 'Forward Policy' of setting up posts in disputed areas led to repeated clashes. On 20 October 1962 war broke out in both sectors at once, and the unprepared Indian army was defeated. On 21 November China declared a unilateral ceasefire and withdrew in the east to north of the line of actual control. The war dealt Nehru a heavy blow, and Defence Minister Krishna Menon resigned. India greatly increased defence spending afterwards, and the boundary question remains unresolved.

events.title: India's first sounding rocket
events.short: Scientists led by Vikram Sarabhai assembled a rocket in a church at the fishing village of Thumba in Kerala and launched India's first sounding rocket, beginning the Indian space programme.
events.detail: The physicist Vikram Sarabhai believed space technology could help developing countries with communications, weather forecasting and education. Thumba, close to the magnetic equator, was ideal for studying the upper atmosphere; the local St Mary Magdalene church and bishop's house were given over as offices and laboratories, and rocket parts were carried by bicycle and bullock cart. On 21 November 1963 an American-made Nike-Apache sounding rocket was launched there, with the young engineer A. P. J. Abdul Kalam among the team. Sarabhai founded the Indian Space Research Organisation in 1969 and is honoured as the father of India's space programme. The church is now a space museum.

events.title: Death of Nehru
events.short: Nehru died of a heart attack after 17 years as prime minister, having laid the foundations of India's parliamentary democracy, secularism, planned economy and non-alignment; Lal Bahadur Shastri succeeded him.
events.detail: Jawaharlal Nehru, from a Kashmiri Brahmin family, was educated at Harrow and Cambridge, became one of Gandhi's closest followers and was jailed nine times. Prime minister without interruption from 1947, he upheld parliamentary democracy and the secular state, pursued state-led industrialisation and founded the IITs and the atomic energy and space agencies, while championing non-alignment abroad. He was also criticised over the war with China, Kashmir and slow economic growth. His health declined sharply after 1962, and he died on 27 May 1964. His birthday, 14 November, is India's Children's Day, for he loved children, who called him 'Chacha Nehru', Uncle Nehru.

events.title: The anti-Hindi agitation in Tamil Nadu
events.short: The constitution made Hindi the sole official language from 1965, sparking mass protests in Tamil Nadu; the government finally guaranteed English could continue indefinitely.
events.detail: The constitution-makers fiercely debated the official language and settled on Hindi in Devanagari script as the official language of the Union, with English continuing as an associate language for fifteen years, until 26 January 1965. As the deadline approached, the non-Hindi-speaking south, Tamil Nadu above all, feared disadvantage in jobs and examinations. In January 1965 mass protests broke out in Madras State: students struck, some burned themselves to death, and clashes with police killed dozens. Prime Minister Shastri promised that English would continue as long as non-Hindi regions wished, a pledge given legal force in 1967. Riding the wave, the DMK won the state election in 1967, and Congress has never since governed Tamil Nadu.

events.title: The Indo-Pakistani war of 1965
events.short: Pakistan infiltrated fighters into Kashmir, India opened a new front in Punjab, and large tank battles followed before a ceasefire demanded by the UN Security Council.
events.detail: In spring 1965 India and Pakistan clashed in the Rann of Kutch in Gujarat. In August Pakistan launched Operation Gibraltar, sending armed infiltrators into Indian-administered Kashmir in hope of sparking a local uprising, which did not come. When the Pakistani army attacked in the Chhamb sector of southern Kashmir in early September, India crossed the international border towards Lahore. Some of the largest tank battles since the Second World War were fought around Asal Uttar and Sialkot in Punjab. On 22 September both sides accepted a ceasefire demanded by the UN Security Council, with the fighting at a stalemate. Prime Minister Shastri's slogan 'Jai Jawan, Jai Kisan', hail the soldier, hail the farmer, became popular.

events.title: The Tashkent Declaration and Shastri's death
events.short: With Soviet mediation Shastri and Pakistan's President Ayub Khan signed the Tashkent Declaration, withdrawing to prewar positions; Shastri died suddenly in Tashkent the next day.
events.detail: Lal Bahadur Shastri, from a modest family in the United Provinces and known for his honesty and simplicity, succeeded Nehru as prime minister in 1964. After the 1965 war Soviet Premier Alexei Kosygin invited the Indian and Pakistani leaders to peace talks in Tashkent in Soviet Uzbekistan. On 10 January 1966 Shastri and Pakistan's President Ayub Khan signed the Tashkent Declaration, agreeing to withdraw their forces to positions held before August 1965, restore diplomatic relations and settle disputes peacefully. In the early hours of the next day Shastri died of a heart attack in Tashkent, aged 61. Congress chose Nehru's daughter Indira Gandhi to succeed him.

events.title: Indira Gandhi becomes prime minister
events.short: Nehru's daughter Indira Gandhi was chosen prime minister by Congress elders; she unexpectedly took firm control and dominated Indian politics for nearly two decades.
events.detail: Indira Gandhi was Nehru's only child and no relation of the Mahatma; her surname came from her husband Feroze Gandhi. Raised amid the national movement and educated at Oxford, she served as her father's aide and hostess while he was prime minister. After Shastri's sudden death the Congress elders known as the 'Syndicate' chose her as prime minister, thinking they could control the woman opponents mocked as a 'dumb doll'. She soon proved a tough politician, broke with the elders in 1969, splitting Congress, and won the 1971 election with the slogan 'Garibi Hatao', remove poverty. India's only woman prime minister, she remains one of its most controversial and influential leaders.

events.title: The Green Revolution
events.short: India adopted high-yielding dwarf wheat and rice with irrigation and fertilisers; grain output soared and the country ended its dependence on food imports.
events.detail: In the mid-1960s India suffered successive droughts and lived on American food aid, a situation described as 'ship to mouth'. The agricultural scientist M. S. Swaminathan invited Norman Borlaug to introduce the high-yielding dwarf wheat bred in Mexico, and from 1966 it was spread widely in well-irrigated Punjab and Haryana, together with fertilisers, pesticides, tube wells and guaranteed government procurement prices. The 1968 wheat harvest set a record, celebrated with a commemorative stamp. By the late 1970s India was self-sufficient in food grains. The Green Revolution also widened regional disparities and caused groundwater depletion and soil degradation.

events.title: Bank nationalisation
events.short: Indira Gandhi's government nationalised the fourteen largest commercial banks, directing credit to villages and small businesses, a landmark of her turn to the left.
events.detail: In the 1960s India's big banks were mostly controlled by a few industrial families, and loans went mainly to large firms while villages and small businesses struggled for credit. On 19 July 1969 Indira Gandhi nationalised by ordinance the fourteen largest commercial banks, holding about 85 per cent of deposits. The move was also part of her struggle against the conservative party elders and proved hugely popular. Afterwards the banks opened many rural branches and gave priority lending to agriculture and small enterprises, raising savings markedly, but also bringing inefficiency and political interference. Six more banks were nationalised in 1980.

events.title: The Indian Space Research Organisation
events.short: Vikram Sarabhai founded ISRO; in 1975 India's first satellite, Aryabhata, was launched on a Soviet rocket.
events.detail: On Independence Day 1969 the space research committee under the Department of Atomic Energy was reorganised as the Indian Space Research Organisation, led by Vikram Sarabhai, with the aim of using space technology for national development. On 19 April 1975 India's first home-built satellite, named after the ancient astronomer Aryabhata, was launched from Kapustin Yar in the Soviet Union. In 1980 India launched the Rohini satellite on its own SLV-3 rocket, becoming the seventh nation able to launch satellites independently; the project director was A. P. J. Abdul Kalam. The INSAT system later served television, communications and weather forecasting.

events.title: Operation Flood and the White Revolution
events.short: Verghese Kurien spread the Anand milk cooperative model of Gujarat, organising millions of smallholders and making India the world's largest milk producer.
events.detail: In 1946 dairy farmers of Kaira district in Gujarat, with Patel's backing, formed a cooperative to escape the low prices paid by private dealers; it later adopted the brand Amul. The engineer Verghese Kurien came to Anand, helped build a modern dairy plant and made milk powder from buffalo milk for the first time. As head of the National Dairy Development Board from 1965, he launched Operation Flood in 1970, using donated European milk powder and butter to raise funds and spreading the 'Anand pattern' nationwide: village cooperatives collected smallholders' milk, paid by quality, and unions processed and marketed it. By 1998 India had overtaken the United States as the largest milk producer, and Kurien was called the 'father of the White Revolution'.

events.title: The 1971 war and the birth of Bangladesh
events.short: The crisis in East Pakistan drove nearly ten million refugees into India; India intervened in support of the Bengalis and after 13 days Pakistani forces surrendered in Dhaka, creating Bangladesh.
events.detail: In Pakistan's 1970 election the Awami League of East Pakistan won a majority, but the military government in the west refused to hand over power. In March 1971 the army launched a crackdown in East Pakistan, killing huge numbers of civilians, and nearly ten million refugees fled into West Bengal and other Indian states. Indira Gandhi sought international support, signed a friendship treaty with the Soviet Union in August and aided Bengali guerrillas. When Pakistan's air force struck airfields in western India on 3 December, India went to war in full; under army chief Sam Manekshaw its forces advanced rapidly with the guerrillas. On 16 December some ninety thousand Pakistani troops surrendered in Dhaka, one of the largest surrenders since the Second World War, and Bangladesh became independent.

events.title: The Simla Agreement
events.short: Indira Gandhi and Pakistan's President Bhutto signed the Simla Agreement, pledging to settle disputes through bilateral talks and renaming the Kashmir ceasefire line the Line of Control.
events.detail: After the 1971 war India held some ninety thousand Pakistani prisoners and some Pakistani territory. At the end of June 1972 Pakistan's President Zulfikar Ali Bhutto came to the Himalayan hill station of Simla to negotiate with Indira Gandhi. On 2 July they signed an agreement to respect each other's territorial integrity and settle differences peacefully through bilateral negotiation without force; troops withdrew to the international border, and the Kashmir ceasefire line was renamed the Line of Control. India later released the prisoners. India has since cited the agreement to insist that Kashmir is a purely bilateral issue.

events.title: The Chipko movement
events.short: Himalayan villagers hugged trees to stop commercial logging, with women at the forefront; it marked the beginning of India's modern environmental movement.
events.detail: In the early 1970s the forests of the hill districts of Uttar Pradesh (now Uttarakhand) were sold in large lots to outside timber merchants; deforestation brought floods and landslides, while villagers were refused even a few trees for farm tools. In 1973 villagers of Mandal, organised by the Gandhian Chandi Prasad Bhatt, first stopped loggers by hugging the trees. In March 1974, when the men of Reni were away, Gaura Devi led 27 women to guard the forest until the loggers withdrew. 'Chipko' is Hindi for 'to cling'. Publicised by Sunderlal Bahuguna, the movement won national attention, and in 1980 the central government banned felling in the Himalayan forests for fifteen years.

events.title: The first nuclear test
events.short: India set off an underground nuclear explosion code-named Smiling Buddha at Pokhran in Rajasthan, calling it peaceful, and became the sixth country to test a nuclear device.
events.detail: After the 1962 war and China's nuclear test in 1964, India began secret research on nuclear explosives. On 18 May 1974, the Buddhist festival of Buddha Purnima, India detonated an underground device of about 8 kilotons at the army range at Pokhran in Rajasthan's Thar Desert. The scientist in charge, Raja Ramanna, reported to the prime minister in code: 'The Buddha is smiling.' The government called it a 'peaceful nuclear explosion' with no military purpose. India thus became the first country outside the five permanent members of the UN Security Council to test a nuclear device. The test prompted the formation of the Nuclear Suppliers Group and a long embargo on nuclear technology to India.

events.title: Sikkim joins India
events.short: In a referendum the Himalayan kingdom of Sikkim voted to abolish its monarchy, and it then became India's 22nd state.
events.detail: Sikkim was a small kingdom between Nepal, Bhutan and Tibet ruled by the Buddhist Chogyal dynasty; from 1950 it was an Indian protectorate, with India in charge of its foreign affairs and defence. The Nepali-origin majority resented the monarchy, and in the early 1970s a movement for democratic reform arose. In an April 1975 referendum an overwhelming majority of voters backed abolishing the monarchy and joining India, and on 16 May Sikkim formally became a state of India. The king, his supporters and some other countries criticised the conduct of the vote. Its capital, Gangtok, is now a popular Himalayan destination.

events.title: The Emergency
events.short: After a court found Indira Gandhi guilty of electoral malpractice and the opposition demanded her resignation, she declared a national Emergency, jailing opponents and censoring the press for 21 months.
events.detail: In the early 1970s inflation, unemployment and corruption fuelled discontent, and the Gandhian Jayaprakash Narayan launched a movement for 'total revolution'. On 12 June 1975 the Allahabad High Court found Indira Gandhi guilty of electoral malpractice in 1971 and voided her seat. The opposition called nationwide protests demanding her resignation. Late on 25 June the president, on her advice, declared a national Emergency. Tens of thousands of opponents were detained without trial, the press was strictly censored, fundamental rights were suspended and elections postponed. Her son Sanjay Gandhi pushed forced sterilisation and slum clearances that caused widespread resentment. The Emergency is regarded as the darkest period in India's democratic history.

events.title: The film Sholay
events.short: The action film Sholay opened and ran for five years at one Bombay cinema; Amitabh Bachchan's 'angry young man' became the idol of a generation.
events.detail: Sholay, directed by Ramesh Sippy, drew on American Westerns and Japanese samurai films: a retired police chief hires two petty crooks to take on the bandit Gabbar Singh, who murdered his family. Shot among the rocky hills near Bangalore, it opened to a lukewarm response but grew through word of mouth and ran for five years at the Minerva cinema in Bombay. Gabbar Singh's lines and the film's songs became part of everyday speech. One of its stars, Amitabh Bachchan, played a series of 'angry young men' rebelling against injustice in the 1970s, catching the public mood around the Emergency, and became Bollywood's biggest star, dubbed the 'star of the millennium'.

events.title: Congress loses power for the first time
events.short: Indira Gandhi unexpectedly called elections; voters punished the Emergency, the Janata Party won, and Morarji Desai became the first non-Congress prime minister.
events.detail: In January 1977 Indira Gandhi unexpectedly called elections for March and released most opposition leaders. The opposition parties quickly merged into the Janata Party, campaigning on the choice between 'democracy and dictatorship'. The result stunned the country: Congress was almost wiped out in the north, Indira Gandhi and her son Sanjay lost their seats, and the Janata alliance won a majority, with the 81-year-old Morarji Desai as prime minister, the first time since independence that Congress lost power at the centre. The peaceful transfer showed the resilience of Indian democracy. But Janata was riven by factions; its government fell in 1979, and Indira Gandhi won the 1980 election.

events.title: India wins the Cricket World Cup
events.short: Kapil Dev's unfancied Indian team beat two-time champions West Indies at Lord's to win the World Cup, and cricket became India's national passion.
events.detail: Cricket came to India in colonial times and was long the preserve of princes and urban elites. At the 1983 World Cup in England, India started at odds of 66 to 1. In a group match against Zimbabwe they slumped to 17 for 5 until captain Kapil Dev hit 175 to turn the game. In the final at Lord's on 25 June India made only 183, but brilliant bowling dismissed the mighty West Indies for 140 to win the title. The victory set off nationwide celebration just as television was spreading, cricket quickly became the dominant sport, and India later became the economic centre of world cricket.

events.title: The first Indian in space
events.short: Indian Air Force pilot Rakesh Sharma flew into space on the Soviet Soyuz T-11 and spent nearly eight days aboard the Salyut 7 space station.
events.detail: Under the Soviet Intercosmos programme India selected two air force pilots in 1982 to train at the Gagarin Cosmonaut Training Centre near Moscow. On 3 April 1984 the 35-year-old Rakesh Sharma lifted off from Baikonur with two Soviet cosmonauts aboard Soyuz T-11 and conducted remote-sensing and yoga-in-weightlessness experiments on the Salyut 7 station. When Indira Gandhi asked him by video link how India looked from space, he replied with the poet Iqbal's words, 'Saare jahan se achha', better than the whole world. The first Indian citizen in space, he received the Ashoka Chakra, India's highest peacetime gallantry award.

events.title: Operation Blue Star
events.short: To expel Sikh militants occupying the Golden Temple at Amritsar, the army stormed the shrine; hundreds died and Sikhism's holiest site was badly damaged.
events.detail: In the early 1980s Sikh militancy rose in Punjab; the preacher Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale demanded greater autonomy, some called for an independent 'Khalistan', and assassinations and violence multiplied. From 1983 Bhindranwale and armed followers occupied and fortified the Golden Temple complex at Amritsar. In early June 1984 Indira Gandhi ordered the army in to clear them out. The militants were well armed, the army brought in tanks, and fighting lasted several days; Bhindranwale was killed, the Akal Takht was badly damaged, and hundreds died, including many pilgrims. The operation deeply wounded Sikh feelings, and months later Indira Gandhi was assassinated.

events.title: The assassination of Indira Gandhi
events.short: Indira Gandhi was shot dead by two Sikh bodyguards at her residence; anti-Sikh riots in Delhi and elsewhere killed thousands, and her son Rajiv became prime minister.
events.detail: On the morning of 31 October 1984, as Indira Gandhi walked through the garden of her Delhi residence to an interview, two Sikh bodyguards, Beant Singh and Satwant Singh, opened fire; she died that day, aged 66. The killing was widely seen as revenge for Operation Blue Star. As the news spread, mass violence against Sikhs broke out in Delhi and other northern cities; mobs searched house to house and many were burned alive, with official figures of nearly three thousand dead in Delhi alone, and some local Congress figures were accused of inciting the mobs. Her son Rajiv Gandhi, a former airline pilot, was sworn in as prime minister the same day, and Congress won a record majority in elections that December.

events.title: The Bhopal gas tragedy
events.short: Union Carbide's pesticide plant in Bhopal leaked tonnes of toxic methyl isocyanate; thousands died that night and hundreds of thousands were harmed in the world's worst industrial disaster.
events.detail: Union Carbide's pesticide plant in Bhopal, capital of Madhya Pradesh, stored large quantities of highly toxic methyl isocyanate; with the plant losing money, its safety systems had long been neglected. Late on 2 December 1984 water entered a storage tank, triggering a violent reaction, and about 40 tonnes of gas poured out over the crowded slums nearby. Residents awoke choking and fled in the dark, many collapsing in the streets. The official toll was about 3,800 immediate deaths, with other estimates of eight to ten thousand; tens of thousands more died of related illness over the following decades, and hundreds of thousands suffered lifelong harm. In 1989 the company settled with the Indian government for 470 million dollars, which victims considered far too little, and the site has still not been fully cleaned up.

events.title: The Shah Bano case
events.short: The Supreme Court ruled that the divorced Muslim woman Shah Bano was entitled to maintenance from her ex-husband; after conservative protests Rajiv Gandhi's government passed a law overturning it.
events.detail: India applies separate personal laws to members of different religions in marriage, inheritance and family matters. Shah Bano, a 62-year-old Muslim woman, was divorced by triple talaq after more than forty years of marriage and sought maintenance under the criminal procedure code. In April 1985 the Supreme Court ruled in her favour and urged a uniform civil code. Conservative Muslims saw the ruling as interference in Islamic law and protested on a massive scale. In 1986 Rajiv Gandhi's government passed the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, effectively nullifying the judgement; critics called it a surrender to religious conservatives, and Hindu nationalists accused Congress of 'appeasing' minorities. The case became a focal point of India's debates on secularism.

events.title: The television Ramayan
events.short: State television broadcast the serial Ramayan; on Sunday mornings streets emptied as tens of millions watched, making it one of the most watched series in the world at the time.
events.detail: In the 1980s colour television spread quickly in India after the broadcast of the 1982 Asian Games, and the state broadcaster Doordarshan was the only channel. From January 1987 Ramanand Sagar's adaptation of the epic Ramayan aired on Sunday mornings for 78 episodes. As it played, streets in towns and villages fell empty; many viewers lit incense and offered flowers before their sets and treated the actors like gods. Each episode is estimated to have drawn over a hundred million viewers. A Mahabharat series followed from 1988. Scholars note that the serials reinforced a nationwide image of the epics and fed into the Ram temple movement that followed. A rerun during the 2020 lockdown set new viewing records.

events.title: Implementing the Mandal Commission
events.short: V. P. Singh's government announced, following the Mandal Commission, a 27 per cent quota in central government jobs for 'Other Backward Classes', sparking fierce protests by upper-caste students.
events.detail: The constitution already reserved seats in legislatures, education and government jobs for Scheduled Castes and Tribes. In 1979 the Janata government appointed a commission under B. P. Mandal to identify other socially and educationally backward castes; its 1980 report estimated these 'Other Backward Classes' at about 52 per cent of the population and recommended reserving 27 per cent of government posts for them, but it was shelved for a decade. In August 1990 Prime Minister V. P. Singh announced its implementation; upper-caste students in the north protested on a large scale, and some set themselves on fire. In 1992 the Supreme Court largely upheld the policy but capped total reservations at 50 per cent. Regional parties of the backward castes then rose rapidly, transforming northern Indian politics.

events.title: The assassination of Rajiv Gandhi
events.short: Former prime minister Rajiv Gandhi was killed by a female suicide bomber of Sri Lanka's Tamil Tigers while campaigning in Tamil Nadu.
events.detail: Rajiv Gandhi, prime minister from 1984 to 1989, promoted telecommunications and computers and cut some tariffs, earning a reputation as a moderniser, though his standing suffered from the Bofors arms scandal. In 1987 he sent an Indian Peace Keeping Force to Sri Lanka, where it fought the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, earning their enmity. On the evening of 21 May 1991, at an election rally at Sriperumbudur in Tamil Nadu, a woman stepped forward to garland him, bent to touch his feet and detonated a belt bomb, killing him and more than a dozen others. He was 46. Weeks later Congress won the election amid a wave of sympathy.

events.title: Economic liberalisation
events.short: With reserves enough for only two weeks of imports, the Rao government and Finance Minister Manmohan Singh launched reforms, scrapping licensing and opening to foreign capital, ushering in rapid growth.
events.detail: In 1991 the Gulf War raised oil prices and cut remittances from workers abroad; on top of chronic fiscal deficits and the collapse of the Soviet Union, India faced a severe balance-of-payments crisis, with reserves enough for only about two weeks of imports, and the government had to fly gold to London as collateral for loans. The new prime minister, P. V. Narasimha Rao, appointed the economist Manmohan Singh finance minister. In his budget speech on 24 July Singh quoted Victor Hugo, 'no power on earth can stop an idea whose time has come', and announced the abolition of most industrial licensing, the 'Licence Raj', a devaluation of the rupee, lower tariffs and opening to foreign investment. Growth accelerated after the reforms, and hundreds of millions escaped poverty.

events.title: Demolition of the Babri Masjid
events.short: In Ayodhya, crowds mobilised by Hindu nationalist groups tore down the sixteenth-century Babri Masjid, which they claimed stood on Rama's birthplace; communal riots followed across India.
events.detail: The Babri Masjid in Ayodhya was built in 1528, reputedly by a general of the Mughal emperor Babur. Many Hindus believe the site is Rama's birthplace and that the mosque was built over a destroyed temple, a dispute dating back to colonial times. In the late 1980s the Vishva Hindu Parishad and the Bharatiya Janata Party launched a campaign to build a Ram temple there, and in 1990 BJP president L. K. Advani toured the country in a vehicle decorated as a chariot. On 6 December 1992 more than a hundred thousand volunteers gathered at Ayodhya, broke through the cordon and demolished the mosque within hours with tools and bare hands. Riots followed in Bombay and elsewhere, killing about two thousand people. In 2019 the Supreme Court awarded the site to the Hindu side for a temple and allotted other land for a mosque.

events.title: Panchayati Raj enshrined in the constitution
events.short: The 73rd Amendment came into force, requiring every state to hold elections for three tiers of rural self-government and reserving one-third of seats for women.
events.detail: Gandhi had long advocated village self-rule, believing Indian democracy should be rooted in the village. After independence some states set up panchayats, but in many places elections were irregular and the bodies powerless. The 73rd and 74th constitutional amendments, passed in 1992 and in force from 1993, required every state to establish panchayats at village, block and district level, elected every five years and given some financial and development-planning functions, with seats reserved for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and women, at least one-third for women, later raised to half in many states. India thereby gained some three million grassroots elected representatives, over a million of them women, the largest experiment in local democracy in the world.

events.title: The 1993 Bombay bombings
events.short: Thirteen bombs exploded within two hours at the Bombay Stock Exchange and other sites, killing 257 people in what was then India's deadliest terrorist attack.
events.detail: After the demolition of the Babri Masjid, Bombay suffered two waves of communal riots in December 1992 and January 1993 that killed about 900 people, most of them Muslims. On the afternoon of 12 March 1993 a bomb exploded in the basement of the Bombay Stock Exchange, followed by blasts at the Air India building, hotels, markets and elsewhere, thirteen in all, killing 257 and injuring over a thousand. Investigators concluded that the attacks were organised by the crime syndicate of Dawood Ibrahim in revenge for the riots. After more than a decade of trials over a hundred people were convicted. Despite the blow, the exchange reopened for trading two days later.

events.title: The Pokhran-II nuclear tests
events.short: Vajpayee's government conducted five nuclear tests at Pokhran and declared India a nuclear weapons state; Pakistan answered with tests, and the US and others imposed sanctions on both.
events.detail: In March 1998 a coalition led by the Bharatiya Janata Party took office with Atal Bihari Vajpayee as prime minister. On 11 and 13 May India secretly conducted five nuclear tests at Pokhran, including a thermonuclear device, under A. P. J. Abdul Kalam of the Defence Research and Development Organisation and R. Chidambaram of the Atomic Energy Commission; to evade American satellites the scientists wore army uniforms and worked at night. Vajpayee declared India a nuclear weapons state and added 'Jai Vigyan', hail science, to Shastri's slogan. Pakistan tested two weeks later. The US, Japan and others imposed sanctions on both, mostly lifted within a few years. 11 May is now India's National Technology Day.

events.title: Bangalore and the IT boom
events.short: After the reforms a software outsourcing industry centred on Bangalore grew rapidly; Infosys, TCS and others served clients worldwide, and India was dubbed the 'back office of the world'.
events.detail: From the 1970s firms such as Tata Consultancy Services wrote software for overseas clients. In 1981 N. R. Narayana Murthy and six fellow engineers founded Infosys with ten thousand rupees. After the 1991 reforms the government set up Software Technology Parks offering satellite links and tax breaks, and multinationals opened research centres in Bangalore. In the late 1990s Western companies needed armies of programmers to fix the Y2K bug, and India's English-speaking, low-cost engineers were in great demand. By the 2000s IT and business process outsourcing were among India's largest export industries; Bangalore became known as India's Silicon Valley, and Hyderabad, Pune and Gurgaon grew too.

events.title: The Kargil War
events.short: Pakistani soldiers and militants crossed the Line of Control and seized heights at Kargil; Indian troops fought for over two months on peaks above 5,000 metres to retake them.
events.detail: In February 1999 Vajpayee travelled by bus to Lahore and signed the Lahore Declaration with Pakistan's Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif. Yet that winter Pakistani soldiers disguised as militants crossed the Line of Control and occupied Indian posts on the mountains of Kargil in Ladakh, vacated for the winter, overlooking the Srinagar–Leh highway. Discovering the intrusion in early May, India launched Operation Vijay; soldiers climbed sheer peaks in thin air and bitter cold and, supported by air strikes and artillery, retook positions such as Tololing and Tiger Hill one by one. Under American pressure Pakistan withdrew in July. More than five hundred Indian soldiers died. 26 July is observed as Kargil Vijay Diwas.

events.title: The Golden Quadrilateral
events.short: Vajpayee's government launched the Golden Quadrilateral, nearly six thousand kilometres of upgraded highway linking Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata.
events.detail: Independent India's roads long lagged behind; most national highways were two-lane, and lorries crawled between cities. In 1999 Vajpayee's government announced the National Highways Development Project, whose first phase, the Golden Quadrilateral, began in 2001, linking the four metropolises of Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata with four- and six-lane highways about 5,846 km long; named for its four-sided shape, it was largely complete by 2012. North–south and east–west corridors followed, along with the Prime Minister's rural roads scheme to connect every village. The projects cut transport costs and spurred industry and towns along the routes.
