events.title: The Delhi Metro opens
events.short: Under E. Sreedharan, the 'Metro Man', the first line of the Delhi Metro opened; it rapidly became one of the largest metro networks in the world.
events.detail: Delhi's population was booming and traffic congestion and air pollution were worsening. In 1995 the Delhi Metro Rail Corporation was set up under E. Sreedharan, an engineer famed for finishing the Konkan Railway ahead of schedule and known for strict discipline and punctuality. On 24 December 2002 the first 8 km stretch from Shahdara to Tis Hazari opened, and crowds flocked to ride it. The network expanded steadily to over 390 km by the 2020s, carrying millions daily, and inspired metros in more than twenty cities including Mumbai, Bangalore and Chennai. It was among the first rail projects to earn UN carbon credits.

events.title: The 2002 Gujarat riots
events.short: After a train fire at Godhra killed 59 Hindu pilgrims, severe communal violence broke out in Gujarat, killing over a thousand people, most of them Muslims.
events.detail: On 27 February 2002 a train carrying Hindu volunteers back from Ayodhya caught fire near Godhra station in Gujarat, killing 59; the cause was disputed, and a later court verdict held that a Muslim mob had set it deliberately. Over the following days mass violence engulfed Ahmedabad and other places: many Muslims were killed, homes and shops burned and tens of thousands displaced. Official figures put the dead at about 1,044, some 790 of them Muslims, with unofficial estimates higher. The state government was criticised for failing to stop the violence promptly. Many cases went through years of trials and some people were convicted; a Supreme Court-appointed investigation later found no prosecutable evidence against the then chief minister, Narendra Modi.

events.title: Kalpana Chawla's death
events.short: Kalpana Chawla, born in Haryana, the first woman of Indian origin in space, died when the shuttle Columbia broke up on re-entry.
events.detail: Kalpana Chawla was born in the small town of Karnal in Haryana and loved watching aircraft as a child. She studied aeronautical engineering at Punjab Engineering College, went on to a doctorate in aerospace engineering in the United States, became an American citizen and joined NASA. In 1997 she flew on the shuttle Columbia, the first woman of Indian origin in space. In January 2003 she flew again on Columbia; on 1 February the shuttle broke up on re-entry, killing her and six other astronauts. She was 40. She inspired many Indian girls to study science, and an Indian weather satellite was named after her.

events.title: The Indian Ocean tsunami
events.short: A great earthquake off Sumatra unleashed the Indian Ocean tsunami, devastating the Tamil Nadu coast and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and killing over ten thousand in India.
events.detail: On the morning of 26 December 2004 a magnitude 9.1 earthquake struck off northwestern Sumatra, unleashing a tsunami across the Indian Ocean that killed some 230,000 people in more than a dozen countries. The waves reached India's southeast coast about two hours later, devastating Nagapattinam in Tamil Nadu, Chennai's Marina Beach and the coasts of Kerala and Andhra, while parts of the Nicobar Islands nearest the epicentre were almost wiped out. More than ten thousand died in India and hundreds of thousands were left homeless. The government declined foreign aid, led its own relief effort and sent the navy to help Sri Lanka, the Maldives and Indonesia. India afterwards set up a tsunami warning centre.

events.title: The Right to Information and rural job guarantee
events.short: Manmohan Singh's government passed the Right to Information Act, letting citizens obtain government records, and a rural employment law guaranteeing each household a hundred days of paid work a year.
events.detail: In 2004 the Congress-led United Progressive Alliance won the election and the economist Manmohan Singh became India's first Sikh prime minister. In the 1990s a farmers' organisation in Rajasthan had exposed corruption by publicly auditing village accounts, launching a movement for transparency. The Right to Information Act of 2005 entitled citizens to demand information from public bodies within 30 days; millions of requests are filed each year, uncovering many corruption cases. The National Rural Employment Guarantee Act of the same year guaranteed every rural household a hundred days of paid work on public projects; later named after Mahatma Gandhi, it is one of the largest public employment programmes in the world.

events.title: The 2008 Mumbai attacks
events.short: Ten gunmen who landed by sea attacked the main railway station, the Taj Mahal Palace hotel and other sites in Mumbai over nearly four days, killing 166 people.
events.detail: On the night of 26 November 2008 ten gunmen of the Pakistan-based Lashkar-e-Taiba landed in south Mumbai in inflatable boats and split up to attack Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus, the Leopold Cafe, Cama Hospital, a Jewish centre and the Taj Mahal Palace and Oberoi hotels. They fired into crowds, threw grenades and took hostages; televised images of the Taj's burning dome shocked the world. National Security Guard commandos needed some sixty hours to end the siege. Nine attackers were killed, and the only one captured alive, Ajmal Kasab, was executed in 2012. The attacks killed 166 people and plunged India–Pakistan relations into crisis again.

events.title: The India–US civil nuclear deal
events.short: India and the US signed a civil nuclear agreement, and the Nuclear Suppliers Group made an exception for India, allowing it international civil nuclear trade without joining the NPT.
events.detail: Indo-US relations improved after the Cold War. In July 2005 Manmohan Singh and President George W. Bush announced that India would separate its civilian and military nuclear facilities and place the civilian ones under International Atomic Energy Agency safeguards, while the US would help India obtain civil nuclear technology and fuel. The deal sparked fierce debate in India; the left parties, arguing it compromised foreign-policy independence, withdrew support in 2008, and the government narrowly survived a confidence vote. In September the Nuclear Suppliers Group granted India a waiver, and in October the two countries signed the agreement, ending the nuclear isolation India had faced since 1974 and opening a new phase in Indo-US relations.

events.title: Chandrayaan-1
events.short: India's first lunar probe, Chandrayaan-1, was launched; its instruments found evidence of water molecules on the Moon's surface.
events.detail: On 22 October 2008 ISRO launched the Chandrayaan-1 probe on its own Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle from Sriharikota island in Andhra Pradesh. In lunar orbit it released an impactor that struck near the Moon's south pole, carrying the Indian flag to the lunar surface. The probe carried eleven instruments from India, the United States, Europe and elsewhere; NASA's Moon Mineralogy Mapper detected signs of water and hydroxyl molecules widespread on the surface, a finding that caused a sensation when announced in 2009. Contact was lost after about ten months. The whole mission cost less than a hundred million dollars.

events.title: Aadhaar, the biometric ID
events.short: India began issuing every resident a 12-digit biometric identity number, Aadhaar, which within a decade covered 1.3 billion people, the world's largest ID system.
events.detail: Many poor Indians had no birth certificate or identity document, making it hard to open bank accounts or receive government benefits, while fraud and leakage were rife. In 2009 the government created the Unique Identification Authority under Infosys co-founder Nandan Nilekani to record each resident's fingerprints, irises and photograph and issue a unique 12-digit number; 'Aadhaar' means 'foundation' in Hindi. On 29 September 2010 villagers of a tribal hamlet in Maharashtra received the first numbers. By the 2020s Aadhaar covered about 1.3 billion people and was used for bank accounts, subsidy payments and mobile registration. It also raised privacy concerns, and in 2018 the Supreme Court limited its use.

events.title: India wins the 2011 World Cup at home
events.short: M. S. Dhoni's India beat Sri Lanka in the final at Mumbai to win the World Cup for the first time in 28 years, fulfilling the dream of the 'god of cricket', Sachin Tendulkar.
events.detail: The 2011 Cricket World Cup was co-hosted by India, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh. On 2 April India met Sri Lanka in the final at Mumbai's Wankhede Stadium. Sri Lanka made 274, and India lost both openers early, including Sachin Tendulkar playing his last World Cup on home soil. Gautam Gambhir steadied the innings with 97, and captain M. S. Dhoni finished the match with a six, India winning by six wickets to become the first team to win the World Cup at home. The country celebrated through the night, and the players carried Tendulkar on their shoulders around the ground. Tendulkar retired in 2013 and in 2014 became the first sportsman awarded the Bharat Ratna.

events.title: Anna Hazare's anti-corruption movement
events.short: The Gandhian Anna Hazare fasted in Delhi demanding an independent anti-corruption ombudsman, drawing massive urban middle-class support and spurring passage of an anti-corruption law.
events.detail: Around 2010 a series of huge corruption scandals came to light, over the Commonwealth Games, the allocation of 2G telecom spectrum and coal mining rights, causing intense public anger. In April 2011 the 73-year-old activist Anna Hazare began a fast at Jantar Mantar in Delhi, demanding a Jan Lokpal bill to create an independent anti-corruption ombudsman. Arrested again in August, he fasted for twelve days at the Ramlila Maidan, where tens of thousands of young people in white 'I am Anna' caps gathered and television covered it around the clock. Parliament passed a resolution, and the Lokpal Act followed in 2013. One organiser, Arvind Kejriwal, later founded the Aam Aadmi Party, which won power in Delhi.

events.title: Mangalyaan reaches Mars orbit
events.short: India's Mars Orbiter Mission entered Mars orbit at the first attempt, making India the first Asian nation to reach Mars, at a cost lower than the Hollywood film Gravity.
events.detail: On 5 November 2013 ISRO launched the Mars Orbiter Mission from Sriharikota on a Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle; its Hindi name Mangalyaan means 'Mars craft'. Because the rocket's thrust was limited, the probe raised its orbit around Earth several times before heading for Mars, a journey of about ten months. On 24 September 2014 it fired its engine and entered Mars orbit, making ISRO the fourth space agency to reach Mars, after the Soviet Union, NASA and the European Space Agency, and the first to succeed at the first attempt. The mission cost about 74 million dollars, less than the film Gravity, demonstrating India's low-cost space capability. It appears on the back of the 2,000-rupee note.

events.title: Modi leads the BJP to victory
events.short: Gujarat chief minister Narendra Modi led the BJP to an outright majority in parliament, the first single-party majority in thirty years.
events.detail: Narendra Modi, from a lower-caste family in Gujarat, helped his father sell tea at a railway station as a boy, later became a full-time worker of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh and from 2001 served thirteen years as chief minister of Gujarat, known for promoting economic growth. In 2014 the BJP made him its prime ministerial candidate, campaigning on 'development' and 'good days are coming' and making extensive use of social media and hologram rallies. Some 550 million voters turned out; the BJP won 282 of 543 seats, while Congress fell to 44, its worst defeat ever. Modi was sworn in on 26 May and was re-elected in 2019 and 2024.

events.title: Demonetisation and digital payments
events.short: Modi abruptly declared 500- and 1,000-rupee notes invalid to fight black money and counterfeits, causing severe cash shortages but spurring digital payments such as UPI.
events.detail: At 8 p.m. on 8 November 2016 Modi announced on television that from midnight the 500- and 1,000-rupee notes, about 86 per cent of the cash in circulation, would cease to be legal tender, a move the government said would fight black money, counterfeiting and terrorist financing. For weeks long queues formed outside banks and ATMs, and cash-dependent street vendors, farmers and daily labourers were hit hard. The Reserve Bank later reported that about 99 per cent of the cancelled notes had returned to the banks, casting doubt on the policy's effect. Yet the cash crunch pushed many people to pay by phone, and the Unified Payments Interface launched that year spread rapidly; it now handles over ten billion transactions a month.

events.title: The Goods and Services Tax
events.short: A nationwide Goods and Services Tax was launched at a midnight session of parliament, replacing a tangle of central and state indirect taxes and creating a single national market.
events.detail: India's centre and states used to levy more than a dozen indirect taxes, excise, VAT, service tax, entry tax and more, and goods crossing state borders queued at checkposts to pay, lorries often waiting for days. After more than a decade of debate, parliament passed a constitutional amendment in 2016 creating a GST Council of central and state finance ministers. At midnight on 30 June 2017 parliament held a special session in its Central Hall, where the president and prime minister pressed a button to launch the tax from 1 July, with several rate bands. State-border checkposts were abolished. Small businesses at first complained of complex rates and glitches in the filing system, which were gradually simplified.

events.title: The Statue of Unity
events.short: The statue of Vallabhbhai Patel on the Narmada in Gujarat was unveiled; at 182 metres it is the world's tallest, honouring his integration of over five hundred princely states.
events.detail: To honour Vallabhbhai Patel, independent India's first deputy prime minister, who integrated the princely states, the Gujarat government under chief minister Modi proposed a colossal statue. It stands on an islet in the Narmada below the Sardar Sarovar Dam, 182 metres tall, about twice the height of the Statue of Liberty including its pedestal, a reinforced-concrete structure clad in bronze designed by the sculptor Ram V. Sutar. Modi unveiled it on 31 October 2018, Patel's 143rd birth anniversary, now observed as National Unity Day. A viewing gallery inside overlooks the dam and the Satpura hills; it has become a popular attraction, though its cost and impact on local tribal villagers drew criticism.

events.title: Ending Jammu and Kashmir's special status
events.short: Modi's government revoked the special autonomy granted to Jammu and Kashmir by Article 370 and split it into two union territories, Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh.
events.detail: Under Article 370, written into the constitution in 1949, the state of Jammu and Kashmir had special status, with its own constitution and flag; apart from defence, foreign affairs and communications, central laws applied only with the state's consent, and outsiders could not buy land there. The BJP had long called for its repeal. On 5 August 2019 the government declared by presidential order and parliamentary resolution that Article 370 no longer applied, and parliament then reorganised the state into two union territories, Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh. Beforehand the authorities deployed large numbers of troops, cut internet and phone lines and detained many politicians, including former chief ministers. Pakistan protested strongly. In 2023 the Supreme Court upheld the decision.

events.title: COVID-19 and the national lockdown
events.short: India declared a national lockdown and millions of migrant workers walked home; the Delta variant drove a devastating second wave in 2021, followed by mass vaccination.
events.detail: India recorded its first COVID-19 case in Kerala in January 2020. On the evening of 24 March Modi announced a 21-day national lockdown from midnight, one of the largest in the world, covering 1.3 billion people. Millions of migrant workers who suddenly lost work and shelter in the cities, with trains and buses halted, walked hundreds of kilometres home with their belongings and children, some dying on the way. In April and May 2021 the Delta variant drove a second wave; hospitals ran desperately short of oxygen and crematoria burned day and night. The official death toll was about 530,000, though many studies put it far higher. India mass-produced and administered vaccines, giving more than two billion doses by 2022 and supplying many other countries.

events.title: Chandrayaan-3 lands near the lunar south pole
events.short: Chandrayaan-3's Vikram lander touched down near the Moon's south pole, making India the fourth country to soft-land on the Moon and the first near its south pole.
events.detail: In 2019 Chandrayaan-2's lander lost contact about 2 km above the surface and crashed. ISRO learned from the failure and strengthened the lander's software and legs. Chandrayaan-3 was launched from Sriharikota on 14 July 2023, and on the evening of 23 August the Vikram lander, named after Vikram Sarabhai, touched down gently at about 69 degrees south, watched live by tens of millions of jubilant Indians. The Pragyan rover then drove out and travelled about 100 metres, detecting sulphur and other elements. India became the fourth country, after the Soviet Union, the United States and China, to soft-land on the Moon. The site was named Shiv Shakti Point, and 23 August is National Space Day.

events.title: The G20 summit in New Delhi
events.short: As G20 president India hosted the summit in New Delhi, which adopted a joint declaration and admitted the African Union as a permanent member.
events.detail: From December 2022 to November 2023 India held the G20 presidency under the theme 'One Earth, One Family, One Future', hosting more than two hundred meetings in over fifty cities and presenting itself as a voice of the Global South. The summit was held on 9–10 September 2023 at the new Bharat Mandapam convention centre in New Delhi. Despite deep divisions among members over the war in Ukraine, a joint declaration was adopted on the first day. The summit also admitted the African Union as a permanent member, the group's first enlargement since its founding. India's use of the ancient name 'Bharat' on its nameplate during the summit attracted attention.

events.title: The world's most populous country
events.short: By UN estimates India's population surpassed China's in 2023, making it the world's most populous country; the same year parliament passed a bill reserving a third of seats for women.
events.detail: At independence India had about 340 million people, and its population has grown rapidly ever since, though the fertility rate has fallen from about six children per woman in the 1960s to about two in the 2020s. By UN estimates, in mid-2023 India's population reached about 1.429 billion, overtaking China as the world's most populous country. Its people are relatively young, with a median age under 30 and a large working-age population, but face enormous pressure to create jobs and education. The census due in 2021 was postponed because of COVID-19. In September 2023 parliament passed a constitutional amendment reserving a third of seats in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies for women, to take effect after the next census and delimitation.

events.title: The 2024 general election
events.short: Held in seven phases with nearly a billion eligible voters, the largest election in history saw the BJP lose its single-party majority, while Modi's alliance stayed in power.
events.detail: From 19 April to 1 June 2024 India's election to the 18th Lok Sabha was held in seven phases. Some 970 million people were registered and about 640 million voted, using electronic voting machines at over a million polling stations; officials even set up a booth for a single voter in the Gir forest. When the votes were counted on 4 June, the BJP had won 240 seats, short of the 272 needed for a majority, and had to rely on its National Democratic Alliance partners, while the Congress-led opposition alliance did better than expected. On 9 June Modi was sworn in for a third term, the second prime minister after Nehru to win three consecutive terms. The election again showed the scale and vitality of the world's largest democracy.
